div.p: Tatty!.
- _ THE STOCKING SONG. Supper is over, the hearth is swept. And now, in the wood-fire's glow, The children cluster to hear a tale

Of the tints so long ago; When grandmamma's hair was golden brown And the warm blood came and went O'er the face that could scarce have been sweeter then Than now in its rich content. The brow is wrinkled and es.nsworn now, And the golden hair is grey; But the lig'st that shone in the young girl's eyes Has never gone quite away. And her Aedlea catch the red fire's light, As in out they go, With the clicking music that grandmamma loves, Shaping the stocking toe; And the waking children love it too For they know that stocking so= Brings many a tale to grandmamma's mind, Which they shall hear ere long. But it brings no story of olden time To grandmamma's heart to-night— Only a parable, short and quaint, Is sung by the needles bright. "Life is a stocking," grandmarnma says, ".And yours is just begun; But I am knitting the toe of mine, And my task is well-nigh done. "With merry hearts we begin to knit, And the ribbing is almost play; Some are gay coloured, and some are white, And some are ashen grey. "But the most are formed of many a hue, And many a stitch set wrong, And many a row to be sadly ripped Ere the whole be fair and strong. "There are long plain spaces without a break, That in youth are hard to bear, And many a weary tear is dropped As we fashion the heel with care. "But the saddest happiest time is that Which we sigh for and yet would shun • When our Heavenly Father breaks the thread And tells us our work is done." The children come to bid good night, With tears in their bright young eyes; While in grandmamma's lap, with a broken thread, The finished stoeking lies.

CON. FOB FEMALE ECONOMISTS.—WouId the prohibition of tight-lacing be a violation of " freedom of contract ?" Punch. "Can you steer the mainmast down the forecastle stairs?" asked a sea captain of a new recruit. "Yes, air, I can," was the reply," if you will stand below and coil it up." It is not genius that tells on the world, but downright and honest hard work. Your brains may feiment and effer- vesce like a yeast pot, but unless you can settle down to steady toil you are worth no more to the community than a soap babble, which bursts so soon that it is hardly worth one's while to atop to look at and admire it. A good black- smith is worth a round donen of geniuses who wear long hair and Byronic collars and wonder why the world does not adore them. Persons who can laugh heartily may be said to have the elements of worth strong in them, and a ready means of se- curing much happiness; hence they should indulge in it as frequently as possible, for nothing is so good for toning up the system and exhilarating the mind as deep, hearty laughter. It also shows one character to a certain extent; for bad people rarely laugh heartily. Laugh when you can, then; and, while it may not make you fat, it will at least improve you mentally and physically for the day. Lord Oxford used to relate a dispute that once arose in the way of raillery between the late Earl Temple and the first Lord Lyttelton, on the antiquity of their families. Lord Lyttelton concluded that the name of Grenville was originally Green field; Earl Temple insisted that it was de- rived from Grand Ville. "Well, then," said Lord Lyttel- ton, " if you will have it so, my family may boast of the higher antiquity, for Little Towns were certainly antecedent to Great Cities; but if you will be content with the more humble derivation, I will give up the point—for Gre,n fields are certainly more ancient than either." DomEsTic METI4OROLOGY.—(By a Fireside Philospher.)— " Relative " Humidity. Tendency to tearfulness on the part of materfamilias and the girls, on paterfamilias saying that he "can't afford a holiday this year."—Dew-Point. The point attained—lachrymally—when paterfamilias, after an hour's argument, requests, imperatively, that he may "have no more nonsense !"—Tension of Vapour. Phenome- non manifested on the first signs of relenting on the part of papa.—Drying Power. Immediate influence of the appear- ance of the cheque-book.—Puneh. TERlFf.—Thrift is an old-fashioned, homely virtue. It wears well. It brings comfort, independence, and along train of blessings. It has health in it. It builds homes. Itirears children. It plants vines and fig trees, and sits under their branches to eat the fruit thereof. And it finds more com- fart and joy, more self-respect and manliness, more honour anl more hope in the little honestly-earned and carefully- saved and wisely-husbanded, than millionaires get from their wild speculations. And this thrift, which is the hope of a people and the secret of permanent prosperity, we have nearly lost and must recover.—Clanstian at Work (Ameri- can). THE SPIRIT Or INDEPESDESCE IS AMETIICA.—No TIPS. —The effect of the democratic institutions of America may be noticed in the total absence of that system of "tips" which renders travelling both in England and Europe gene- rally so disagreeable to most people. When you leave an American hotel, you are not surrounded by waiters and chambermaids, who expect to be rewarded for services which have already been paid for. Not the least annoyance of this kind meets the traveller from one end of the States to the other. The same comfort is experienced on the rail- ways. There the officials have too much self-respect to hang about the carriage doors in expectation of having gratuities surreptitiously slipped into their hands. The conductor of a train, indeed, is as much a gentleman as any of the passengers. If you offered him money, he would deem himself so much insulted that he would—well, he would probably stop the train and order you to leave it! If you offered him r cigar, ten to one he would, if he took it, offer you another in exchange. Daring the whole time I was travelling about the States, I did not pay, and I was not expected to pay, a single cent for anything but ser- vices I had received. Even many services of a valuable kind were rendered, not only without payment, but without any expectation of it. An amusing instance of the inde- pendence which early in life takes possession of the Ameri- can people occurred at a friend's house. My friend's son— a smart, intelligent lad of some 10 or 12 years—had been put to a good deal of extra trouble on my account. On the day I was leaving I called him aside. But the moment he B3W my hand in my pocket, he turned on his heels and dis- appeared. Nor could I get speech with him afterwards. I learned subsequently that his own explanation was, that he was too oldrnow to receive presents from his father's guests. If this is the spirit of the youth of America, anybedy can understand that the dignity of the elder people will forbid them from asking for what they have not earned. It is, perhaps, to this same spirit that the country is indebted for its freedom from another evil—beggary. There may be beggars in America; indeed, there is at least one State in I the Union which has enacted penal laws against them; but I was never importuned for alms myself, nor did I see any- body else. What I did see, however, was a young lad who sold newspapers in the streets of Chicago, who kept and educated an orphan sister out of his earnings, and who was as proud of the girl as any father in the States of his own child.—" Our American Cousins." By W. E. Adams." AN AMERICAN TRAGEDY.—Fiie-arms are so commonly used in certain parts of the country that a schoolmaster at Paris, Kentucky, was wounded with a pistol by one of his pupils, whom he had corrected for failure in his studies! Perhaps, however, the most terrible incident in which re- volvers played a part was that which occurred at Knox- line, Tennessee, in October, 1882. The persons concerned f'n this affair were prominent citizens of Knoxville, one of them being a banker, another holding the rank of general in the United States service, and the third occupying the position of justice of the peace. Differences had arisen be- tween Major O'Connor, the banker just mentioned, and the family of General Joseph A. Mabry. O'Connor had ad- vanced money to Mabry on the security of some property, had foreclosed the mortgage, and had thus become possessed Of the Mabry estate. The first life lost in the quarrel which ensued from these trans ictions was that of William Mabry, C eon of the general's, who was killed by Don Lusby in an affray on the Christmas Eve of 1881. Out of this homicide there arose a feud which has since resulted in the death of no fewer than five of the parties concerned. Don Lusby And his father, Moses Lusby, were killed by General Mabry and his !on Joseph on the 26th of August, 1882, the offen- dere being afterwards acquitted on the ground of self- defence. A still more terrible encounter occurred a fetv weeks later. The elder Mabry, .meeting O'Connor on the fair ground at Knoxville on the 10th of October, accused ofhohwise::;l, Wip.rielvlieantuted The ioiusn- him of procuring the inu!der tervention of mutnal friend!, consequences for the time being. It was arranged that the quarrelsome officers should keep out of eachother'sws. But Mabry soon afterwards was seen to pass O'Connor bank. The gallant major accepted this as a challenge, wished into the street with a shot-gun, and wounded the general in such a way that he shortly afterwards died. Another son of Mabry's—Joseph Mabry, junior--who had recently been elected a justice of the peace, and who was actually engaged at the time in trying a case about a hun- dred yards from the scene of the murder, now appeared to take up the quarrel. The younger Mabry and the fiery O'Connor seemed to have both fired together, the one with a pocket revolver, the other with a fresh gun which had been handed to him from his office. The banker fell dead on the aide-walk, the justice of the peace on the tramway track. Three of the most prominent citizens of Knoxville had slaughtered each other in the public thoroughfare. So eaded for the day this terrible vendetta.—" Our American ("ein4 9" by W. E. Adame.

PROLIFIC WHEAT.— , Mr... Walter Price, Sudbury, planted one grain of wheat ir came up and there garden amongst his potatoes. It 'Pere 50 ears from it, yielding 2,595 grains' It was '.4 tomnron red wheat, planted early in Sep- tember.

POTAinEfi..—Mr. F. H. Hill, gardener to Mr. A. _Ruggles Brise, of Durwards Hall, Rivenhall, lifted a root of the "Mr. Breese" potatoes, grown with native guano, containing 37 potatoes. The six largest weighed 21bs. loz., 11b. 20z., 130 z., 121-oz., 90z., Soz. The whole root weighed 13Ib. 3oz. This prolific crop has been sent by the grower to be exhibited at the Native Guano Company's stand at the Fisheries Exhibition. INCENDIARY FIRES.—A valuable haystack, the property of Mr. W. Bligh, St. Botolph's Farm, Sevenoa.ks, was dis- covered to be on tire shortly before midnight on Tuesday, and, despite the combined efforts of the local brigades, it was almost completely destroyed. This makes the fourth fire of the kind which has occurred within the district during the last fortnight. In one instance four ricks were burnt down, and in another a rick, the property of Lord Sackville, was very much damaged. The whole is attributed to incendiarism, and much alarm is felt over the matter. SELECTING POTATO SEED.—An American farmer says his way of selecting seed is to walk along after the diggers with a small basket and pick up the choice potatoes, of perfect shape and with large eyes, from these hills. When the bas- ket is full, it is carefully emptied into a bushel box, and the sun shines. As soon as a few are filled they are taken to the cellar and set away till the tubers are through sweating, when they are laid (not poured) in barrels and coveted up , from the air, not to be moved again till planting time. THE FALL OF TILE LEAF.—An early falling of the leaf may be anticipated this year, as the result of drought, and irrespective of the early frosts which usually determine the matter. On the 29th of August a very considerable fall of the leaves of limes, planes, and chestnuts was noticeable in the suburbs of London and in all the drier parts of the southern counties. Since that date the leaves of those and other trees have been falling freely. In many instances chestnuts have made a second leaf growth, and show patches of golden green upon a ground of dingy russet, the "new wine" not agreeing well with the "old bottles."—Gardener's Magazine. HAY HAULING EXTIIAOILDINARY.---A correspondent states :—Thomas Turner, of Troutbeck, who is nearly three- score years and ten, evidently does not believe in the plan adopted by the farmers in the district where he resides of gathering in their crops by the aid of horses and carts. He recently, with the help of his handmaid, cut a field of about six acres in extent, and secured the whole in good condition by carrying it away, a wheelbarrow-load at a time, to his homestead, about half-a-mile distant from the field.

TENANTS BECOMING THEIR OWN LANDLORDS.—The Settled Estates Act has just been put into operation for the first time in Cornwall, when Mr. G. L. Bassett's, a large landed property in the southern part of that county, was offered for sale by auction, at Holston. There was a large attendance of tenant-farmers, to whom it had become known that the properties would be offered on conditions that made it comparatively easy for them to become purchasers, Mr. Bassett having offered to cover two-thirds of the purchase money on mortgage bearing interest at 4 per cent., this be- ing for the benefit of the sitting tenants in order that they might not be disturbed in their holdings, but become owners in due course. Mr. A. P. Vivian, M.P. for West Cornwall, purchased one of the largest estates for £6,255. Several others were bought by sitting tenants, some of them at prices which were said to be in excess of the reserve, but in other cases the bidding was not brisk, as the reserve was regarded as excessive. CONVERSION OF SEWAGE GRASS TO HAY.—We have dried in the "Gibbs" harvest-saver the yield from 94 acres of irrigated rye-grass, and from 40 acres of meadow. This last, when nearly ready, was caught in the rain and carried to the machine water-wet. Our irrigated rye-grass is nearly impossible to make into hay, even if we have two or three weeks of unbroken fine weather; and as there is only about four weeks from the time one crop is cut to when the other is ready, it cannot be made on the land on which it is grown, but has to be carted to some piece of spare land to be finished. It then requires turning and making in the ordinary way every day, or at least every other day, for 14 to 21 days, and by that time is so spoilt by long exposure to dews and sun, that it will be neither good hay nor even good litter. By the aid of the harvest-saver we clear our fields in three or four days after mowing. I find the beat plan is to " ted-out" on the next day after mowing, wind- row, ted-out again, collect with a horsers.ke, and carry to the rickyard. We heap it there into large cocks of about three loads in each cock, as near to the feeding end of the machine as we can. We let it remain in these cocks for about a week, by which time the hay will be found hot and brown in the middle. The cocks nearest the machine are passed through first, and the others are then drawn up on sledges, which for this purpose are much better than carts, as they save the labour of two men. It will be understood that irrigated rye-grass must cost more for coal and coke than meadow grass. The calculation I made last year was Is. 10d. per ton of hay made. I think it will be leas this year, but I shall find this out more correctly at the end of the season—it is undoubtedly more economical than the labour required for even "attempting" to make it in the usual way. We shall be making several more ricks of irri- gated rye-grass this season, and I shall be pleased to show anyone who is interested what can be done. If an addressed postcard is sent, I will advise the sender when next working, but I find it impossible to answer the numbers of letters and questions on the subject.— W. IV. Champion, Whitley Maaor Farm, Reading.

THE DECREASE IN THE VALUE OF AGRICULTURAL LAND. —The fall in the value of land in the United Kingdom since 1879 is strikingly shown in the annual report of the Commissioners of Inland Revenue for the year ended March 31st, 1883, recently published, and to be obtained from Messrs. Hansard and Son, through any bookseller, for 61d. The gross annual value of lands assessed under Schedule A. in 1881-82 in the United Kingdom was £68,811,032, being a decrease of £180,941, as compared with 1880-81. But this was not all, for sums were repaid on account of agricultural distress during the year equal to an assessment of £1,243,104; so that the total decrease of annual value of lands in 1881-82 was £1,721,045. In the three years 1879-80, 1880-81, and 1881-82, the total decrease was equivalent to an assessable value of £3,728,663. The Scotsman points out that if this be taken at 23 years' purchase, it shows a decrease in the value of land in three years of no less than £85,759,249. The decrease, at any rate in the last year of the three, has been within a very small fractional percentage the same in England and Scotland. Under Schedule B the decrease in 1881-82, as compared with the assessment of the previous year, was £387,652, of which £324,193 arose in England and Wales, £63,024 in Scotland, and £435 in Ireland. But the Commissioners point out that, in addition to this de- crease, "the sum of £3,600 for duty has been repaid in respect of claims arising out of agricultural depression, and the sum of £5,902 included in schedules of discharge from the same cause." "These together," the Commissioners go on to say," represent a total assessment equal to £1,059,373 in value, besides the £387,652 above recorded in respect of the year 1381-82. In the three years ending with 1881-82 the total decrease in the assessments, including repayments, has been £2,242,566. After all, this is only a little over 3 per cent. reduction, and as rents in some districts have gone down from 30 to 50 per cent., they must have risen in other places. Tithe, however, which agricultural deprossion.can- not reduce, helps greatly to keep up the assessment under Schedule B. The total gross assessment under this schedule for 1881-82 for the United Kingdom was £68,799,405, of which the sem of £51,169,023 belongs to England and Wales, £7,650,123 to Scotland, and £9,980,259 to Ireland. It will be noticed that the assessment under Schedule B for Ireland had only decreased by a very small amount. This shows that the recent rent reductions had not taken place to any appreciable extent when the assessment was made. If owners of agricultural land have lost money, owners of ground rents and houses have gained in greater proportion; for here we have an increase for 1881-82, as compared with the previous year's gross assessment, of £3,411,641, of which £3,204,437 arose in England, £153,895 in Scotland, and £53,309 in Ireland. Of the increase in England no less than £2,023,183 were in the Metropolis. Turning to the assessment of incomes arising from trades, professions, rail- ways, &c., under Schedule D, the Commissioners tell us that there is an increase not equalled since 1874-75. The total increase in the gross assessment is £12,046,275, of which £10,080,703 arose in England, £1,963,594 in Scotland, and £1,978 in Ireland.

PROFESSOR OWEN.—Richard Owen, the youngest son of Richard Owen, of Fulmer-place, Bucks, was born at Lan- caster on July 20, 1804. In early youth he served as mid- shipman on his Majesty's ship Tribune, but all prospects of naval advancement were speedily clouded by the peace which ensued at the close of the American war of 1814. The youthful middy returned to school on shore, and subse- quently studied medicine under Mr. Baxendale, a surgeon of his native town. In 1824 he matriculated at the University of Edinburgh, and two years later received the diploma of the Royal College of Surgeons in London, where, as a stu- dent at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, he acted as dissectorl under the famous Dr. Abernethy, who quickly recognised his remarkable talent. A visit to Paris was the next turn- ing-point in his life. There he worked in the laboratory of his master and friend, the great Cuvier, then at the zenith of his fame as a comparative anatomist. On returning to England Mr. Owen procured an appointment as assistant- surgeon in the Navy, but was induced to resign it through the energetic representations of his staunch old friend, Dr. Abernethy, whose influence secured him a more congenial post as assistant to Mr. William Clift, F.R.S., then engaged in cataloguing and arranging the magnificent collections of John Hunter, purchased by Government, and transferred to the museum of the Royal College of Surgeons, of which Mr. Clift was conservator. For some time the young sur- geon also practised in Serle-street, Lincoln's-inn-fields, and although his keen insight and great abilities would proba- bly have ensured him wealth and distinction as a physician, he gradually abandoned the medical profession for a life's devotion to research, content with smaller emoluments and greater leisure to work hard for the advancement of science and the increase of knowledge. That his life has been one of unintermittent labour his published works fully testify, for he has toiled with almost superhuman energy and per- sistent regularity, investigating the structure of all classes of the animal kingdom. His contributions to literary and ' •,cientific periodicals abne number nearly four handr.d. Many of these are important memoir, =bodying new facts and valuable discoveries.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

CABBAGE.—These should now be ready for planting out into their winter quarters, and the best plants should be selected. The smaller ones may be equally useful, and may attain in time the size of the large ones, but the latter should be ready first. Apart from that, the plot when planted will have a more uniform appearance if a continued selection is made instead of planting them haphazard. In planting it is our practice to put the plants thicker than is usually done, and we have found it to answer remarkably well. The plants are put out a foot apart each way, and in the spring, as soon as they begin to heart, we tie the most forward up, and in a week or ten days they are pulled up for use. Others plant 18 inches or 2 feet each way. We there- fore consider that our plan has a decided advantage, inae- ' much as our produce is nearly as much more. All the plants should be inserted so deep that the lowest leaf rests on the soil. LETTUCL—The last sowing of these are nice plants, and should be pricked out 6 inches apart in a sheltered position, so that they may stand over the winter. It is a good plan to plant them on raised beds which are formed thus : Measure the width of the bed, which should be about four feet. Cut down the sides, and by taking soil 2 inches or 3 inches thick and the width of the spade and throwing it on the bed the latter will be so mach higher, and the space from where the soil has been taken will act as surface drains, inasmuch as they will be 6 inches below the surface of the bed until the latter has settled. We should prefer the form of the bed to be convex. Water will thus pass off more quickly. Stagnant water is detrimental to the lettuce in winter. There is generally a great demand for young plants in the spring. It is therefore worth while to use every available means to preserve as many plants as possible, and so soon as the requisite number has been planted those left in the seed beds should be thinned out 4 inches apart at present, in case slugs should destroy the others. CRLERY.—ShouId any of our readers have discovered white blotches or blisters on the leaves of the celery they i will find on breaking the blister a maggot or two, about the size of those seen in cheese. In some parts of the country crops have been rendered useless by this peat. It therefore behoves every grower to pick off the infected part of the leaves and put it on the fire. It is late in the season for these maggots to spread much, but if those that make their appearance now are destroyed the stock will be that much lees for next season's propagation. TRH FRONT GARDEN.—We have frequently drawn atten- tion to the cultivation of Pinks and Carnations for the front garden. From what we read in The Garden, it appears that the Rev. Chas. Wood of this town must have the best col- lection for some miles round. The Editor of The Garden writes thus :—" The Rev. Charles Wood, of Preston, sends us a very brilliant series of self-coloured and clove Carn- ations. Our correspondent must hale a beautiful autumnal garden." In his communication to the Editor, Mr. Wood says :—" An exhibitor of Carnations, of course, would not look at such flowers; nevertheless, I find them very useful for cutting. Some of the kinds I have had 25 years. They are covered with bloom, and some of the roots are 2ft. in diameter and quite hardy. lam very fond of clove-scented Carnations, and am pleased you take an opportunity of bringing them before the public." We are here tempted to give a list of the varieties that the Editor of The Garden fancied most:—Sing of Cloves, deep purple-crimson; Fire- eater, colour cardinal; Harrogate, rose pink shaded with purple, very fine • Lord Beaconsfield, plum-purple; Elysian Beauty, rose pink; Gertrude Teiguir, delicate flesh pink; Inaperial Purple, deep purple; Jeannie, rose pink; Old Scarlet; Favourite, purple, semi-double; Old Red, deep crimson-red; and W. P. Miller, white. We should like to see a clump of one or more of these in every cottager'e front garden. They require only ordinary care and skill to culti- vate successfully. The exact spot they are to be planted in being fixed upon, the soil, unless it is tolerably good, should be taken out a foot square and about the same depth for each clump of three plants, and be replaced by turfy loam free from wire-worm, to which should be added one-tenth of old mortar, such as is got from the dressing of bricks, and about one eighth of decayed manure. In cold wet localities it would be advisable to remove the soil Sin. or Sin, deeper, and fill part of the space with any rough porous material; and in filling the holes, raise the soil at least 41n. above the surface, to allow for sinking as well as having them at all times slightly elevated. In the majority of front gardens these Carnations will succeed with nothing more in the way of preparation than a little manure added to the soil. Few are aware that the splendid samples of Carnations and Picotees exhibited at the Preston and Fulwood Horticul- tural Society's show last month were grown by a mill hand (Mr. Lord, of Todmorden) in his back yard, in pots, proving the truth of the old proverb "Where there is a will there is away."

THE WINDOW.—Last week we drew attention to the oc- casional practice of exhibiting tender exotics as window plants; our reason being that we consider it has a tendency to paralyse genuine window gardening. The subjects for window gardening are sufficiently numerous without flying to these tender exotics, which cultivators of plants are aware can be grown in the window for only a limited period. Why not cultivate some of the Myrtles, especially the small-leaved kinds such as Jenny Itsitenback, which embodies an agreeable perfume, graceful foliage, with a pro- fusion of innocent-looking globular white flowers? Then there is the Aralia Sieboldi, with its bold glossy green fo- liage; and those who like a few stripes of white in the foliage of their plants should grow Aspidistra Lurida Varie- gala, which is not a total stranger to the cottage window. Again, if the cottager has an ungovernable desire for Palms, we commend to his notice Phoenix Dactylifera or the Date Palm; not that we think he would ever get dates therefrom, though we can assure him that it is not at all improbable that every date he sowed would produce a plant.

THE SHAPIRA MSS.—Surely an E is wanted ?—Punch. O's SIMPLE DUTY.—Doing coe's very best is one's simple duty. Anything short of this is a shame to any men. There is never a fair excuse for doing fairly well— if doing better were possible to the doer. Not how much you do, but how well you do it, is the true measurn of your success in any line of action or of purpose. "Though thou have time But for a line, be that sublime; Not failure, but low aim, is a crime."

A CLEVER HOAX.-000 of the cleverest hoaxes ever perpetrated was one invented by Dean Swift, and intended for the public good. Ile caused to be printed and circulated some "last words" of a street robber named Elliston, pur- porting to have been written shortly before his execution, in which the condemned thief was made to say :—" Now, as I am a dying man, I have done something which may be of good use to the public. I have left with an honest man— the only honest man I ever knew—the names of all my wicked companions, the places where they live, and a short account of their chief crimes, in many of which I have been their accomplice, and heard the rest from their mouths. I have likewise set down the names of those we call our set- ters, of the wicked houses we frequent, and all of those who receive our stolen goods. I have solemnly charged this honest man, and have received his promise upon oath, that whenever he hears of any rogue to be tried for robbery or housebreaking he will look into his list, and if he finds the name there of the thief concerned, to send the whole paper to the Government. Of this I here give my companions fair and public warning, and hope they will take it." We are told the dean's ruse succeeded so well that street rob- beries were for many years few and far between.

THE WRONGS OF THE STONIACH.—In most of the early literatures is to be found a dialogue between the Body and Soul, in which each accuses the other of their mutual per- dition, recapitulating the offences which have produced it. Something similar might be written, with good effect, di- viding the imaginary conversation between, let us say, the Stomach and the Man, and making an attack of gout the subject of their recriminations. The Man might accuse the Stomach of having done its duty so badly that he is tor- mented with a burning fire in his extremities, which will neither let him eat, drink, walk, nor rest. The Stomach might plead justification, and say that she had lighted the said fire as the only means of getting a moment's rest from an intolerable taskmaster. Again, the Man might complain that he had lost all enjoyment of life, that his spirits were depressed, his mind gloomy, his appetite gone, his once fine muscular system reduced to flabby indolence; that his food did him more harm than good, so that it had become a misery to eat, and that every meal was followed by a leaden oppression which rendered life an insupportable burden. The Stomach, having listened to all this, delivered in a tone of angry accusation, would reply, "My case is just a.s bad as your own. Before I had well digested your breakfast, you gave me 4,oaeat luncheon to see to; and before I had got that out or the way, you thrust a dinner upon me large enough for three Stomachs. Not satisfied with that, you wound up the day with a supper, drenching me all the time with ale, wine, spirits, tea, coffee, rum, more wine, more spirits, till I thought you had taken leave of your senses; and when I heard you groaning in your sleep, starting up every now and then as if apoplexy had broken into the house, and going to carry you Off, I said to myself, "Serve him right if it did." And in this way you went on year after year, treating all my acquaintances with contempt. I gave you headache after headache; I tried to recall you to reason with half-a-dozen attacks of influenza; gave you a bilious fever; made you smart with rheumatism ; twinged you with gout till you roared. But all to no purpose. You went on making me digest till the work broke my back, and now I can digest no longer." This reproach might be made even pathetic by a description of the Stomach watching its hard tasks come down to it from the regions above between dinner and bedtime. First comes a plate of soup and bread, and a glass of sherry. "I can manage that," says the Stomach; then a plate of fish, with more bread and more sherry; "and that," adds the Stomach, "though the sauces don't quite agree with me." Then comes beef, or mutton, or both, and stout; then game and sherry; then a dish of tart. "Confound this pastry," says the Stomach; "it gives me more trouble than anything else ; but if the mas- ter will only stop here, I think, if I put out all my powers, I can get even this rubbish out of the way." But she has hardly taken this hopeful view of the case, when down come cheese, celery, apples, oranges, nuts, figs, almonds and raisins, port, sherry, claret, and a tumbler of hot Hollands- and-water. "Goodness gracious, was there ever such a mess ?" exclaims the Stomach; "what can the man mean? Does he think one pair of hands can manage all this ?" Still the willing slave goes to work, when presently there is a rush of hot tea from above, with a thin slice of bread and butter. And when the Stomach, with infinite labour, has got the hodge-podge in some sort of homogeneous shape, and is preparing to take a nap after her exhaustion, lo! devilled drumstick rushee into the laboratory, two devilled 1 kidneys, a bottle of stout, and three tumblers of hot brandy- and-water !--Ileaith.

div.head: EX_A_MINER, SA TURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883. SOME NOTES ON VICTORIA.
div.p: THE EX_A_MINER, SA TURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883. SOME NOTES ON VICTORIA.

No. VIII. The cost of living and the rate of wages are matters which have the strongest personal interest for the settler in any country. The latter are generally high and the former not very much out of proportion in Victoria. Artisans and manual labourers of all kinds, but especially good agricul- tural labourers, also domestic servants, receive splendid wages in this colony. Masons, bricklayers, and carpenters have their twelve shillings per day, plasterers 13s. or and blacksmiths, wheelwrights, and painters from 10s. to 131. General labourers have Os. to 7s. per day, but pick and shovel men on railways and kindred jobs can com- mand considerably more. Ploughmen and the better sort of farm hands are given 255. per week, with rdtions •, ordinary farm labourers, 20s. to 255.; shepherds, £25 to £6O per an- num, with food; grooms, £4O to £5O, with board and lodg- ing; gardeners, 20s. to 255. par week, with board and lodg- ing; and good general domestic servants, £3O to £4O peryear. Married couples on farms and stations and about gentlemen's residences are able to secure comfortable situations at from IE4O up to £BO a year with board and lodging. Miners working for the companies receive only £2 to £2 103. per week—thne, an occupation which to some of the early searchers for gold has proved a richly rewarded toil is now one of the worst remunerated trades that a Victorian work- ing man earning weekly wages can be employed in. The scholastic profession is pretty well paid, but still there is not much room for tutors and governesses. The ground is well taken up. I would not recommend any such to come out here unless to an assured engagement. Clerks and shop- men also ought to know that there are already more than enough of them here. Unfortunately many of the youth born in Victoria cherish the notion, like far too many else- where, that there is something lowering in labouring with the hands rather than the head, and they look forward to the counting-house and the shop counter in preference to working on the land or acquiring a knowledge of some useful handicraft. Hence the sepply of clerks and shop assistants is vastly in excess of the demand, and the remuneration is proportionately low. From employers of labour in Mel- bourne from contractors and from farmers there is a cry ' that the State should revert to the system of assisted im- migration formerly in force. They urge that it would pay the colony to import some thousands of the horny-handed sons of toil and their families. The eons of toil already here, and doing excellently well, don't, however, see this, and as they are an important factor in the constituencies, it is not likely Parliament will fall in with the request—to any large extent at any rate. lam personally disposed to think that a wholesale system of immigration would he a great curse to the country. As it is the distributing sec- tion of the community is more than equal to the wants of the colony, and of unskilled labour there is in most branches sufficient if properly utilised. A modified scheme of assisted immigration might be resorted to with great advantage and probably will. The people that are mostly wanted here are skilled artisans, handy agricultural labourers and servants, and intelligent farmers, with moderate capital, and ready and willing hands. For these there is an opening, and a good one, and the Govern- ment might very wisely and safely make an effort to draw them thither. The helping to Victoria of a few hundred families from the farming districts of England or the grape- growing districts of the South of Europe would be an ex- cellent preliminary step. The workmen in Victoria have almost uniformly adopted and secured the eight-hours system, and so far at any rate as concerns those of the metropolis, they are thorough believers in the principle of union for trade purposes. There are few towns in the old country which have so extensive a building, owned by the united trades as a place for their society meetings, as that of the Melbourne Trades Hall. The cost of living is not greater, but less, in respect of food than in England. The four-pound bread loaf is pur- chasable for Od. and 60. at the bakeries. Mutton ranges in Melbourne, where it is a little dearer than in the country, from 2d. to 41. per lb.; beef from 3d. to Bd. per lb. (the last- mentioned figure being the price for prime rump steak) ; milk is 4d. per quart; good tea can be got at two shillings and two-and-sixpence per lb.; and sugar, butter, and eggs are, lumped together, much the same in price as in the old country. Butter is selling sometimes at Pd. and is. per pound in the metropolis, but there have been dry periods latterly when 3s. per lb. has had tif be paid. Eggs tzf..., when scarce fetch as much as 2s. 6d. per dozen; more often they are at Is. and Is. 3d. or Is. 4d. Barn-door fowls are if anything a little dearer to purchase for the table than they are in England, but rabbits are dirt-cheap. In the country, where they abound, they are of course to be had for the catching or shooting, and in come parts, so numerous have they become, that a wholesale poisoning plan has to be ' followed. Fine rabbits that have been trapped or shot can in the town, however, notwithstanding the cost of carriage, be bought for Is. and le. 3d. to ls. 6d. per co4ple. In various classes of vegetables and fruits exceedingly low prices prevail. Potatoes are cheaper than in the English markets. A huge vegetable marrow or big "Turk's head" is obtainable for a few coppers, and beet-root and tomatoes, both of which are dear with you, are here ridiculously cheap, especially the tomatoes, which can be bought at one half- penny, and ordinarily a penny per lb. Some fruits, as apples and pears, are higher a little in price than in Eng- land, but several kinds are much cheaper—among them grapes, which throughout six or eight months a year are at fourpence or sixpence a lb. retail for the very best. For those who favour the juice of the grape as found in wine, an article of colonial produce officially declared by European wine judges to be a sound and wholesome drink, may be purchased at the rate of one shilling up to eighteennPnce a bottle. This is sold by the glass in colonial Wlue shops at threepence or sixpence. Without claim Ing to be an expert in this line, I shall be safe la anerting that there is far less mischief in a bottle of the commonest colonial wine than there is in a much less quantity of colonial or imported spirits, and from this point of view a total abstainer might not hesitate to wish the wine-making industry of the colony success.

Sufficient figures have been quoted above to establish the fact that one can live famously here at a moderate cost, but lest there should be some scepticism under this head I would mention that anyone can in Victoria be provided with board and lodging of a superior character for twenty and twenty-live shillings per week, and that in the restaurants a capital repast of several courses is served at prices ranging from sixpence to a shilling. The sixpenny eating-houses are those affected by the artisan classes, and there are plenty of these places in Melbourne where a bowl of soup, a plate of meat with vegetables and bread, and some sort of pudding or pastry to wind up with, are supplied for the modest coin just mentioned. I believe that in New South Wales the main necessaries of life are if anything a little cheaper than they are in Victoria, but the facts as regards the latter colony surely indicate that on a fairly moderate income a man may live quite luxuriously. In Melbourne a family man who is not his own landlori has to pay a heavy rent. It is so, too, in the New South Wales capital and in Adelaide, the South Australian capital. Gas and fuel (chiefly wood for household purposes) are also costly save as to the bush, where the selectors have more firewood than they need. The cost of transport makes the wood dear in the principal towns, well nigh as expensive as the coals from New South Wales. It must be remembered, however, that except for cooking and the washing of clothes the production of heat is not required in the colonial house- hold many weeks in the year. Furniture cannot be ob- tained at as low a figure as in England—even the cheaper kinds and the main articles of wearing- apparel are con- siderably dearer in Victoria than in the old country. All things taken into account, the working man in Victoria who is in receipt of his two pounds ten shillings per week is as well off as the working man in the English manufacturing centre who may be making his two pounds. There are hosts of the class in England who would deem themselves rich if they were receiving two pounds a week while here two pounds ten shillings, and more often three pounds per week are the lowest current in the trades. It follows from the particulars I have adduced respecting the cost of living, dEc., that the colonist who is paid three pounds ten shillings per week—and, as has been shown, this is not an ex- travagant wage—is in a position to live well, appear respect- able, and put away a nice little sum every week as a saving. He is, indeed, doing far better for himself than he could hope to do if labouring side by side with his equals in a land where the struggle to get on is keener. Then the climate of Victoria is simply delightful, spite of some drawbacks to which reference will be made. The winter lasts about three months in the year, and it is no- where, not even in the mountainous parts of the colony, what in Great Britain would be called at all severe. On the lowlands snow is never seen, or, if seen, looked upon as something perfectly astonishing. During my first winter in Victoria there was one morning a slight fall of snow in the neighbourhood of Melbourne. Such a thing had not been known for 20 years before, and so singular was the spectacle that it furnished the subject for a picture in the illustrated journals of the colony. Spring and summer, and I was going to add autumn, only the change from summer into what is called winter is almost immediate, are for the most part a succession of bright and beautiful days, daring which hardly a cloud is to be seen in the sky. Sometimes there are long spells of such weather in the drier parts of the colony, and then there are reports of a great want of rain for the parched ground; but in other parts, south and west, there is usually quite sufficient, without being too much moisture north, or hot wind days, in the height of summer December, January, and February are intensely disagree- able, and to young children and aged people are doubtlesa trying; but there are never more than two or three of such days together, and the total of them is very small. When the temperature in the shade gets over 100, and the dust is being driven about rather freely, a summer day is not alto- gether enjoyable. But then a change is at hand; there is a delicious downpour of rain, if only for a few minutes, and the coolness is all the more refreshing. The dust, which is not confined to north wind days of summer, but is a little too much troublesome at other times, is an undoubted draw- back, but this, which is much less annoying than formerly, is nothing to the nuisance of the flies, which in the bush are terribly tormenting. Then there are in some places more snakes than are pleasant, though it is but right to add of these latter that they must be more than usually of a re- tiring and inoffensive disposition, for the newsp ipers— which report aore personal detsils than do those in Eng- land—only rarely contain an account of a fatality arising from an encounter with one of these unsavoury reptiles. Snakes, therefore, need not after all be taken into account. Flies and dust remain, and they are really of small moment when set against the splendid enjoyment derivable from outdoor life in this sunny south land. After the rain and fog and the slush, which are so much concomitants of life in the large towns at home the climate of Victoria must be pronounced as, in truth, thstsof another world. I am unable to supplement this with any very laudatory opinions regarding the scenery. There are, undoubtccUy,

romantic spots, but chiefly they have to be sought for. In some parts of Gippsland, the lake district, for instance, and on the coast in the western district, and about Port Phillips' shores there are charming bits of the picturesque, albeit, generally speaking, the face of the country is monotonous.
ARRIVAL OF MR. SHAW, THE MIS- SIONARY, AND MRS. CAREY.

By the Garth Castle, which reached Plymouth on Mon- day from South Africa, a number of persons in whom con- siderable interest is centred arrived in England. These are Mr. Shaw. the missionary who was imprisoned by the French at Tamatave ; Mrs. Carey, the widow of the notorious James Carey; and the witnesses who have come from South Africa to give evidence in the trial of O'Donnell, Carey's assassin. A correspondent, who went as far as Madeira to meet the Garth Castle, has been able to gain a good deal of information as to the treatment to which Mr. Shaw was I subjected, and his account tends very strongly to confirm the original account of Admiral Pierre's high-handed action and to demonstrate the truth of Lord Hartington's remark that the release of Mr.Shavr did not terminate the Tan3atave incident. His release came suddenly, and was on the double ground that no offence had been proved against him, and that he was a British subject. He is now, it appears, ad- vised to claim £lO,OOO as compensation for Ha Imprison- ment. Mrs. Carey and her seven children did not land at Plymouth, but, in the company of the Dublin detective who had charge of them throughout the voyage, proceeded to Southampton. The Rev. G. A. Shaw addressed a crowded meeting in Exeter Hall on Thursday night, in connection with the London Missionary Society, and related the circumstances of his imprisonment by the late French Commander in Madagascar. At the close of his address a resolution was adopted, in which the belief of the meeting was expressed that the action of the French naval officers in imprisoning Mr. Shaw could not have the approval either of the French Government or the Frenoh people.

div.head: TRIAL OF CAREY'S ASSASSIN.
div.p: TRIAL OF CAREY'S ASSASSIN.

On Tuesday afternoon O'Dminell was brought up at Bow- street Police Court, and charged with the murder of James Carey.—Mr. Poland and Mr. Thomas proseckted.—Mr. A. M. Sullivan, who defended the prisoner, complained that the accused had been refused all opportunity of communi- cating with his solicitor with a view to his defence, and the magistrate, after stating that he could not understand why there had been any refusal, gave an order that O'Donnell should be allowed to see his solicitor at any time he chose. The prisoner left the court, and after a short interview with his solicitor returned, when the case for the prosecution was proceeded with.—James Parish, a servant to offie,..rs on board the Melrose, who saw the murder committed, having identified the prisoner as the man who fired the shots, his cross-examination was deferred. Evidence was given by Thomas Jones, the boatswain; Thomas Francis Carey, eon of the deceased ; Richard Edward H. Beecher, second officer ; Captain James Rose, the master of the steamer Melrose ; and Inspector J. Cherry, chief of the police at Port El;za- both. Some sensation was produced in court by a state- , ment made by young Carey, who asserted that after the shots were fired O'Donnell remarked to Mrs. Carey: "Shake hands with me, Mrs. Carey; I was sent to do it." Inspec- tor Cherry gave interesting evidence as to the examination at the prisoner's trunk. He stated that he found in it be- sides a pistol and cartridges a cutting headed, "Irish Revo- lutionists in America," a supplement of the Weekly Freeman containing a portrait of James Carey and four small pic- tures at the corners entitled, " He swears in his victims," " Look at the man in the grey suit," "Ho informs," and "As Crown witness." There were also papers of the 11th and 17th of May. showing that at that time the prisoner was in America, a certificate showing that he was a citizen of America, and papers showing that he was in Ireland in June. It was mentioned that there were two other wit- nesses to examine—the doctor and Mrs. Carey; and as an adjournment was necessary it took place at this point, Mr. Flowers fixing the next bearing for Friday. The prisoner was not returned to Millbank, but was taken to Newgate, where a strong force of police is on duty.

div.head: LOWTON MURDER.
div.p: THE LOWTON MURDER.

Yesterday (Friday) afternoon week, the remains of Joshua Rigby, 73 years of age, of Cheetham's Fold Farm, Lowton, who had been murdered the previous Monday or Tuesday, were interred at Winwick churchyard. The rector, the Rev. Canon Hopwood, read the burial service. The " mourners" included Mrs. Gibbon, mother to the man in dristody on a charge of being the murderer, and sister of the deceased; Thomas Gibbon, a brother of the prisoner; James Rigbv, brother; and some nephews and cousins of the old man. Prior to the conveyance of the body to the church the re- latives, in the interest of the accused, brought Dr. Anderton, of Leigh, to examine the state of the remains. Mrs. Gib- bon had an interview with her husband in the police cell on Friday morning, and she states that he was in fair spirits. The prisoner expressed a hope that he might be permitted to attend the funeral of his uncle, but was tsid that this was impossible. Mrs Gibbon mentioned that o of the stacks was in danger of firing through excessive heat. Prisoner suggested that it should be turned over, and men were set to work to do this during the afternoon. Old Rigby farmed 30 Cheshire acres, and had been there all his life, his father being the previous tenant. The prisoner was brought before Mr. Booth on Friday, and again remanded. The police are pursuing their investigation of the cir- cumstancea ai.tending the death of the old farmer. For a few days after the discovery of the murder very little pro- gress was made, but link by link the chain of evidence is being woven whereby the crime may, perhaps, be traced home. Two men, named William Richardson and Thomas Bent, were working on the farm last Tuesday morning week, and when the time CAM 3 when their allowance of beer was due, though it had been the practice of the deceased to serve it, on this occasion the ale was given to them by the prisoner. A remark was made as to the absence of the de- ceased, whereupon Gibbon went upstairs with the remark that the old man would not come down again until he was carried. As against the theory of suicide, irrespective of the evidence given by Dr. Perrin, as to the result of his post-mortem examination, there is the fact that the deceased on Monday evening was at the neighbouring public-house, the Jolly Cater, where he drank a glass of gin, and seemed to ke in, for him, an exception- ally good humour. During Friday night Inspector Charn- ley and Sergeant Dunn made an important discovery. They entered the house of a relative by marriage of the prisoner Gibbon, and they there discovered what they had vainly searched for at the farm, viz, the will of the murdered man, as well as his bank book and other papers. According to these the deceased had about £l7O in the bank, and, reckon- ing the value of his stock of hay ;and cattle, it is not at all improbable that the deceased was worth hetween £7OO and £BOO. The will is in favour of the priaoner. After the remand on Friday Gibbon was taken to Strangeways Prison. Two or three passengers in the same carriage asked him, when between Leigh and Tyldesley, "Did you do it ? " (meaning the murder).. The pi isoner replied that there were lots of Lowtoners who would say Rigby ought to have been killed long since; but if he (Gibbon) had done any foul play to the old man, might God strike him down dead that minute.

The prisoner has always been looked upon as a steady, sober, and industrious young man, and popular sympathy is certainly in his favour. This was shown so late as Tuesday last, when, after the inquest, he drove away from the Jolly Carter in charge of the police amid shouts of "Keep thi heart up ;" "Good-bye " and similar sym- pathetic expressions from a large number of persons. No doubt further light will be thrown upon the murder when the inqueet is resumed next Wednesday. - ADJOURNED INQUEST. • _

An adjourned inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. T. W. Barker, the district coroner, at the Jolly Carter Inn, Lowton Common, on Tuesday forenoon, Mr. rage being the foreman of the jury. The young man John Gibbon was present in the custody of the police; and Mr. Richardson, solicitor, of Bolton, was in attendance on his behalf.

Before the proceedings commenced, Mr. Richardson ob- served that he wished the jury to dismiss from their minds ail that had been in the papers; much of which was very unfair. The papers had incriminated tbe prisoner, and he thought the jury should not be lead away by what they would have read.
The Coroner endorsed the remarks, and said they must dis- miss all from their minds, and come to a decision only upon the official evidence.

Samuel Ward, a collier residing in Lowton, was the first witness called. He said he was in the Jolly Carter Inn on the night of the Monday preceding the deceased's death. Gibbon came in about seven o'clock, and remained until eleven. The deceased came in by himself between nine and ten o'clock, and seemed to be sober. Wit- ness saw him have one glass of gin only. He remained about half an hour and then left by himself, seemingly as sober as when he came in. Witness had known him all his lifetime, and that night the deceased seemed as hearty and jovial as ever. They bid each other "Good night." Thomas Bent said he was a silk weaver and resided at Lowton. He was employed by the deceased for four or five days before his death. He went on the Tuesday morning at a quarter to eight o'clock and saw John Gibbon "milk- ing " in the shippon. He afterwards saw the prisoner go towards the house with the milk, and remembered Richard- son coming about nine o'clock. Prisoner said his uncle was in the house samewhere, and he and Richardson went in together. In about tea minutes Richardson came out and shouted to witness, in coarse of which he (witness) went into the house. The prisoner said that witness should go uppirs and look at his uncle, and witness and Richardson went upstairs together. On looking towards the right hand side at the top of the stairs they SAW a bed with no one on it, but on looking further SAW the deceased in a crouched position between the bed and the wall. In helping to assist the deceased up witness found that he was dead. He saw blood on his throat and right shirt sleeve, and also saw the knife and razor produced. The razor was on the pillow and the knife opposite to him. They were both open, and there were grey hairs and blood upon the knife. Someone had apparently slept in the bed Deceased had his shirt on only, and witness said to Richard. son that they should let things remain as they were until they fetched the police. On the arrival of Police-constable Naylor the body of deceased was put on the bed.—By Mr. Richardson: There were no others to attend to the farm ex- cept the prisoner and the deceased. Richardson came in about an hour after witness got there, and asked if there was anybody abdut.—ln reply to the Coroner, witness said Richardson came for some beer. He saw a bottle t.f beer on the table inside the "loase.—By Mr Richardson : Lis did not hoar it said that It was straw

the man was not up. When witness saw the deceased he did not feel faint or feel sick but he felt frightened. He did not see James Rigby there before nine o'clock. He was downstairs crying and leaning against the chest. He saw James Rigby and the prisoner talking together. He be- lieved it was the prisoner who told him that James Rigby wanted the bank book. He (witness) said to Gibbons he must not part with it because "I know that all is left to thee." Witness knew that because he was one of the at- testing witnesses to the will. He did not know where the will was kept. He had known the prisoner ever since he was a little boy, and he had never known anything bad about him. He was steady, sober, and industrious.--By the foreman: Gibbon was the first person I saw each morning daring the seven days I worked for the deceased.—By , Supt. Jackson: The bed clothes and sheets were clean as if I nothing had been in.—ln reply to a juror, witness added that the things in the room did not appear to be disturbed. There were no signs of a struggle. The deceased was cold when he found him.

William Richardson, farm labourer, Lowton, said be was working for the deceased at the time of his death, and went to work mowing in the fields at seven o'clock on the morn- ing of the day in question. He arterwards went to the house for some beer, and saw John Gibbons on the hay-rick in the yard. Gibbons said it was something strange that his uncle was not up, and he would go and see where he was. Witness saw him go upstairs, and in about half a minnte he came down and said, "My uncle will not come down till he is carried down; you and Bent go up and look at him." They went upstairs, and the prisoner pointed out the deceased in a crouched position between the bed and the wall. They did not touch him, though he was dead. They saw the knife and raaor produced, both open, on the bed. Witness went fora policeman, and returned with one. He did tot notice any'appearance of a struggle. He never saw the deceased use the knife to cut bread and cheese with.— By Mr. Richardson: He told some persons on the way to the police station that he thought the deceased had " stucken " himself.—Sapt. Jackson: Did you see any- thing to lead you to believe that he had " stuck" himself ? —Witness: Nothing but the blood on the bed.—The Coroner: What made you think he had stuck himself ? Witness : Because the knife was on the bed.

_ Isaac Wilcock, a silk twister, residing at Lowton, said he had known the deceased all his lifetime. On the Tuesday morning in question he went to the farm, on being told that there was something amiss there. It would be about nine o'clock. There was no one downstairs but witness, the policeman, and two other persons, who went upstairs into the deceased's bedroom. They found the deceased on the floor with his head between the bed and the wall, and his face towards the window. The policeman asked them to lift the body on the bed, and when they were doing so, wit- ness saw his throat cut—as if it had been done with a stab. Ile also saw two wounds on the head—one on the top, and another on the right hand side of the head. Witness noticed that the bottom sheet of the bed was all right and straight, but the top clothes were rolled upon the floor. In witness's opinion the bed had been slept in. The deceased had nothing on but his shirt and a flannel night-cap. Witness first men- tioned the wounds on the head when he was eoming down stairs.—By Superintendent Jackson; The stab on the throat was the only wound I saw apart from those on the head. John Percy, rent and debt collector, residing at Lowton, said he had known the deceased for over 40 years. On the Tuesday morning be heard something about the deceased and went to the farm. He went upstairs with some other people, and saw the old man down on the floor, on his left side, between the bed and the wall. The bed appeared to ' have been slept in hlthough the bed clothes were off—about the feet. He noticed a little blood on the right hand sleeve, and saw on the bed a razor and a pocket - knife. They were open, and about eighteen inches apart. The handles were towards the body of the deceased. He saw the prisoner before be went upstairs, and he seemed in very great distress. Witnesa asked if he had noticed the deceased being any different overnight, and the prisoner replied that he had not noticed anything unusual. Heals, asked him if he had heard the deceased in the night, and he replied that he had not.—By Mr. Richardson: I have known the young man Gibbon from boyhood, and I have always known him to have a good and steady character.—The Foreman: Do you think the deceased could have fallen by the bedside as you found him ?—Wit- ness: Well, I don't know.—The Coroner: That is a matter of opinion for the jury to consider.—By Superintendent Jackson: I did not notice any appearance of violence. Ido not think the deceased could have fallen where he lay with the knife and razor in the position in which they were.— By a Juror: I did not notice any blood on the deceased's , hands.

James Thorniey, a labourer on the railway, said on the Tuesday morning in question he went to the farm and arrived there about five minutes past nine e'clock. He asked the prisoner if it was "true about the old man?" and he replied, "Yes, it's true enough." Witness and some others went upstairs with the prisoner, and they went into the bed- room—the prisoner stopping at the top of the stairs. The body was found in the position described by previous wit- nesses.

Thomas Boydell, landlord of the Jolly Carter Inn, re- membered seeing the deceased in his house about half-past nine on the Monday night before his death. He was sober, and was in about a quarter of an hour. He went out by himself. That was the last time he saw him alive. On the following morning in consequence of what he heard he went to the farm and saw the prisoner. He was crying. He asked him if he would let him see his uncle, and he took him up. He saw something like a gash in the throat, and 8611fli blood on the shirt front. The policeman CaM3 in while he was there. Witness assisted to put the body on the bed.—By the foreman : The deceased had some potatoes to eat in my house. lie did not cut them with a knife. I have never seen the pocket knife produced previously. The inquiry had now lasted for several hours, and the Coroner observed that as there were other witnesses to call it was quite impossible for thorn to finish that night. He thought, therefore, that they had better adjourn, and the only questi,m for them to consider was what day would suit their convenience.
After a C:onversation among the jurymen, it was decided that the inquest should be resumed on Wednesday next at half-past eleven.

011 ! TEOSE BOYS !—The following advertisement appeared in the Daily News :—" A Comfortable Home Wanted for an amusing little Monkey, to be Sold cheap." Alas, here is another unfortunate parent who is unable to solve the great question of the day, namely, " What shall we do with our boys ?"—Punch. _ _

On the way home, after his duel with O'Connell, in a hackney coach, Lord Alvanley said, "What a clumsy fellow O'Connell must be to miss such a fat fellow as I am. He ought to practice at a haystack to get his hand in." When the carriage drove up to Alvanley's door, he gave the coach- man a sovereign. Jarvie was profuse in his thanks, and said, "It's a great deal for only having taken your lordship to Wimbledon." "No, my good man," said Alvanley, "I give it you, not for taking me, but for bringing me back." Quaint Mr. Slick once said—" Foddering cattle, going to mill, and chopping oven wood ain't jest the thing to rile up the poetry in a feller's bosom," but the reason is that there may be no poetry there to" rile" up. Many a man thinks he could be great if he only had time to attend to the mat- ter, and growls about the circumstances which hamper him; but Gladstone is just as much of a statesman when cutting trees in the forest as when making a speech in the House of Commons, and Tennyson cuts hay and sings about Lady Clara Vere de Vere at the same time. We should all be greater than we are if we would only admit that we are as small as we are. While half conscious that we are merely frogs, we are determined to swell to the size of an ox, and the process is painful and the result is disastrous. GOD'S CARE.—There was a beautiful engraving on the wall of the Matterhorn mountain. We were remarking that the wondrous works of God were not only shown in those lofty, snow-clad mountains, but also in the tiny mosses found in their ravines. A friend present said : "Yes, I was with a party at the Matterhorn, and while we were admiring the sublimity of the scene, a gentleman of the company produced a pocket microscope, and having caught a tiny fly, placed it under the glass. He reminded us that the legs of the household fly in England were naked, then called our attention to the legs of this little fly, which were thickly covered with hair, thus showing that the same God who made the lofty mountains rise, attended to the comfort of the tiniest of creatures, even providing socks and mittens for the little flies whose home these mountains were."—T. Newberry. COMPLIMENT TO A. Sr. HELENS POLICE TNSPECTOR.—At the close of the business at the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday morning, A ldermin Harrison being in the chair, Mr. Superintendent Johnston said :—I am sorry to inform your worship that this is the last time that Mr. Inspector Wood will assist me in the performance of my duty here. The chief constable has ordered that he be trans- ferred to Widnes, a more Important position, to replace In- spector Barnett, who has been promoted to the rank of superintendent, and transferred to Ashton-under-Lyne division. Mr. Wood has been with us now in St. Helens for about fifteen years.—Alderman Harrison said : 1 am sorry that we have to part with Mr. Inspector Wood. He has always been a most efficient and courteous officer, and always attentive to his duties. I hope, Mr. Wood that you will have every success wherever You go.—Mr. Wood then, in a few words, suitably returned thanks for the kind refer- ence which had been made to him. During the fifteen years Mr. Wood has been in St. Helens, both as constable, ser- geant, and inspector, he has earned the respect and goodwill of all classes.

THE FOWLER'S ART IN Sr. ICILDL—After our levee with the inhabitants, we were escorted up the hill to see a speci- men of the fowling art, which is their chief occupation. It was, without exaggeration, an "awfully interesting" sight to Bee a man dancing down a precipice of 500 or 600 feet with a rope round his waist, his bare feet against the rock, and a wand in his hand with a horsehair snare at the top, while two men, well planted on the brink above him, lowered the rope rapidly in accordance with the directions he sang out to them, like a chaunt, all the way down. About half way down he stopped at a narrow grassy ledge, and began to poke about. Then we saw him stretch down his wand and instantly draw it up again, with a white bird (a fulmar) fluttering at the end of it. He took the bird, stuck its head and neck under his waist-belt, and did the same thing over again to two other birds. Then he was hauled up, but disengaging the rope from his waist when about 100 feet from the top, he made his way up unassisted, through a fearful chasm which, looked at from above, seemed perilous even for a goat. We breathed more freely when we saw him safe on the grassy brink. It was satiefac• tory to hear that accidents in this "dreadful trade" are very rare, which says much for thecombined hardihood and Oil- Ition of those who practise 11.—Gasi Ward.
