whale of the bottle nose species has been caug tiorbreck, close to Blackpool. The first Diocesan Conference ever held in Newcastle took Place on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Hill, mineral water manufacturer, of Irby-in-the Marsh, died on Tuesday from the effects of having a tooth draws. A destructive fire took place on Saturday night at the Great Eastern Railway Company's Works, Stratford, %ex. A lagely attended meeting was held on Tuesday night, h Exeter Hall, London, to protest against the imprisonment Of Miss Booth in Switzerland. • At Monkweermouth, on Monday, about twenty thousand Persons took part in the proceedings in connection with the uteening of a Salvation Army barracks. The Lords of the Admiralty have decided that black or Coloured men are not to be entered for service in the navy Without the special sanction of the Admiralty. A passenger train from Birmingham to Dudley, on the leireat Western line, ran into a siding step block at Dudley Oti Monday evening, and several passengers were injured. The Rev. T. M. Hughes, a clergyman, was brought up again at the Birmingham police court, on Tuesday, on the Charge of bigamy. The case was not concluded, and a further remand was granted. John Edward Peyton, a solicitor, of London, was on Sat- Urday committed for trial by the migistrates at Driffield, Charged with endeavouring to obtain money by false pre- tences. • hansom cab driver was fatally injured while driving DP-r053 Ludgate- circus, London, on Tuesdey afterneon, throughhis horse bolting and upsetting a vehicle, after coil- cling with an omnibus. The two police constables charged - witli causing the death of the man Parkinson, at Manchester, who died from the effects of a blow received during a disturbance, have been committed for trial at the assizes. SOON TIRED OF LIFE —At the Liverpool police court, on Tuesday. Thomas Barns, a youth, aged 15, was close ged with attempting to commit suicide by taking carbolic acid. The prisoner gave as his reason that he was tired of life, his father and mother being in the hibit of beating him %ad quarrelling. He was remanded. Mr. Jamas Caw, who in 1840, while in command of the Edinburgh Castle steamship, at Margate, became the nnwh- tag instrument of the landing of Prince Charles Louis &Napoleon and his band of followers In their abortive at- tempt to rouse the soldiers at Boulogne, died last week at Greenwich, ani, was buried in the Shooter's Hill Ceme- tery. A SENTENCE " LIKELY TO ATTRACT NOTICE "—Private James Bibb, of the Royal Warwickshire Regiment, has been neat to gaol for three months by the magistrates of that county for stealing four pennyworth of apples, though this h his first offence. The report adds that the sentence is "likely to attract notice," and few people will dispute this Probability. A FATAL QUARREL BETWEEN MAN AND WIFE. -- On Saturday night, George Steven, a dock labourer, at Leith, While drunk quarrelled with his wife, whom he assaulted. Shortly afterwards Mrs. Steven was found in her house dead. A post-mortem examination made on Tuesday !bowed that death resulted from heart disease. Steven is cust9,l7, tau LATE lottsst fluourt4.—kt Balinoral for the last few days workmen have been busily engaged in preparing a foundation for the statue of the late John Brown, whiclf is about to be erected by command of the Queen. It is ex- Pected that the work will be ready early in October. The Cite is to be south of Balmoral, and will be visible from the Windows of the castle. CHARGE AGAINST A BANE MANAGER—At Newcastle, on Monday, William Alexander Ogilvie was charged with hay- lug conspired with other persons not yet in custody fo de- fraud the directors and shareholders of the Northern Coun- ties Bank, of which he was manager, by means of falsifica- tion of accounts and documents. The case was adjourned to the 15th October. THE GLASGOW DYNAMITE CONSPIRATOBS.—Eight of the Sine men in Glasgow prison charged nith the dynamite Outrages have presented a petition to the Justice General of Scotland for "running their letters." The petition was ranted, and the Crown authorities will now be recraired to °dog on the trial in 60 days unless they should ask for another 40 days' postponement. LONDON TO JOHN 0' GROATS ON I TRICYCLE.—Mr. Alfred Nixon champion of the London Tricycle Club, who last year made the first and at present only tricycle journey trent John o' Groat's to the Land's End, a distance of 1,007 relies, in a fortnight, has just accomplished the Above-men- tioned ride, a distance of 750 miles, also for the first time, On a tricycle in 8 days 23 hours. TRH ALLEGED FRAUDS BY I,POST-OFFICE CLERK.—Wm. George Linville, post-office clerk, has been agein charged at Leamington with stealing two registered letters containing 4.1e500, consigned to Lloyd's branch bank at Leamington, On July 29. The prisoner was in charge of the Leamington Poet-office, and absconded with the letters, and was arrested In London. He was committed for trial at Warwick assizes. THE NORWICH HOSPITAL BAZ.AAR—At a meeting of the governors of the Norfolk and Norwich Hospital, on Satur- daY, it was stated that the total receipts from the recent baz tar, inaugurated by the Duke and Duchess of Con- naught, amounted to £6,328 9s. Bd., the nett results being £5,779 ss. 31, It is hoped that this will be found sufficient to cover the entire cost of fitting and furnishing, as well as any amount that may be due on the fabric itself. DIYSTHRIOUS 81100rING APPIIR i NOBTIL WALES.—As reral young men were proceeding from Wrexham to .83reoed early on Sunday morning, a shot was fired at them 4rOln behind a hedge, and Henry Roberts, of Wrexham, was 1491 Anded in the head and face. His injuries were attended by an eeeisteet to Dr: Devies, and it is thought they will Cot prove dangerous. The person who fired the shot has Rot vet been found. but the police are said to have a clue. HOYAL ALBLIL. ASYLUM —The thire geinquennia.l festival aid of the Roval Albert Asylum for Idiots was held on Monday at Lancaster. Lord Winmarleigh occupied the -Chair at the business meeting. The report of the Central Committee stated that the past year had not been less pros- perous than former years. -There were at present 516 Patients in the Asylum, and there was a prospect of the 'whole of the vacant accommodation being utilised before IlH2g. THREATENING AN M.P.—Joseph Betts, Northumberland - Street, Heigham, commission agent, has been committed for trial at Norwich for sending a letter, signed "Another In- Lincible," to Mr. Colman, M.P., threatening to murder him. %lee letter was eimila to that which the prisoner was some rahntha ago chatged with sending to the Bishop of Norwich, Who at last assives withdrew from the prosecution, and the Wilmer was bound over to appear for judgment when called uPon. Eatereerry AT BOLTON.—A. case of peculiarly brutal as- was before the Belem magistrates on Monday. A la„..bOttrer named Andrew Laryin kicked a young man named mortis, who had interposed on behalf of an old woman whom Lervin was kicking. After he had been told that he had broken Morrie's leg Larvin dealt him another kick, and was ,aho guilty of the almost incredible atrocity of "taking cold of the broken limb and twisting it round." The fel- low was committed for trial. Symrsitsta CHt4PIONSHIP OF LA.NCASHIRE.-0a Tues. _LILLY night the 500 yards swimming championship of Lance- :eke was decided at Oldham, the competitors being J. Vnhey, Oldham, one mile champion of England; J. Col- -ISt, Salford, 1.000 yards English champion; J. Frost, Sit- toed; and J. Mills, Oldham. The latter retired after going ▪ fourth of the distance, and Finney, who was in front alt the way, won by 44 yards. Collier was a length ahead of crost. Time, 'tirnin. 55sec. The professionals' handicap was won by J. Rasa &Ilford ; A. Rebineon, Leeds, second; C. Rotherham, Salford, third. INGRATITUDE AND DISIIONESTY.—Robert Dauks, con- 1 tleatial clerk to Ar. Jesse Harbert, barrister, Birmingham, , haying absconded, it has been ascertained that during the Past two years he hts been forging cheques and receipts Which will involve his employer in the loss of many hun- dreds of pounds. Some years ago Danks was sentenced to fieeve years' penal servitude, which, by the exertions of Mr. Merbert, who acted as his counsel, was reduced to fifteen Months. When released from prison Mr. Herbert took Danks into his employ, and the latter has since been a prominent 131. ember of a local religious body, and is said to have been Rithly respected. aa Exreteeourawenv Camas AGAINST A lons-sums iii*CdOOLMASTER.—The remarkable charge against a National 11.5hoolmaster, named Randall, was gone into on Saturday by the magistrates at Driffield. Randall had employed e fisher- I luau to commit a violent assault on a girl of 15, who was formerly a teacher in the National Schools, but the man Pee information to the police and the prisoeer was appre- flooded. The girt and her parents now gave evidence to Show that the prisoner, who was a married man, had formed an extraordinary liking for the girl, and that he had pro- Dosed to take her abroad and marry her, an arrangement Which the parents very naturally scouted. The prisoner was Committed for trial. TRH Qom/ A A PAINTER.— Under Mr. Leitch's in- !dr, action, Her Majesty attained to great proficiency in paint- • On the occasion of one of his visits, Mr. Leitch saw a drawing of a subject behind Buckingham Palace, which :ter Majesty had done entirely by herself, and which Mr. Leitch described to me as "really admirably well done." Jle liked it so much that he obtained leave to take it away rin order to have it properly mounted. It was lying in his Studio for this purpose when Stanfield called, and observing the drawing he asked by whom it was painted. Mr. Leitch eaid it was by a pupil of his. Oh, nonsence," Stanfi-ld fte id. "Yes," said Mr. Leitch. "and it is by a lady." Stan- "add looked at it again and said, "Well, she paints too well 4er an amateur. She will b• soon entering the ranks as a Professional artist."—Good Words. RXTRAORDINA.RY CONDUCT or A GIRL.—At Birmingham .4_1214 Saturday, a girl of 15 was reminded on a charge of 'Waling 8s 6,1 from a woman with whom she had lodged. Z'sue prosecutrix stated that for some time the girl had be- Zit,l,ged to the Church Army, and she had discovered that the --ren3', which had been taken from her pocket, had been EtiLt by the prisoner to the army. She had also stolen two e °folios from her mother, with one of which she bought "Hallelujah bonnet" and a dress, giving the other to a Zeptain. The girl had recenrly lost two situations through neYing out to attend the army meetings till nearly mid- zah.t ; in fact, her ass miation with it had practically ruined •

'A-LCUTTA. EXTILBITION.—There is every Indication that this fichibition will be a groat success The number f visitors is Pected to be so large that arrangements are being made for al4 encampment outside the city. All the space set apart for lecidbitors is already bespoke. We understand that Oadbury taxvi been appointed Elo's Purveyors of the Cocoa and —'oool4le,tioueetned at the Exhibitioa.—..ant.

A heavy gale prevailed iR Liverpool on Thursday, as in other parts of the district, but no (min tee WAS reported. A respite has been granted in the case of the murderer Gouldstone, to allow of an inquiry to be made respecting his sanity. 111 A. bronze statue of Sir Francis Drake by Mr. Baehem, pre- e ited to Tavistock by the Duke of Bedford, was unveiled en Thursday by the Portreeve. The Gas Committee of the Manchester Corporation, as the result of the year's working, are able to make the usual grant of £52900 to the Improvement Committee. The British Association concluded its congress at South- port on Wednesday. In the afternoon a general meeting wee held, at which thanks were voted to all who had laid he association under obligation. On Wednesday, a farmer of Entwistle, named Foy, at- tempted to cross the line at Oaks Station, near Bolton. H- was knocked down by a passing train and cut to pieces. De- em vete leaves a widow and nine children. MINE DESASTER.—A large quantity of rock and earth suddenly fell, on Thursday moreing, at Cook's Kitchen Mine, near Camborne, burying ten men Tne dead bodies of two have been recovered, and it is feared that others have also ben killed. GARROTTE ROBBERY ON BLACKHEATII.—A. gentleman residing in the vicinity was garotted and robbed on Black- heath, London, on Tuesday evening, between eight and nine o'clock. A gold watch (No. 5,227), locket, and chain, and about £2 in money, were stolen from him. REPORTED EXTENSIVE FORGERIES—It is reported that forgeries to the extent of over £6.000 have been committed on several London banks by a professional man, for whose arrest a warrant has been issued. The forgeries are said to have been effected by means of bills of exchange. AFFRAY WITH POACHERS.—A desperate encounter between poachers and police took place early on Thursday morning on Lard Warwick's estate, Oakley Wood, Warwick. Blud- geons and stones were freely used. One poacher was severely wounded, but escaped. Two were captured. AN ABSCONDING BANK MANAGER. A warrant was issu el by the Birmingham magistrates on WAnesdey even- ing for the arrest of John Alfred Burean. manager of the Birmingham Union Bank, who has absconded, and who is chargeel with forgery on the bank. The defalcations are ascertained to be £15,000. SEASIDE SABBATH DESECRATION —The Rev. C H. Wain- wright, Vicar of Christ Chutch. Blackpoel, referred at a meeting held in that town on Wednes lay night to the great amount of poverty existing amongst the residents, and ex- pressed his conviction that it was a punishment for the Sabbath desecration for which Blackpool, he said, was pro- minent among watering places. SETTING FIRE TO A HORSE —Before Sheriff Barclay, at Perth, on Wednesday, James M'Doneall, labourer, pleaded guilty to having on Saturday, the 15th inst., in the parish of Kirkmichael, Perthshire, cruelly illtreated a horse yoked to a cart loaded with bay, which horse he was driving, by tying a quantity of hay round its hind legs and setting fire to it. He was ordered to pay £3 of a modified penalty or suffer a month's imi risonment. EXTRAORDINARY LICENSING PROSECUTION--Mary Smith, landlady of the White Swan, Derby, was on Wednesday tined 5s and costs by the Derby magistrates for selling liquor during prohibited hours on the morning of Sunday, 16th inst. The sexton of St. Peter's Church, finding there wee no wine for Communion, went across to defendant's house, and she let him have a bottle of port. He was ob- served by a policeman as he left the house. Tbe. sexton was fined is. THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER AND MR. BRADLAUGH.— At the Newcastle Diocesan Conference, on YV ednesday, Mr. B. C. Browne, who read a paper, said it was a mistake on the part of Mr. Bradlaugh's friends to suppose Christians op- , posed his return to the House of Commons, because be was' a good social reformer.—The Bishop of Manchester said he corecurred in this. A good Christian might even be a Socialist and Republican, and might co-operate with others in real , Christian work. DREADFUL SUICIDE OF A GLASGOW GENTLEMAN —On Thursday morning, as a charwoman entered the office of John P. Paton, marine insurance broker, 3, Royal Ex- change Buildings, Glasgow, she found him dead on hischair and a discharged revolver at his feet, whereupon she nearly fainted. He had put the revolver to his mouth, as the ball had passed through his head and struck the roof. The act must have been committed during the night. The deceased was aged fifty. A MOTHER SHOT BY HER &N.—A peculiarly painful occurrence is reported from Lancaster. Mr. Holden, on of the district coroner, was shooting rabbits on Wednesday near Quernmore Park his mother and an being with him. Un- fortunately his gun accidentally exbToded whilst the ladies were in the line of fire, and Mrs. Holden was shot in the breast, her injuries causing death a few hours later. Her sister also received portions of the charge, and is said to be in a serious condition. YOUTHFUL GALLANTRY REWARDED —On Wednesday evening, at Accrington, Master J. Berry, a youth of only thirteen years, was made the recipient of a portrait and medal for an act of bravery. At some risk to his own life, Berry gallantly plunged into a pond of water and rescued a drowning child. The portrait was the gift of the child's father, and the medal was presented by the Accrington Swimming Club. The presentation was made at a public swimming gala. MARRIAGE OF THE LORD MAYOR OF LONDON'S DeuGnren.—The marriage of Miss Knight, daughter of the Lord Mayor of London, to Mr. Aitken, took place at St. Paul's Cathedral on Wednesday morning in the presence of a large congregation. The Archbishop of Canterbury per- formed the ceremony, and among those present were Alder- men Carden, Fowler, De Keyson, and Cotton. The presents were very numerous, and included one of plate, costing 125 guineas, subscribed by the Court of Aldermen, and a silver and glass epergne, by the Court of Judges. The pair will go to Christchurch for the honeymoon. HOMICIDE IN MANCHESTER.-00 Saturday night Wm. M•Derrnott, a young man, was intoxicated and violent in Gresham-street, Openshaw. His father, Henry M‘Dermott, a labourer, tried to get him away and was struck several , times. He retaliated, striking his son several blows. The last blow knocked the young man down, and he died in the I street. Henry ill‘Dermott, who is a man of good character, I was taken into custody charged with causing his son's death, and was rem tnded at the Manchester County Police Court, on Itilonday.—M•Dermott was committed for trial on Wednesday by the Manchester magistrates. Ex CRORDINLRY FAGGOT VOTING.—An objection WAS lodged by the Liberals at the Revision Court at Oxford on Tuesday against the Rev. Washbourne West, Bursar of Lincoln College, on the ground that be did not occupy the house for which he claimed. It was stated that Mr. West was one of the largest faggot-voters in England, and he admitted that at the last election be voted seventeen times, and then was obliged to miss seven places where he was en- titled to vote. He claimed to be represented in Parliament be 64 members. The objection was over-ruled, as Mr. West stated that he owned the house, and had used it during the year. EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPE. An extraordinary escape from suicide was reported on Wednesday in Birmingham. A. tradesman in the town in a state of delirium jumped through a bedroom window three storeys high, but his night- shirt caught upon a hook in the sill, and he hung sus- pended for ten minutes above the heads of the people. His wife, bearing cries, ran upstairs, and had the presence of mind to close the sash of the window, thus affording addi- tional protection, as the garment by which her husband was suspended was rapidly giving way. Amidst considerable excitement a ladder was procured, and the unfortunate man was rescued from his perilous position. A SALVATION " DEMONSTRATION."—tir'eorge Hill, " cap- tain " of the Accrington detachment of the Salvation Army, was on Wednesday summoned, with five members of his following, for assaulting Mr. Edmundson, a local cab owner. Some days ago the defendants interfered with Edmundsen's progress as he was driving along a street in Accrington at a time when they were " demonstrating " in the newel man- ner. They stopped the horse, beat it about the head with , their tambourines, and finally assaulted the prosecutor. Two I were discharged, and fines ranging from lOs to twice that I amount were imposed upon the remaining defendants, who refused to pay, preferring to undergo the alternative im- prisonment. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents amongst others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal, were sealed during the week ending Septembor 22nd, 1883 : William Mather, Salford, engineer, improvements in machinery for printing fabrics; William Hargreaves and Robert liarwuod, Bolton, for improvements in the construc- tion of fly-wheels and pullies for rope driving; John Fer- ran, Manchester, improvements in machinery for spinning and doubling fibrous materials; Henry Yates, Manchester, improvements in machinery for sectional warping; Thoinas Bibby, James Bibby, and John Baron, Burnley, and William Baron, Rochdale, improvements in machinery used in the manufacture of paper bags; John Stones, Ulveraton, and , Thomas Kirby, Barrow-in-Furness, improvements in machinery or apparatus for automatically opening and clos- ing or working the doors or shutters of hoists or lifts; John Thompson and Thomas Barker, Manchester, improvements in machines for combing cotton, silk, and other fibres; Samuel Lowe and William Lamb, Nottingham, improve- ments in knitting machines.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E., Fat. Inst. P.A., 4, St. Ann's Square, Manches- ter. TRAGEDIES.—On Wednesday, at Leeds, Stephen Kelly aged thirty-two, dyer, was committed for trial on the charge of having caused the death of James Gillman, a labourer. The evidence showed that the prisoner had stabbed Gillman in the head with a knife during a street fight, after finding that deceased was too powerful for him.—At the Thames Police Court, Hugh Armstrong, forty years of age, a sea- man, was remanded, charged with attempting, without ap- parent provocetion, to murder a female in a public-house by cutting her throat._TWO most desperate attempts at suicide were made at Hanley by a servant girl, named Mary Jane Jackson. She first jumped into a pool of water, and being rescued ran to her sister's house and inflicted a terrible gash in her throat, with a bread knife. A number of persons tried to take the knife from her, but only succeeded by breaking it in her hand, several of them being cut in the attempt.— At Honiton, William Dowell, Eliza Williams (his sister), and Amos French, all of Branscombe, were charged with the wilful murder of William Perryman, a latiourer, on Saturday, the Bth inst. The theme, of the prosee.ution was that the accused hav:ng had a quarrel with one David Pyle, the prisoner Dowell waited one night for Pyle on his return from work, and in Mistake shot Perryman, who came that way. Williams asd French were charged as acces- sories before and after the fact. After hearing evidence for the prosecution, the Bench discharged the pr;soners without hearing the case for the defence. A SHORT ROAD TO HEALTH AND WEALTII.—InStOAd at a bottle of champagne every day at dinner, drink a bottle of CARMACR'S sparkling POIMETTE.—.Idvt.

div.head: 14',XAM1NEP, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.
div.p: THE 14',XAM1NEP, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.

PERSONAL._ The Duke and Duchess of Albany arrived at Balmoral on Tuesday. Earl Granville arrived at Hawarden, on Monday, on a visit to Mr. Gladstone. Sir Stafford Northcote sailed from Jersey, on Monday, on board Mr. Smith's yacht Pandora. Sir Arthur Sullivan has again visited Leeds and rehearsed the choruses for the forthcoming festival, which opens on October 10. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught make a short stay :a England after their return from Germany, and then leave for India. On Tuesday, Mr. John Bright, who is at present the guest of Sir James Caird, of Cassencarrie, visited Kirkcudbright, and drove through the town. The Princess Beatrice opened a bazaar in Aberdeen on Thursday in aid of the Sick Children's Hospital. A great procession of the trades and friendly societies, magistrates, and local authorities afterwards proceeded to Duthie Park, which was formally opened by her Royal Highness. • Sir Moses Montefiore will next month complete only his 99th year. Although physically somewhat weak, he is perfectly free from disease of any sort. His intellect and memory are particularly clear, and he takes a very active interest in everything that passes in the world. He usually drives out for an hour ithen the weather is mild and fine. Mr. W. E. Forster, Sir James Anderson, and Mr. John ('ender, M. P., Captain Shaw, superintendent of the London Fire Brigade, and other gentlemen, dined at the British Legation, Athens, on Monday evening. Some of the Greek ministers, together with members of the diplomatic body in Athens, were invited to meet them. Mr. Forster• and his party left Athens for Constantinople on the 27th inst. Mr. Gladstone, in the Pembroke Castle, reached Graves- end on Friday week, and on landing was heartily cheered. The right hon. gentleman accepted an address from the local Liberal Association, and in expressing his gratitude for the welcome given him remarked that the trip had given all his party—and not the least his friend the Poet Laureate—such an additional stock of strength and spirits as would enable them old as they were, to start again on their career, with the 1;ope to render in their respective spheres some little further service to their fellow-creatures before they died. The Premier proceeded by special train to London, and walked from the Charing Cross. Station to Downing-street. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Hawarden, on Saturday evening. They met with a hearty reception at Chester. There was a large congregation in Havrardan Parish Church, on Sunday morning, including many visitors. The Premier read the lesson.

POLITICAL. Lord Randolph Churchill will not speak at Bournemouth on Thursday, nor attend any public meetings till December at Edinburgh. Replying to a resolution of Carmarthenshire colliers, Mr. Gladstone writes that he has every hope the present Parlia- ment will deal with the question of the county franchise. A meeting of the Lewes Conservative Association was held on Wednesday evening, when Mr. F. %V. Cosens was unani- mously adopted as the Conservative candidate at the next election. The Liberals have selected Mr. Robert Crossley, brother of the Mayor. Tam DEAN FORVIT MIN.ERS on Saturday night unanim- ously adopted a resolution in favour of the extension of the borough franchise to counties, and expressing an opinion that no reform bill will give satisfaction unless there be a thorough redistribution of seats. The meeting authorised the executive of the Miners' Union to petition Mr. Glad- stone to include a reform bill in the work of next session. Mr. WALTER Waxer, late member for Wallingford, ad- dressing the Liberal Association of St. Ives, Cornwall. on Monday night, said the assent of the Conservative candi- didate for Manchester to the proposed extension of the franchise showed the process of education was still going on in the Conservative ranks. As Liberals they should never cease to agitate for justice, fair play, equality, and no monopoly. Mn. Rama, memter for Wallingford, and the selected L beret candidate for Bridport, addressed the Liberal As- seciation on Thursday, and was enthusiastically received. Rwiewing the work of the session, he expressed the conv'e ' tion that no rule was more effective than that of grand committees. He was in favour of extending the franchise to counties, but regarded land nationalisation as wild and impracticable. Mr. EDWARD BIRKBECE, M.P., speaking on Wednesday night at a dinner of the North Walsham Agricultural Asso- ciation, said the Grand Committees had proved successful, and but for them the Bankruptcy Bill would not have passed. Credit was due to the Government for introducing the Agricultural Holdings Amendment Act, though he rather preferred Mr. Chaplin's bill. The House of Lords had nearly played the fool over the bill. Lord GEORGF. HAMILTON addressed a Conservative meet- ing at Oldham, on Saturday. ln reviewing the foreign policy of the Governmentt his lordship declared that the action of Mr. Gladstone in Egypt was a clumsy and servile imi- tation of the late Lord Beaconsfield, and that he affected his purpose by the shedding of blood and the overthrow of national institutions in Egypt, whereas Lord Beaconsfield achieved his successes by the moral influence of a resolute will. SIR Joerx Sr. Al/2417, addressing his constituents at Fal- mouth on Saturday afternoon, said that the present condi- tion of India was more satisfactory than for years past. In his opinion the Iltert Bill agitation would end in a corn- promise which would admit of natives gradually obtaining the power proposed to be bestowed on them. Mr. A. P. Vivian, M.P., commended the Corrupt Practices Act, and expressed his belief that the Agriaultural Holdings Act was a fair and earnest endeavour to do justice between landlord and tenant. A WORSINGUEN'S DEmossraanorr, attended by about 20,000 persons, was held on the Town Moor, Newcastle on Saturday, to support the extension of the franchise. INlr. John Morley, MP., expressed the belief that the Govern- ment had not made up their minds on the subject of the county franchise, but a popular agitation of the question would assist them. He believed it would be in the fore- front of the Queen's Speech next session. Mr. Broadhurst, Mr Bradlaugh, and Mr. Stevenson, members of Parliament, were also present. The EARL OF CORE, speaking on Wednesiay at the annual meeting of the Frome Agricultural Society, claimed credit for the Gevernment for having pissed the Agricultural , Holdings Act. He admitted that the importation of foreign cattle was a difficult question to deal with, hut recommended a visit to Deptford to see the precautions taken and the regu- lations enforced with the obj et of preventing the importa- tion of disease His lordship expressed the belief that next session they would see introduced a Local Government Bill, for which they hid waited so long. Replying to a resolution of the Welsh miners protesting against the existing tariffe on foreign cattle and sheep urn- pert!, Lord Kensington, M.P., writes—" I understand you to refer to orders and regulations respecting the slaughter of animals at ports of landing. All such regulations are either directly or indirectly under the Privy Council, or the local authorities acting under the power given them by Acts of Parliament. I am in favour of as little restriction as possible on any trade that would supply food for the people, but, at the seine time, precaution must be taken against the intro- duction of disease amongst the flocks and herds of the country." Mr. P. STEWART 3iIACITER, M.P., speaking OR Monday night at a missionary meeting at Weston-super-Mare, re- ferred to the return of Mr. Shaw, against whom the French had failed to find the slightest cause for arrest. Madagas- car, he felt sure, would not suffer from this attack, nor would France gain anything but a bad reputation. The case of Mr. Shaw was certainly not one that should he over- looked. They could not always remain passive under in- sult ; and while he was far from advising the course of action the Government should take, he maintained that firmness was expected, especially where the rights of con- science were imperilled. MR. BRADLATIOR AND SIR S. NORTHCOTE —Mr. Brad- laugh has addressed a letter to Sir Stafford Northcote recapitulating the principal facts of his conflict, in which he complains that the Conservative leader has involved him. with the House of Commons. He states that Sir Stafford broke his pledge to consider fairly the Government Affirmation Bill, and moved a resolution resulting in his violent expulsion. After enumerating other acts of opposi- tion by the Conservatives, in and out of Parliament, to his admission, Mr. Bradlaugla asks whether Sir Stafford intends to continue the conflict, and adds that while the seat is legally his it is his duty to enforce his rights. Mr. 'Awes Pratt, M.P, speaking at the Lampeter Agricultural Show dinner OD Thursday, combatted the notion that the restrictions upon the importation of foreign cattle were intended as a protection to farmers. They did not want protection, but the surest way of increasing the price of meat would be to allow foreign disease to decimate the flocks and herds of the country. The workingman was equally interested in stamping out disease, for he de- pended chiefly upon this country for his meat supply, and the best means of doing so was restriction upon the re- moval of cattle from place to place, and upon the importa- tion of foreign disease. Sin RICHARD CROSS opened a Conservative Club at Penrith, on Thursday, and at a luncheon held afterwards he spoke of the importance of such institutions in spreading their principles. The Tory party always desired the people to think out political Questions for themselves, and were cer- tain that if they would do so the Liberal Government won,cl be turned out of office at the next election. A general elec- tion could not be far off, and the Conservatives ought to carefully prepare for it. At a public meeting held later, Sir Richard returned thanks for a resolution endorsing the action of the Conservative leaders. In reviewing the con- duct of the Government, he said they bad blundered in Ireland, Zululand, the Transvaal, 'Egypt, and India. Division in council bad produced weakness and rashness in action, and this had been followed by all sorts of failure. MANCHESTER ELtertorr.—Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., has written a letter to the chairman of Dr. Pankhurst's com- mittee, warmly supporting Dr. Pankhurst's candidature, and forwarding a cheque for £lOO towards his election expenses. A letter has also been received from Mr. Ben Brierley stating that he will vote for Dr. Pankhurst in reply to Mr. Houlitsworth's charge of cowardice against the Liberal party. At a large and enthusiastic meeting held in the Cnorlton Town Hall, on Saturday evening, Dr. Pank- burst made a statement as to the course it his intention to pursue at the general election. The Mayor (Mr. Alderman Hopkinson) received the writ calling upon him to take the official steps neceseary in the election of a successor to the late Mr. Hugh Birley, the Conservatative representative of that city. The Mayor has fixed Saturday next as the day on which nominations may be made, and the following Thursday, the 4th proximo, for the polling.
i REIGN INTELIAGENIE.

Mr. Edgar Vincent has accepted the post of financial ad- viser to the Egyptisn Government. It is reported from Pretoria that the chiefs Mampoer and Mapoch have been sentenced to death by the Boers. Mr. Edgar Vincent's acceptance of the post of financial adviser was notified to the Egyptian Government on Tues- day. A report has reached th 3 Mauritius from Madagascar that the llovas have recaptured all their positions on the west coast.
Cardinal Manning is expeeed shortly at the Vatican, to discuss among other questions the establishment of a Catholic University in Lon4on. _

The Sultan's berat, approving of the appointment of Sir Evelyn Baring as British diplomatic agent and consul- general in Egypt, has arrived at Cairo. RAILWAY COLLISION IN FRANCE—A train coming from Arcachon, on Monday morning, ran into the Bayonne ex- press at the Saint Jean Station. Fifteen of the passengers were slightly injured, but a post office employe was seriously hurt. LORD COLERIDGE IN AMERICA. —Lord Coleridge was entertained on Tuesday night at Chicago, as the guest of the bar and the principal citizens. The company numbered over 350, and Lord Coleridge had an enthusiastic reception, which he acknowledged in a graceful speech. GERMANY AND THE VATICAN.—The Prussian bishops who have been expelled from their dioceses have been au- thoris.ed by the Vatican to negotiate with the Government under certain conditions with a view of being allowed to return. Doubts are, however, entertained here regarding the success of the negotiations. Rua I'ACHA.—No small importance is attached la the diplomatic circles of Cairo to the almost unanimous election of Riaz Pacha, on Saturday, to the Egyptian Legislative Council, as the high popularity of the ex•minister. of which it is an evidence, is attributed to his having quitted office in consequence of his disagreement with the Sultan. THE KING OF SPAIN AND GERMANY.—Speaking at the State banduet at Homburg, the King of Spain expressed the pleasure which it had given him to become acquainted with the German army. It is thought that the speech may be taken as confirming the statements made, with all appear- ance of authority, that his Majesty has resolved to join the Mil-European Alliance. INTERNATIONAL SANITARY CODES.—AII the Powers, according to a telegram from Rome, have signified their adheson to the propssal of the Italian Government to summon a conference at Rome, with the object of making sanitary regulations and the drawing up of international sanitary codes. Signor Mancini, Minister for Foreign Affairs, will shmtly address a circular to the Powers on the subject. RAILWAY DISASTER ON THE COTINENT.—A despatch from Kufstein states that a collision occurred on Wednes- day afternoon near that place between an express and a goods train owing to a mistake made by the pointsman. The engine of the express train was greatly shattered, and many of the passengers were braised and shaken. The goods train, which was loaded with casks containing spirit, caught are. TIM PRINCE or BCLGARIA.—A Reuter's telegram from Berlin states that during his stay there the Prince of Bul- garia freely expressed his wish to renounce the throne and return to Germany. He told some of his former comrades in the German army that the state of affairs in Bulgaria is often almost unbearable, and that probably in the end he would be forced to leave the country. Tim a JESCITS.—Tbere are at the present time assembled in Rome Jesuits representing all provinces of the order from every part of the world, who have come here in order to elect a vicar-, who shall eventually succeed to the office of general of the Society of Jesus. Father Becks, the present general, is anxious, owing to his advanced age, that his successor should be appointed. OUTRAGE BY AN IRISHMAN AT A BRITISH CONSULATE.— A man named John Feeny, a.n Irishman. entered the outer room of the British Consulate at New York, on Tuesday, and, drawing a seven-chambered revolver, fired two shots apparently without any definite aim. No one was hurt. The man has a sickly appearance, and is about 26 years of age. He wa's arrested. He had recently been discharged from the hospital at Buffalo, and declared that he had come purposely from Canada to kill the Consul, who had been libelling him. The prisoner is evidently of unsound mind. Tim SMYRNA COASTING TRADE.—Reuter's Athen's corres- pondent telegraphs that, according to a report which has reached there from Constantinople, Mr. Wyndham, the British chargé d'affaires, has addreiseda remonstrance to the Porte against the monopoly in the Smyrna coasting trade granted to a Turkish ehiisowner, and has claimed the same privileges for English ships as are enjoyed by Turkish ves- sels. He has also informed the Turkish Government that British trade with Turkey has been brought to a standstill on accennt of the uncertainty existing with regard to the tariff, and has re-affirmed the right of England to the most favoured nation treatment. THE SI,AYE TRADE IN MOROCCO —lt is stated that the slave trade in Moroce) is as brisk as ever. Since the second week in April of this year seventy-one slaves have been sold in the market place in Tangier, and many others privately. A correspondent at Casablanca, the place at which a number of girls were publicly flogged, writes that a dealer in slaves arrived there recently, and drove what he calls a herd of them through the streets like cattle, offering them for sale. They included boys and girls from eight years of age upwards, and men and women between the ages of eighteen and forty. Several of the children, it was ascertained, had been kidnapped from their native villages.

CRIME IN TIPPERARY. —.Notices appear in Tuesday night's Dublin Gazette stating that five townlands in the County Tipperary, in conscroence of the existence of out- rage in them, require additional constabulary. DISASTROUS FIRE AT SLIGO.—An extensive bobbin fac- tory and saw mills at blip were burnt down on Tuesday night. The da:nage amounts to several thousands Of pounds, and a large number of the workpeople are thrown

idle. -TnE Lone) LIEUTENANT left Dublin on Saturday on a visit to the North. His Excellency before going attended a meeting of the Privy Council, at which important busi- ness was transacted. Sir Edward Sullivan, Master of Rolls, was sworn in as Lord Chancellor. THE LABOURERS' DWELLINGS ACT.—At tbe North Dublin Union Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, Mr. M‘Mahon, the Nationalist candidate far Limerick, suc- ceeded in carrying a motion to obtain the necessary forms for putting the Labourers' Dwellings Act into operation. SIR S. NORTIICOTE'S VISIT TO IRELAND.—A meeting of the Conservatiws of Newry, held on Monday evening, adopted an address to Sir Stafford Northcote, on the occa- sion of his visit to the North of Ireland, and appointed a deputation, including Mr. Thompson, M.P., to make the present. CAPTAIN Bovoyrr's POPULARITY.—A Claremorris cor- respondent states that Captain Boycott held a ceurt in that town on Tuesday for the collection of his rents. All the tenlnts were loud in their praise of him as he allowed them their fixed rents since the time of the service of their I notices. Carrus Disxase is now rapidly abating in Ireland. The new outbreaks last week show a decrease of 129 compared with the previous seven days ; while the decrease in the total number of animals attacked was nearly 3,000, only nine of the animals died and four were killed, while 10,693 recovered, showing a mild form of disease. A Youvuran 13loaxisr.—At Dublin Police Court, a girl named Bridgfoot, aged 18, was charged with bigamy, having married a man named Kavanagh, her husband, a soldier, being alive in England. The prisoner admitted the offence, and said she had committed it as her husband bad told her never to expect to see him again. She was sent for trial. ATTACK ON A LADY BY A DISCHARGED PRISONER.-011 Tuesday night a desperate attack was made upon Miss Laird, of Limerick, by a discharged soldier named King, who was discharged from Nenagh Gaol on Tuesday morning,after undergoing two years' hard labour for stealing from Gal- way Barracks and supplying to Fenians 30 rifles. King has been arrested. TatuntnaNG A Winow.—At Billyhaunis, Ballinlough, county Roscommon, a man named Flynn was on Wednesday arrested for having on the previous night broken the door of a widow's house, and placed on the threshold a scooped turnip with a light inside resembling a human head. The woman is suffering from the shock. The prisoner was re- manded without bail. THE CHARGE AGAINST k COLONEL'S SON.—The young gentleman named Partridge, the son of a colonel, and who, having failed in his examination, recently enlisted as a soldier, was again charged at Dublin, on Wednesday, with stealing a clarinet, belonging to a college student. The magistrate, not wishing to ruin the defendant for life. con- victed him of illegal possession, and imposed a fine of £2 103. which was at once paid. AN ENCYCLICAL Or THE POPE WAS read in the Roman Catholic chapels on Sunday referring to the institution of the Rosary in honour of the Blessed Virgin in the 12th cen- tury, as having enabled the Papal aethority to crush the Albigensian heretics afterwards, and enjoining the faithful to devote the whole of the month of October to the cele- bration of the Rosary with a view to check the flow of • infidel and social disorder throughout the world. DEATHS FROM DISUSED MEAT—The inquest on the bodies of Patrick Farlong and James Whelan, who died from poisoning, caused by eating diseased meat supplied to them whilst employed in harvest work by dr. Leigh, J.P., of Rose Garland, county Wexford, was concluded on Saturday. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the evidence. About forty other persons who were affected by partaking of the same food have recovered.

exaa-TANT CONDUCT or A LADY.—Tnformation reached . nobin, on ,:tealay, of a.gallant rescue front drowning at Grevstones. a little girl was bathing with her French governess a a•ave carried her away, and she was rapidly being carried out u u ' sea. MURDEROUS AFFRA.V.—A murderous affray is reported from Cloninore, in the north•east of county Tipperary. The combatants, all named Vitzpatrick, were eight or nine in numLer, there being on one side the uncle, aunt, and three or four cousins, and on the other three brothers, sons of a widow, who were attacked, the quarrel ari!ing, out of a long- standing agrarian diipute. A gun, four-pronged pitchforks, and a turf spade were among the weapons handled by the attacking party. In the first place dogs were set upon the three brothers, who, however, drove the brutes off ; then a desperate encounter took place, in which one of the widow's sons Lawrence, was shot in the ribs by his uncle, and the other brothers were wounded with pitchforks. All six astaii, ante were arrested by the police, and were taken before a magistrate and remanded. The young man, Lawrence Fitz- patrick, lies in a precarious condition. NATIONiCL LEAGUE MEETINGS.—A largely attended meet- ing, convened by the local branch of the National League, was held at Tullow, County Carlow, on Sunday, at which Mr. Biggar, M.P., Mr. Gray, M.P., and the Lard Mayor of Dublin, M.P., were present. Mr. Biggar, in supporting resolutians calling for self-government for Ireland and amended land laws, said they had been told recently that they would receive home rule for Ireland, because Mr. Herbert Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain had intimated so much, and the latter had said something in favour of it; but he (Mr. Biggar) warned his hearers that those were men who would soon eat promises if they got the chance. He looked upon the settlement of the land question as impossi- ble until they had the land parcelled out at prairie value, the payment of the purchase money extending over a term of years. In conclusion, he remarked that of course be should have to speak against outrage, but at the same time if a member of the league took land from which another had been eviated, he thought he ought to be asked to cease to be a member, and he thought he was a man with whom he should not be inclined to associate. The proper way was to keep them outside in their social arrange- ments, and to some extent in their business arrangements. A meeting was held at Bandon, on Sunday, for the pur- pose of establishing a branch of the Irish National League. About 2,000 persons attended, the principal speakers being Messrs. J. P. 0 Connor, M.P., and T. D. Sullivan, M.P. Re- solutions were passed expressingconfidence in the Irish Par- liammtary party, declaring the Land Act of lt4Bl insuffi- cient, and demanding the establishment of a peasant pro- prietary. Mr: Sullivan declared that the Irish party would never rest until they bed obtained the land for the people who tilled it. Mr. O'Connor said they had already dealt heavy strokes at the vicious system of landlordism, but nothing short of its extirpation from the country and the restoration of the'r native Parliament would satisfy them. —On Tuesday, in spite of the Orange warnings, Mr. Par- nell's party commenced their campaign in the County Tyrone. The meetings were held at Pomeroy and Stra- bane.

DARESBURY LLCENSING SESSIONS. The adjourned licensing sessions were held in the Sessions House, Daresbury, on Tuesday, before Mr. Edward Greenall, Mr. Rotrrt Pierpoint, and Mr. James Marson. OUTRAGE BY A RUNCORN GAME- KEEPER. A FRODSHAM COMPLAINANT. At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magis- trates were engaged for some hours hearing a charge of assault brought by a young man named William Walker, who lives with his father at Alvanley, near Frodsham, against James Turner, a gamekeeper in the employ of Mr. Brundrit, of Runcorn.—Mr. Dickson, solicitor, of North- wich, who appeared for complainant, stated that on the 27th of August his client, who is a cripple and subject to epileptic fits, went on the Cliff at Alvanley, on land belong- ing to the Earl of Haddington, for the purpose of cutting ferns for bedding cattle, a privilege which Mr. Dickson said had been enjoyed by the inhabitants of that neighbourhood for many 'years. The complainant was met by the game- keeper, who asked him what he was doing there, and why he did not go further up; and without further preface he threw the complainant on the ground, got astride of him, and put his knee into the poor fellow's ribs, the result being that one of his ribs was broken and severe hemorrhage ensued. blood gushing from his mouth and nostrils. After severely beating the young fellow' striking him on the head and giving him a black eye, he dragged him to the edge of the cop and pitched taim over, complainant rolling down into the road. He was then allowed to go home, where he presented himself in a most deplorable condition. Dr. Robinson was called in, and complainant was under his hands for some time.—The fur- ther hearing of the case was then stopped in a peculiar manner, Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, of Nurthwich, en behalf of the defendant, taking the preliminary objection that the matter involved a question of right, and therefore ousted the jurisdiction of the magistrates. He said that if the in- habitants of the district claimed the right to get ferns upon that land it would make a serious difference to the Earl of Haddington and to Mr. Brundrit who had the right of shoot- ing there.—Mr. Dickson, on behalf of the complainant, said he must insist upon the right of the defendant to get ferns there, which he had done since his boyhood.—The keeper (Turner) was then c illed, and stated that the place where the affair occurred was not near the road, as had been alleged on behalf of the complainant, but that it was upon an enclosed wood. This wood was a pheasant preserve, and the defendant was mowing down the cover for the birds.— Both sides declining to waive the nu,stion of right, the Chairman of the bench, while expressing the feeling of the bench that it seemed castrary to common sense that so seri- ous an alleged case of injury should not be within their jurisdiction merely because the question of right was involved, said it was no use going on with the matter as the law stood. The question would have to be decided in another court.

RUNCOIN SCIENCE SCHOOL (449). The annual meeting of this school was held in the directors' coom at the Gas Works on Monday. There was a good attendance of young mm, and Mr. J. R. Fritn occu- pied the chair. Mr. Simkin and Mr. Knowles, the teachers, and Mr. Pope, the secretary, were also present.—The Cuain- MAN said he was pleased to meet the students, and to have the pleasure of distributing the prizes and certificates they had succeeded in obtaining. He was quite sure the the study of scientific subjects was beneficial, far above the value of prizes or certificates, in the habits of steadiness, and thirst for knowledge acqoired. After some further observations, Mr. Frith said he should be glad at some future time to show the students of the school there the gas works, and describe the cons!ruction of the plant, which would be interesting to the Building Class, and explain the process of the manufacture of gas, which would be interesting to the Chemistry Class. Mr. Frith then distiibuted the prizes, a list of which has appeared in The Ezaminer, making a few appropriate remarks to each recipient,—Mr. POPE gave a few interesting facts with regard to the school. He said he had compared the success of the Runcorn school with the average results throughout the country. The comparison was very favourable. Although in building construction the success of the school was 2 per cent. below the average, ' in chemistry the results were about 15 per cent. above. He pointed out to those present that the payment the teachers ' ' received for their labour depended upon the attention they paid to the teachers directions. The school was self-sup- porting; no outside help being asked for, and the fee of 3s. was not used for the salaries of the teachers. lithe students failed to pass the ex tminations, the teachers only received a very small fee, *fact which ought to spur those who entered the classes to exert themselves to the utmost.—Mr. Sams; explained the scope of teaching in building con- struction, and expressed his satisfaction at the students' work for the past two years.—Mr. KteowLEs defined the range of the teaching in chemistry—elementary and advanced.—A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the directors of the Gas Company, and to Mr. J. R. and Mr. J. N. Frith, for allowing the school the use of a room, and preparing it for the students' reception. It was observed that this generous provision was a valuable contribution to the usefulness of the school, greatly reducing its expenses. The room is used two or three nights each week for six months in each year free of rent, and no charge is made for tire and gas —Mr. J. 11. FRITH suitably acknowledged the vote, observing that he was glad to hear someone speak well of the directors of the gas company. who, he was sure, would have the heartiest satisfaction in allowing the school the use of the room for another session.—We may state that it is proposed, if sufficient students are enrolled, to teach the following subjects during the coming winter :—Praotical, plane, and solid geometry, building construction, machine construction and drawing, and inorganic chemistry (theoretictl). In connection with the city of London Guilds Institute there will be a class in alkali manufacture, and the allied branches conducted by Mr. Knowles. This class will meet in the laboratory at Camden works. It is also con- templated to start a class in carpentry and joinery in con- nection with the same institute if sufficient students can be found. _ _

THOMAS'S SICK AND BURIAL SoCIETY: ANNUAL TEA PARTY.—The annual tea party in connection with St. Thom is's Sick and Burial Society was held in Heath-lane schoolroom on Monday evening. About 60 of the members sat down to ;an excellent tea after which a ball was held, the masters of ceremonies being Messrs. E. Ogden and A. , Smith. The St. 'Thomas's Braes Band, under the conductor- , ship of Mr. Livesley, capitally rendered the various selec- tions of music. THE CHURCH SCUOOLS.—Iu consequence of the observa- tions made by Her Majeety's Inspector of Schools in his report on Farnworth elementary schools, respecting the dis- tance which separates the boys from the girls' schools, we understand that the vicar, the Rev. George Bond, contem- plates the erection of another block near the girls' school, and will shortly make an appeal to the public. TEMPERANCE ENTERTAINMENT. On Tuesday evening the senior branch of the Farnworth Church of England Temperance Society gave a capital entertainment before a crowded audience in the girls' schoolroom. The Rev. Jos. I Holden presided, and ma-de a few appropriate observations. Songs, recitations, and dialogues were given in good style by the members, and the glee party sang the Canadian boat song in capital style. The sketch, " A regular Tartar," was performed in a very creditable manner, and was heartily enjoyed by the company. FRODSHAM. In the class list of the Cambridge Local Examinations, just issued, the name of the Rev. E. H. Bamford, Trinity Manse, Frodsham, appears as a successful candidate. INDEPENLENT ORDER OE RECHABITES —The thirtieth high moveable conference of the Independent Order of Rechabites was held at Douglas, Isle of Man, on the 7th and Bth August last, and a report of the proceedings has been published in pamphlet form. The Frodsham Tent is in the Winsford and Norley district, and we gather from the re- port that Messrs. %V. Dutton and J. Alcock were the repre- sentatives. With regard to local tents, Warrington appears to have been stationary, as there were 89 financial members in 1831 and the same number in the year 1883. On the other hand, the Winsford and Norley district had 1,135 financial members in 1881, and 1,415 in the year 1883, or an increase of 230, a fact which speaks well for the efforts made by the officers of our local tents of the Irdependent Order of Rechabites. THE FRODSHAM CATTLE MARKET.—At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Peter Harrop had been sum- moned at the last sessions for neglecting to cleanse a sale- yard at Frodsham after the auction sale.—On the case being called, the Clerk said that the matter had been adjourned in order to allow Sergeant Johnson to report what had been done since attention was called to the matter.—The Sergeant stated that the present condition of the yard was such as complied with the orders of the local authority, the place had been thoroughly drained, and the floors laid with tiles in a satisfactory manner.—The Chairman said the arrange- ment on the last court day was that if the orders of the local authority were complied with there would be no neces- sity for the defendant to attend the present sitting, and as the police had made a favourable report the case would be dismissed on payment of enstg. FATAL FALL FROM A BEDROOM WINDOW AT RUNCORN.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the con net for the honor and fee (if' Halton, held an inquest at the Dev•mshire Hotel Runcorn, on Mon lay afternoon, touching the death of George Massey, aged two years, son of William Massey, g ocer. ff,•Bruns- wick-street, Runcorn. On Thursday nigbt the child slept with hs sister Esther Ann, who arose shortly after seven o'clock in Friday morning, leaving him in led. About a quarter to ei,ht she was in the kitchen when she heard a .110is2 as it s.imethin, were falling into the yard. but think- ing the hens were the cause she took no further notice. EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A CHILD AT ST. HELENS.

An inquest was held at St. Helens, on Thursday afternoon, by Mr. Barker. county coroner, on the body of Margaret J )hnson, 18 month old, who lived with her parents at 19, Doulton-street, but who on WAneslay afternoon met with her death in an extraordinary manner.—Elizabeth Johnson deposed that about ten minutes past three she left the house to go to a shop some little distance away, leaving a mug of dough, which was ready for baking, on the kitchen Seer. When she went out the child was playing in another part of the kitchen, and the dough was covered with paper. She was away about 20 minutes, and on returning found the child head-downwards in the dough, the paper having been removed. She took it out and screamed for assistance, upon which two neighbours came in, but the child was lifeless.— Sarah Timmins, a next door neighbour, said she ran in, and found the child dead in its mother's arms. She had heard the child screaming ten minutes previously, but did not know the mother was out. It w.,s probably about the time when the child was falling into the mug. She must first have polled the paper away, then have leaned over the side and fallen in.—Both this witness arid a Mrs. Middlekurst, who gave corroborative evider,u, spoke to the great distress the mother appeared to bs in.—The Coroner s4id this seemed to be purely an accident. It was a pity the mother had left the child alone, but nobody would anticipate anything of this kind occurrireg.--The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

Barker were also present and took part in the proceedings, was severely handled, and had his coat torn.—The prisoner LEIGH. was sent to gaol for one month for assaultiog the constable, The Leigh licensing justices on Monday refused to renew and for the damage to the uniform he was ordered to pay tiO off licenses, and there are now only 24 such licenses in 103. and costs, or 14 days' hard labour.—John Doyle was the division. , charged with being drunk and assaulting P.C. Barker.— The officer proved that whilst he was struggling with Fal- low, Doyle ca.ne up to the crowd, took a running kick at the officer's head, but happily missed him.—Prisoner was tined 20s. and costs for being cirtink and disorderly, but the. charge of assault was dismissed, the magistrates saying there was a doubt in the case.—P.C. Laing proved the. charge of drunkenessn.
OVER.

FAIR.—The annual onion 'fair of Over was a contrast to last year, when the amount of stock was, in variety and value, far in excess of previous years. The orders in council prohibiting the movement of cattle militated against a good supply of cattle. Of onions there was no lack, and prices were good. With people young and old the fair was as busy apparently as in most prosperous years. RELINFORD. - - -- •

TRAVELLING WITIIO-TJ-T- A TICKET.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, ma Monday, a young in in named James Arthur Catelv was charged with having travelled in a train on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway without having pi:viously obtained a ticket.—Mr. J. 0. Swift prose- cuted.—The defendant, who pleaded guilty, it appeared was a clerk employed at Wigan, but living at Ormskirk. On the evening of the 11th inst. ha was noticed to leave a train at Rainford Junction and to go around the rear of the train and attempt to leave the station as if he were not a traveller. He, however, on being closely questionrd, ad- mitted that he had travelled without a ticket.—A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed. ROBY.

HAAVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT ST. BAUTHOLO- MEW'S CHURCII.—The apptarance of Roby Church on Sunday last was most pleasing. The decoratim.s, whilst sufficiently ample to form a most effective feature of the service, did not tend to hide the architectural beauty of the edifice. The biptismal font, the first object to meet the eye, was richly surrounded at its base with fruit of every clime, grapes hung in clusters from the caps of the support- ing pillars, and in the basin more fruit and flowers were artistically grouped, the whole being surmounted by a corn stack in miniature. The pulpit was adorned with a mono- gram in wheat, and encircled with growing fruit. The lectern had a marvellously worked cross of plaited rye, reaching to the fluor. The floral devices in the choir and chancel were of high merit, whilst along the aisles and on the lintels of the windows were varied arrangements of wheat, barley, rye, oats, &c., the whole work having been done by ladies of the congregation, who, with the donors of fruit, desire to remain anonymous. The, grain, Ire., was given by the following farmers :—Messrs. Gore, Ashton, T. Rivington, Abbinett, and Bowling. There was a large con- gregation iu the morning. 'no sermon was preached by the vicar, the Rev. G. J. Banner, from the text, "The har- vest is the end of the world, and the re.pers are the angels " —St. Matthew 13th chapter, part of the 3Nh verse. In !he evening the Rev! F. G. Nett occupied the pulpit, preaching from St. Mark 4th chapter, 26 to 29Lh verses. The mualcal portion was well rendered by the organist and choir, under the direction of Mr. T. Hough. Spec,ally commendable, was the rendering of the anthem, "I will magnify Thee.' Order of service :—Morning: Voluntary, Pas:oral,Psalms of the day—Foster, Gauntlett ; To D i Dm, Garrett n F ; an- them, "I will magnify Thee," Goes; hymn 030; sermon; voluntary', Silver Trumpet. Evening: Psalms for the day, Rumbalt, Goodenough ; Mag,niticat, Burnett in F; Nunc Dimittis, Bennet in F ; anthem, "I will magnify Goes; hymn after sermon, 370, Fugue, Handel. Offertory eollections were taken on behalf of the choir fund, and is. Bd. was realised.

LECTURE ON SINGING AT RUNCORN. As an appropriate introduction to a curse of lemons on vocal music, which will be conducted during the coming winter by Mr. J. Ha'ford, the choirmaster of the Methodist Free Church, a lecture on " How to learn to sing" was, delivered in Ellesmere-etreet Schoolroom on alonday even- ing, by Mr. J. Graham, (I.T.S.C. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Craig, 8.A.. and there was a large and intelligent audience. The chapel choir occupied seats on the platform, and during the evening sang several pieces of music in capital style, the tasteful intonation being very observable as there was no accompaniment. Mr. J. H.,)1 ford conducted. In a few appropriate Observatione the Chairman introduced the lecturer, who said those people who could speak should be able to sing, and in 99 cases out of every 100, ordinary persons could sing. Except in cases of physical affliction, such as deafness and dumbness, there was a general ability to sing, and if people would only begin to cultivate the faculty of singing, no matter at what age, they must suc- ceed. By means of diagrame the lecturer described the physiological mechanism by which sourid was produced, ex-• plaining the construction and action of the diaphram, the lchest, the lungs, the throat, and the larynx. The mouth, ' he said, was not made to breathe throueh, but to speak, sing, and eat with. The nostrils were the proper channels to le.-eatiae through, and the impurities of the atmosphere, such. as ehemical gases, did not then reach and injure the lungs. If people when they left an heated room would only breathe through their nostrils instead of their month they wouldf not ran so much risk of bronchitis and such complaints, They heard people speaking of falsetto, head, chest, and throat voices, and he wondered they did not have a "boots' voice"—(laughter)—but be wished to point out that there were no such voices. Musical sounds were only produced by the vocal cods of the ithroat, and the changes in the voice were caused by the propergurseeof effect u"proen the gisteirss.'i'ngiTnhg. e position of the singers had a at e should stand upright with their chest forward, head up- right, giving "voice box," or " Adam's apple" plenty ot room to play in, and keep the mouth open-. He had had the pleasure of knowing Mr. llolford for some time, and last. winter he examined e dos of his to test their musical ability. They had only had one coarse of lessons, and they must not expect much from them that evening, but some ot them, who at the beginning knew nothing perhaps of music,. could now sing at first sight. To make sure that they had not seen the music before he had composed a little tune for them. Mr. Graham then banded a copy of the music to, each member of the choir, and they Rang it in a very credit- able manner. Tbe lecturer remarked how pleasant it would le! if each one of those pre-ent had that ability. It was _ waat everybody could have, and he hoped that they would I not go away with the idea that they had no voice. If they persisted in neglecting to cultivate their voices, they were I robbing themselves of the foretaaate of that heavenly joy when they would ell sing perfectly. 'The question arose which notation should they use. Music was the same what- ever the signs they used. A great mina- people seemed to have a repugnance to the tonic-sol fa notatiou, but although they had great uphill work with the Government and their inspector, it was now taught in about SCA per cent, of the schools in which ally nonvion was used. Dr. Steiner and Mr. McNaught were now appointed inspector and assistant inspector, and as these gentlem: n were enthusiastic tonic- sol-faists the system was adopted in hundreds of schools. Ile hoped Runcorn would not he bebindhand, but would go in for reading music like reading a newspaper. (Applause.) —The Chairman made a few complimentary observation& with reference to the lecturer, and the choir having sung another piece of music, the National Anthem was sung by the company and the meeting terminated. itr79d

LOCAL COMMISSIONS.—The London Gazette of Tuesday night contains the following :—War Office, Pall-mall, Sept. 25-3rd Battalion the King's (Liverpool Regiment), Cap- tain James Matthew 'Taylor resigns his commission; dated 26th instant. 4th Battalion the King's (Liverpool Regi- ment), Lieutenant Reginald Arnulph Aylmer from sth Battalion Royal Irish Regiment, to be captain; dated 26th instant. 21st Lancashire, Charles Balshaw to be quarter- master ;_ dated 26th instant.

THE 'MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL —At the meeting, on Wednesday, of the directors of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, it was mentioned that the Chamber had been invited by the secretary to the Ship Canal Provisional Committee to appoint a delegate to the conference which it is proposed to hold in the Mayor's Parlour at the Town Hall, on the 28th inst., " to.consider the future steps to b 0 taken in the promotion of the Manchester Ship Canal." The secretary was instructed to reply that the directors of the Chamber did not feel themselves authorised to appoint a delegate to represent the Chamber at the proposed confer- ence.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—BRSiDeSS generally in the iron trade of this district continues flat. There was a fairly good attendance on 'Change on Tuesday, but, except that for prompt specification there is still a pressure for finished iron, there is only a very limited amount of buying going on. The pig iron business con- tinues extremely dull. Nominally quotations are un- changed; Lancashire makers still hold for 458 to 45s 6d, less 21 for forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester, and for good brands of Lincolnshire, delivered Jere, 44s 10d to 458 10d, less 21 is still quoted. Only a very trifling business is, however, being done at these figures and to secure any orders of weight concessions of about 6:1 Per ton are necessary. Some of the makers decline to give way, but there are sellers ready to meet buyers, and orders are being taken at 6d under the quoted rates. In finished iron the weight of forward buying continues only small, bat makers are, in most cases, so full of present orders that any thing like quick delivery is difficult to obtain, from either the local or North Staffordshire houses, and prices are Erin on the basis of £6 2s 6d to .£6 5s as the minimum for ordinary bars, £6 12s 6d. for hoops, and £8 58 to £8 7s 6d for good qualities of sheets, delivered into this district.--- This has been the quietest September so far as the coal trade is concerned for several years past. The advance prices at the commencement of the month, and the warra weather which has since prevailed, have operated as a cheek upon the demand, and the month is closing with a decidedly less active trade than that with which it opened. The better classes of round coal have kept in moderately good demand, but inferior sorts and common round coal for general trade requirements have not been moving off so freely, whilst engine fuel has continued a drug, burgy being bad to sell, with supplies of sh.ck so much in excess of the demandthat stocks are accumulating heavily at many of the collieries. Quoted prices are without material alteration. At the pit mouth best coal averages 9s Cid to 10i, seconds 78 6d to common round coal 5s 9d to 6s 6d, burgy 4s 6d to 58, an good slack 3s 6d to 3s 9d per ton. The demand for we- ment has fallen off somewhat, and for delivery at the hie level, Liverpool, or the Garston docks, steam coal does eell average more than Is 9d to Ss per ton.
