div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.

A great gathering in support of the assimi- 4,atien of the county and borough franchise "k place at :Newcastle on Saturday, and it `Was so oederly and imposing in character and (:14 reasonable in its demand that we believe its influence will be felt throughout the length -11 d breadth of the land. Newcastle has al- Ways been to the fore in the political move- tents whiar have agitated the country since he Passing of the first Reform Bill • it is oted for its thorough Liberalism, if not 4adicalism and on the extension of the fran- „ellise to the counties it has now uttered no mncertain sound. We hope the excellent ex- trnPle which the borough has thus set may le followed by other constituencies, so that the franchise Government, when they come to deal with , e franchise question—as in all likelihood theyt will during next session—may feel that 7 have the people at their back. It is isuMated that fully 10,000 persons took part ill the procession which preceded the meet- but the number present on the Town t "r is variously estimated at from 20,000 h() 80,000, If, -however, there be any dis- Vte as to the precise number in attendance, ere cannot be any doubt about the enthu- ,a'9lll of the multitude. They came from far arla near, by road, rail, and river, at great 4erlfice of time and money, in order to tes- ti"' their sympathy .with the movement. A thel3-seated conviction that the cause which h eY had espoused was a just one could alone na..ve brought so many thousands together. Ir,"e noticeable feature about the gathering et,a'B this, that those taking part in it were OPosed almost exelusively of the artisan and I.ring class. The pitmen from the col-, of Northumberland and Durham th'erided, the ship carpenters and joiners from irb„e towns and villages contiguous to the eside shipbuilding yards were present, so were the men from the ironworks and 41341 e manufactories in the town ar; neighbourhood. Most of them it i; no doubt, still unenfranchised, but I 0 clearly their intention to remain so no harlßer than they can help They know they teV,,e right on their side, they are determined 'make it known, and to demand, if need be, vihat has so long been unjustly withheld from e„, The demonFtration was, in every re thoronAly representative of the true 41,11'' of the working classes, it will be th `me more significant in its influence, and 4re consequ-ntly exists the stronger rea..on the Government should take cognizance thj`• From six different platforms there was a';iutirnitted a resolution in favour of reform, sew, at each it was carried without a dis- til "ent voice. This resolution was to the b ett that the assimilation of the county and then.ugh franchise is imperatively called for in nterests of those who are now unjustly 11 rived of their political rights, and would, t'retanted, contribute powerfully to the pro- rest;i" arid prosperity of the country. The I)as;ntion further urged the Government to tlegt B,nch a measure of reform during the I)equ,essiun of Parliament; and it was sup- in :each case by vigorous speeches Nv 44f th Or tug men and from „several members jttilkarliament. The sagacious and talented kollscr Member for Newcastle, Mr. JoHm 4nra:Elt. was amongst the speakers, and he sive.to have been more than usually inci- Of to. riis observations respecting the House Ito adrds, of which, ,of course, Mr. MORLEY is ISR 714er, will be mad with interest as show- rttuat e direction in which public opinion ;Nett; necessarily tend in dealing with this Like most other members of Par- 111.r. mottLEY anticipates that next qtl 'll a county franchise bill will be intro- „ ced ule by the overnment, and seeing that bei:nBervative party are slowly but surely thea,,ecmverted to the necessity fo-.• such a mre becoming law, we think there can intr‘occietilY be two opinions that the bill, when 1411 h ced, will pass the Commons without c• acitiffi ulty. The question will then arise c - Will the Lords do ?" who, as Mr.

MORLEY pointedly remarks, "represent no constituency, whom no public body has chosen who has undergone no test of fitness, and who furnish no efficient guarantees of political responsibility." Mr. MORLEY sug- gests these august legislators should have the bill before Easter, for he thinks that the Lords will consider it necessary to throw it out at least once, in which event he advises Parliament should prorogue and in the fol- lowing Session send the bill to the Upper Chamber again. The Peers might then be expected, under pressure of public opinion, to let the bill pass. In that case Mr. MORLEY thinks the Session might proceed, and then in ins Parliament might deal with the exceedingly difficult business of redistribution, which, it must be ad-' mitted, is of as much importance, if not more, than the extension of the franchise. Without, indeed, a scheme of redistribution the extension of the franchise will be of very little value. We hope the dif- ficulty which is inevitable with the Upper Chamber will be got over as easily as Mr. MORLEY anticipates; but we are afraid he takes by far too sanguine a view. The Peers, know full well that any further enfranchise- ment of the people would be the prelude to an addition to the democratic element in the House of Commons, now by far too weak, and suzli an addition would undoubtedly sound the,deathAnell of the Lords as a legislative assembly. Some of those present at the meet- ing on Saturday can doubtless remember the struggle with the Lords in 1832. The Reform Bill had then to be wrung from these irrespon- sible legislators; and it was not until the KING had granted his permission to Earl GREY and to Lord BROUGHAM to create such .a number of peers as would be sufficient to ensure the passing of the bill that the House of Lords showed signs of yielding. It then dawned upon, them that if a number of new peers were created the influence of the Tory Opposition in the House would be en- tirely swamped, and in order to avoid this a number of their lordships decided to absent themselves during the passing of the measure. Thus did the Lords ob- struct the Reformers of 1832, and it is im- possible to point to a single good measure passed by a Liberal House of Commons since which they have not more or less obstructed and destroyed. It would be well if their lordships learned in time the lesson which demonstrations such as that of Saturday are intended to teach, and which lesson was ad- mirably put by Mr. MORLEY, viz., that "The time had come for the English people to be masters in their own house. They had a right to be, they were fit to be, and they had reso- lutely made up their minds that they would be."

PRONBSSOR ANDRE'S ALPINE CHOIR —As will be seen from advertisement this celebrated choir, which has just completed a three months' stay in Blackpool, is to give three of their unique entertainments in the Public Hall, Runcorn, commencing on Thursday evening next. The Rev. Canon Barclay is announced to preside on the first evening. Here, as in other places visited by the Choir, a large house may be expected to receive them.

CHANGE RINGING AT RIINCORN.-011 Sunday eight mem- bets of the Wrexham Society of Change Ringers visited Runcorn, and by the kindness of the Rev. Canon Barclay were permitted to use the bells of the Parish Church. In a little under three hours they rang bolt's 10-part peal of grandsire trebles (Reeves' variation) consisting of 5,040 changes, the execution being all that could be desired. The ringers were :—Treble 1 Alfred Lea, 2 R. W. Evans, 3 Robt. .Jones. 4 Joseph Williams, 5 John Ellis, 6 Thomas Newell, 7 Edward Rowland (conductor), tenor Edward Evans.

AN INDIGNANT WIDNES BUTCHER. —At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Christian B Aver, butcher, Waterloo. road, who bad been twice previously fined for having unjust weights, was fined 40s. and costs for having a pair of •counter scales with a loose adjusting ball.—The defendant went to the table, and flung the ameunt of the fine upon it with a bang, shouting out that there were three persons only fined 20s. and costs last week for a similar offence, while he was fined 40a. and costs.—He was told to behave himself, or he would be charged with committing a breach of the peace.—Putting his money bag in his pocket, and placing tric cap on his head with a defiant air, he then strode wisely out of the court.

OUTRAGEOUS CONDUCT OF A BEGGAR AT WIDNES.-s-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Jonathan Waves, a tramp. was brought before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and Mr. W. L. Evans, charged with twags drunk and disorderly, and also with begging. About RIFf-past six en Mondey evening the prisoner called at P.C. Barker's house and asked for money and food. The officer's wife refused his request, I whereupon he became very violent and threatenti to knock her head off. He then went into the street and created a disturbance. P.C. Barker followed him and took him into custody. He was very drunk.—Barker stated that he had had great complaints about the pr, soner, who had previously gone into .a house and threatened to kill a wonsan.—For being drunk the 'Bench fined the prisoner 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, and for begging he was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. RUNCORN ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.—These see- ' sions were held at Runcoin Police Court, on Monday, before ! Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Reynolds. The only license to be considered Was that belonging to the Swan Inn, which Mr. Husband, of Widnes, asked to be rem wed on behalf of the Halewood Brewery Company.—Superin- tendent Williamson obj-cted as he considered that the house being situated close to a full-licensed house was entirely un- necessary for the requirements of the n, ighbourhood.—Mr. Husband said the late tenant, Selin t 04+,4, had given up ' possession, and the Company propesed finding a tenant who would satisfy the police. They would te tve the license in . the hands of iSaperintendent Williamson until a suitable person was found.—euperintentlent Williamson still objec- ted, as Mrs. Ogden lived at the next house.—The Bench renewed the license on the understanding that Ogden should not again take possession of the premises. ! A NEW VIEW OF THE LAW AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. John Stranger was sum- moned ter wilfully damaging the property of Thos. Carter, of Farnworth.—The complainant, who wore the blue ribbon, said the defendant eln the evening of the 4th Sep- tember, created a disturbance at his house sevesal times, and about 11-0 p.m., when the family was in bed, broke three panes of glass, which were worth is. 9d.—The defendant did not deny breaking the windows, but asked their worships te look at the cause of his conduct. The complainant, who I was his brother-in-law, had kept his wife away from him at 1 his house for a month. He went to the complainant's house to fetch his wife, aud got nothing but abuse; and wes told she was not going to return.—Mr. Geskell, jun., said the de- fendant had no right to break the windows —Defendant re- plied that he thought that if a wife was in a place, the hus- band had a right to make a road to her either through the window or anything. (Laughter.)—The defendant was fined 6d. and costs 7s. 61, and ordered to pay the damage, Ise9d.—Defendaat : I shall have to apply to my wife for the money. She went away and took the money, and she is the cause of it. ROBBERY BY I DOMESTIC SERVANT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Emma Hughes, aged 1 15, as brought up on a charge of stealing a shawl and ' 2s. 64. in mosey, the property of Julius Pollock, furniture broker, IS, High-street, Runcorn.—The Prosecutor said the girl had been in his employ as domestic servant for three months. She left on Sunday morning, about seven o'clock. In consequence of what took place, he followed her and caught her in Queen-street. She was wearing the shawl produced, and said she was going to Warrington.—Esther 1 Pollock said that when she awoke on Sunday morning she i discovered that the prisoner bad gone. She found an old skirt of the prisoner's with a key in it. The key would un- lock her money box. There were two half-crowns in the box on Thursday, but on Sunday morning one was missing. —P.C. Wallace deposed to receiving the prisoner into cus- tody. He charged her with the robbery, and she replied, , "I only put it on. I was going to bring it back on Monday morning. I know nothing about the half-crown."--Mr. Brundrit said this was a bad beginning for a girl of her age, - and in the hope that it would be a warning to her, the itench would only fine her ss. and costs. PRESENTATION TO A. SCHOOLMISTRESS AT RUNCORN.—The singularly happy connection which has for several years existed between Miss Crews' head mistress of the infant department of the Wesleyan day schools, and the Methodist cause in Runcorn, will shortly be broken by the marriage of the lady with the Rev. Thomas Arrowsinith. The signal servieee which Miss Crews has rendered to the cause merited ; conspicuous recognition, and on Tuesday night the members of her society and Bible classes assembled in the Brunswick Sunday sehool, for the purpose of presenting her with a handsome marble clock and an illuminated address. Tea was provided for the members, and after the tables were cle tred, Mrs. Povah, in affectionate terms, referred to the love and esteem which knit them to Mies Crews, end asked her to ac- cept their present, assuring her of the earnest wishes of ti e rneenbers of her classes for her future welfare. Short speeches were also , delivered by the Revs. S. Mees and G. Hack, Messrs. Unsworth and Norman, each c7(ntleman referring in terms of the highest prsise to the sterling vality of :::-..r 1 services which Miss Crews had rendered while in Runcorn. Miss Crews quitably acknowledged the present, and the rest of the evening was spent in a Yfiry iutereeting and enjoyable manner.

div.head: EXAMINEB, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINEB, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.

MERSEY MISSIONS, Rtnecoax.—ln connection with these missions a harvest thanksgiving was held on Thursday evening, the room being tastefully decorated with cerials and flowers. The Rev. T. Patrick, M.A., chaplain to the Mersey Missions, was the'preacher. The choir, accompanied by the harmonium by Mr. George Howard, sang special harvest hymns. RELIGIOUS SERVICES AT THE THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN. —We understand that the committee of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association have made an application to Mr. E. J. Ottley for the use of the Theatre Royal, in which to hold Sunday services during the winter. The lessee generously granted the free use of the building, and ex- pressed his sympathy with the institution from which the application emanated. „,., la ALLEGED EXTENSIVE THEFT AT WIDNES.—AL yr nes, on Thursday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Myer Bir- man, traveller for Mark Steinart' wholesale watch manufacturer, Manchester, was remanded till Monday on a charge of stealing gold and silver watches and jewel- lery, valued at £lB5, under circumstances previously reported. We understand that after the hearing of the case the prosecutor visited the police office to ask for the man's discharge. BOWLING MATCH FOR £5 ASIDE AT RUNCORN.—OR Tues- day afternoon last Messrs. Yarwood and Birch met Messrs. Dainteth and Wright on the green attached to the South Bank Hotel, Runcorn, in order to bring to an issue their en- gagement to play a game of 51 up on level terms for £5 aside. The match eventually ended in favour of Dainteth and Wright by 22 points, the score at the conclusioa being, Dainteth and Wright. 51; Yarwood and Birch, 29. Mr. Samuel Johnson acted as referee. COMING OF AGE OF MR. T. W. SPEAKMAN, OF RUN- CORN:— On Friday last week, Mr. T. W. Speakman, eldest son of Mr. P. Speakman, of Grove House, Runcorn, attained his majority, and the interesting event was celebrated bv a tea party in Camden Sunday Schoch The teachers and officials of Camden and Nelson- street Sunday Schools, of which M. Speakman is secretary, had been invited, and about .40 persons sat down to an ex- cellent repast, prepared by Mr. T. Ba.eley. The teachers took advantage of the occasion to present Mr. Speakman with a token of their esteem and respect in the anew) of a ' handsome volume of travels, and the officials of Nelson- street branch presented him with a silver pencil ease as an earnest of the same good feeling. Felicitous speeches were given by Mr. P. Speakman, Mr. Beckett, Mr. Harrison, Mr. J. Bazley, Mr. W. J. Shore, and Mr. T. W. Speakman. ANOSHER WIDNES GROCER IN COURT.—Hugh N. Whar- ton, grocer, Church-street, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday on a charge of having unjust scales in his nossession.—Superintendent Barker said he visited the defendant's shop on Saturday. and found a pair of scales, the adjusting ball of which was loose and could be taken off at will. The scales were placed behind a heap of butter aril lard and other things, and persons purchasing anything could scarcely see whether they received the right weightor not. He might say that the defendant dealt largely in hams and bacon.—The defendant said his assistant would swear .that the scales had never been used without the ball. There were three or four times as many articles under a pound weighed on the scales as there were over that weight. For those small weights the scales would be no ase if the ball was removed.—The Bench flood the defendant 20s. and costs.

A SUSPICIOUS CASE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Johanngliefferan, a woman of no settled residence, was charged with stealing a shilling from the shop of William Thomas Miller, butcher, Ann-street West. About 10 o'clock the prisoner entered the shop and asked for a quarter of a pound of beef steak. She was served, and tendEred a shilling in payment. The youth in the shop gave her 9d change, and a girl named Sarah Ann Jones then came in for a pound of mutton chops. When he had served her he asked for her money, and she stated she had placed it ou the counter. Immediately afterwards the pri- soner left the shop and went to the Victoria Vaults, where the manager, Harry Webster, supplied her with a pint of beer and a glass of whiskey. She gave him a shilling. He returned her eta, and this'smount was found upon the pri- soner when arrested by P.C. MoMasters.—The Bench said It was a very suspicious case, but the evidence was not quite conclusive, and the prisoner was discharged. A MOONLIGHT FLIT AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty ?ea- eions, on Wednesday, Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, Runcorn, appeared on behalf of the United Cheshire and Lancashire Building Societies to prosecute Samuel Grennan on a charge of illegally and fraudulently removing goods to the value of £1 103 , with intent to defraud.—Mr. Lake stated that the societies were the owners of the house 17, Caroline- street, of which the defendant up to the 27th August, and for some time previously, was the tenant. Be, however, paid his rent very irregularly, and the arrears accumulated to £ll 6s. Daniel Lowry, the agent of the property, made frequent applications for the money, but a variety of ex- cuses was made by the defendant. Several times on the 27th August Lowry visited the house, and in the evening when he called fctr the last time, he was told that the defen- d tnt was at a funeral, but if he would see him in the morn- ing the money should be paid. Early on the morning of the 28th Lowry again went to the house, but only to find that the tenants were non est and the furniture removed. The societies prosecuted not so much for the money as to make an example of the defendant. Tenants so often made excuses of illness, funerals, or bad work, and trespassed on the good nature of their landlords, and when the rent was pressed for a "moonlight flit " took place.—Evidence haying been given in support of this statement, the de- fendant was ordered to pay double the value of the goods, viz, £3, and costa 7s. 61., or in default a month's hard labour.

Rutecoax CRICKET CLUB.—The season finished on Satur- day last, with a match between the married versus single members of the club; the attendance, however, of members being, owing to various causes, small, and, as will be seen, the married, though giving odds, won easily. If the results of the past season have not been brilliant, they may at all events be considered satisfactory, as the Ist eleven playing 10 matches, have been bracketed with six wins, six loses, one tie, and three drawn games, two in favo,t and one against, it being worthy of note that in no single instance was the Ist eleven beaten twice by any of its opponents. The clubs played have been on the whole of a good class, and the scores obtained against have been in most cases small, this being due to the good bowling, which has been the chief feature in the doings of the club, which possesses several of average merit, .while that of two or three has been really first rate; and the average of J. Wood will bear comparison with any similar record in the country, and is worth repro- ducing-viz., total number of overs bowled during the season 192, 62 of which were maidens, taking 79 wickets at a cost of 284 runs, or an average of 359 runs per wicket. RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB.

In consequence of the partial financial failure of the Madrigal Club last season, it was deemed advisable on Mon- day evening to hold a meeting of the subscribers to consider whether the club should dissolve or continue its labours for another winter. In the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, the president, Mr. P. Speakman occupied the chair. After a lengthy discussion pro and con, it was decided that the only musical society in the town should continue to exist, and endeavour to attract a greater share of public favour than it has hitherto done. Mr. J. Argent will, we understand, again nnziertake the duties of conductor, and the club will make its first appearance this winter in a ballad concert. At the end of last season there was a balance of about £7 due to the treasurer, Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, but that gentleman has generously wiped off the debt, and the best thanks of the meeting were accorded to him for his kind act.

div.head: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening, a meeting of ratepayers was held in Bethesda school-room to consider the correspondence between the overseers, the Local Government Board, and Runcsrn Improvement Commissioners, relative to removing the overseers' offices to Waterloo House, and to fix and de- termine, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, what rent shall be paid for the proposed offices. Mr. W. Handiey presided, and there was a moderate attendance of ratepavers.—After a prolonged discuseion, it was decided that the rent be increased from £3O to £35 per annum, for the offices at Waterloo House for the use of the overseers.— It was also resolved, on the motion of Mr. ROBERT SHAW seconded by Mr. MEADowcnoFr, that the cost of removing tite fittings from their present offices, and the provision of additional fixtures, not exceeding £2O. receive the approval of the ratepayers.—On the motion of Mr. Nortmax.'secondeds by Mr. Same', a vote of thanks was accorded the chairman and the meeting cancluded.
PROMOTION OF INSPECTOR BARNETT, OF WIDNES.

Mr. Inspector Barnett, of Widnes, has been promoted to the rank of Supaintendent of the County Police force at Ashton-under-Lyne, and in a few days he Will sever his con- nection with the town. While the law-abiding population of the town will hear with regret of Mr. Barnetes departure, thEy will rejoice at the advancement of an officer whose un- swerving attention to duty and skilful tact has stood the town in good stead on many an exciting occasion. During the seven years he has been in Widnes he has shown excep- tional aptitude in the detection of crime, and in the general management of police business, whilst in controlling a mob he was courageous and forbearing. He has received more than one acknowledgment of his ability from the magis- trates, who have ever shown the greatest ccntidence in his judgment and capabilities. Although a strict disciplarian, he has won the respect and esteen of His men, who regard him with admiration. One trait in his character is des.rv- ie'r of the fullest reuzeition, nn,! ill.t le his humane d'- in with the unfortunate people who sonlietime! come ' under his notice, the prisoners receiving considerat ion con- sistent with his duty. Supt. Barnett will be succeeded by Inspector Wood, of fit. Helens.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
PEACE AND WAR AT HOME AND ABROAD.- THIRD-CLASS TOURIST TICKETS. - PETER- BOROUGH CATHEDRAL.-SMUGGLING PASSEN- GERS.-SMUGGLER SAILORS.-BEAUTIES AND CARICATURISTS. -
LONDON, THURSDAY.

It is curious to see how at a time when the prospects of Europe—France perhaps excepted—are eminently peace- able, all the great Powers are nevertheless if not arming themselves, at least preparing to do so. It is, I suppose, an illustration of the motto ei ris pacem bellron pura. Italy is adding to her armour-clads, but that is merely carrying out a programme which she started years ago. This little king- dom, not so long since a scarcely more important power than Spain, has been resolutely constructing her fleet, and perhaps the most remarkable thing about the advance of Italy as a marine power is that her armour-clads are of home construction. Other great powers occasionally em- ploy England, or take a fly leaf out of as English book. , But from the first Caetellatoare has proved itself a regular Portsmouth. The Italian fleet c3ntains vessels second in tonnage only to our own, and there always rides at anchor in the harbour of Spezzia a guardshiro as fine as any that defend our coast stations. And now I see that France is going to reconstruct her navy. No European navy ueeds it more. France seems the country for starting great ideas and then abandoning them. In the first number of the Cornh ill Magazine, published three and twenty years ago, there was a very striking article showing the contrast between our vessel the Monitor and the French ship "La Gloire." France seemed then to have entered on a new career for her navy, but, in fact, she has not done much since. At last she undertakes these nautical preparations for peace. The world under- stands that England will follow in the lead of the other powers, and that we are to have fresh line of battle ships of even a store costly nature; at least, that is the suggestion of the statement, that the next financial year will show in- creased expenditure in the navy accounts. But there seems a general impression amongst sailors that these enormous vessels are almost as dangerous to the crew as to the enemy, and that no foe is so dangerous to them as a stiff gale of wind. One of the sailors of the Agincourt told me that she was "a brute in a storm," and we have several ships—the Minotaur, for instance—which are of the same build, and, I believe, of the same character. The one lessen of the hay harvest this year, now being rapidly gathered in, has been the development of third- class traffic. It has driven first-class quite out of the field, and yet it has yielded a larger revenue. It would be well if the Thames were not to be boundary between good vehicles and bad. It is singular that all the trains that go north of London are supplied with admirable third-class carriages, and those that go south with very poor ones. Of these the Brighton are the best, and, though it is hard to decide, I think the South-Eastern are the worst. There is another point connected with tourist traffic in which it Would be well for the public, and for the companies too, that uniformity were established. The Great Northern issue their tourist tickets in May, and they are available till the end of the year. The company, in effect, says to its cus- tomers, as we take your money in spring, we'll allow you to consult your own convenience as to when you shall take our conveyances, but we are bound to make up our accounts by the end of the year, so we must assign a limit, and we fix it at the 31st of December. Now, nothing can be more reassnable. Some of the other com- panies give their tourist tickets validity for two months, and if you outstay that time will recognise your payment as one on account, and allow you to complete your journey when you like on payment of the difference between what you have paid and the price of two tickets. This is fair, bet it is not liberal. It is the course adopted by the London and North-Western, and one or two other lines. But at least it is better than that of those other companies who make no allowance for overstayed tickets, and, finding the traveller at disadvantage, take all they can out of him.

I wonder whether the architect who has charge of Peter- borough Cathedral will have the courage to remove those four ugly turrets that used to disfigure the central tower. No one could look at the pile without being annoyed by those excrescences upon it. I believe they owe their origin to the perverse taste and obstinacy of a Dean of Peter- borough three generations ago. lam teld that when he put them up there was a great outcry against both him and them, and that he met it by eying that if he heard much more upon the subject he'd build them twice as high. Ber- nini, the very worst of Italian sculptors and architects, did very much the same thing for the Pantheon. Ile stuck two turrets one at either side of the portico close to the dome. The Italians called them Bernini's asses ears. They re- mained an impertinent disfigurement for two or three cen- turies, but in April this year they were pulled down amidst great acclamation. The structural repairs in Peterborough Cathedral just at present give a great opportunity to the existing De in and Chapter.

French plays are so popular in England and English plays that are popular are so largely taken from French originals, thati seems strange there should he so little interchange of dr,..natic hospitality. Once or twice English companies have gone to Paris, but always with failure. The English visitors preferred to see French plays, and the French residents did not care to see our English ones. The year of the great exhibition Mr. Sothern went over with Lord Dandreary, and was rewarded in his venture by a complete fiasco. I hear that in the coming winter Mr. Augustus Harris will try the effect of lavish management on the Parisians. The theatre selected is the Chiltelet‘ which is certainly the French Drury Lane. Only that the Chitelet is a miserable building inside, large, dirty, and uncomfortable, and that the scenery and ntzse en scene are as a rule very poor. Mr. Harris will take over " Youth " wherewith to make his dibut, and, if he is wise, he will take over his scenery as well. Where so large company, how- ever, has to be brought over, housed and fed, failure would be fell. Smuggling is looking up as one of the accomplishments of the British sailor. The watch that is kept at Dover and Folkestone, and other sea coast places, on passengers land- ing from the continent is practically a farce. It very rarely happens that a lady comes with a skirt improver ballanced with tobacco, or has a tin pocket to her dress filled with brandy or eau de Cologne. As a Frenchman said to sae the ether day, producing from his pocket a few very poor cigars of his own importation, "de Douane Anglaise n'est pas Mauvaise." Strictly speaking, there is very little searching, and still less collaring. I notice, however, at Folkestone, that whenever a pile of luggage reveals dual ownership the astute officers, if they so select a subject for investigation, always chose a lady's trunk. A portmanteau of a decide!), masculine outline passes free, unless its isolated position proves it to be a bachelor's belonging. In such cases the revenue officers, probably because they are married men, are incorruptibly rigid in their discipline. But when there are both portmanteau and trunk, the officers—no doubt for the same reason-- seem to know the habit of husbands, from the days of Adam downwards, to throw the blame upon their wives, and seek her trunk for cigars. " Mais la Donane n'est pas mauvaise," and it is clear that it is professional not amateur smuggling which it is sought to suppress.

Now this professional smuggling is mainly carried on, not by smugglers of the Disk Hotterwick type, but by re- spectable British and foreign sailors, and it is on board the mail boats that the practice most extensively prevails. I suppose ono reason is that as white sheep eat more than black sheep because there are more of them, so the Dover and Folkestone and Newhaven boats are more peccant be cause they have greater opportunities. The authorities are pretty well informed of what is going on, but it is very bard to detect. The contraband cargo may be hid in twenty different places on board the ship, and if the opportunity does not arise for landing it that makes no matter. It can remain where it is. It pays no rent. It crosses the Channel half a dozen times, till at last the fitting moment arrives. I believe to- bacco, unlike Madeira, does not benefit by sailing round the world, but the clgats so imported are destined to be con- sumed by no very great judges. I have stood on the Dover Pier.at midnight, and watched the revenue police keeping as accurate guard over the Ostend steamer as if it were a burglar who was expecting a rescue. Every sailor who went on shore was subjected to a very singular examination. They slapped him on the chest—as if he were a political p.ltient—to Lnsarz his iluhari cciibin3 to his j-rsey ; they looked in his boots, and made him lift his trousers to the knees. All kinds of dodges have been used to defraud the revenue. Oue man bad•an oil can that he Vas always

taking on shore. He took it so often that they got quite suspicious. That an was examined. It revealed nothing but pure, or rather probably impure, lamp .oil. Unfortu- nately a spring gave way, a false bottom opened, and the revenue oflicer'l sleeves were drenched with brandy. lam told that the Ostend bo:ft is especially great offender, much more so than the Calais, and the reason is that the Ostend steamer being Belgian, and flying the tricolour and not the Union sack, cannot be boarded with the same facility as ur.e of our ern 'vassals.

There has been a great show of beauties at Cnicago in the United States, and Lord Coleridge, who is due at that capi- tal, may hear a curious point of law argued and settled in regard to one of these fair ladies. She went in for competi- tion, taking her place as Beauty No. 9, and when the award came out the palm was given to her. Her name is Arabella Johnson, a slight, tall girl with what lady writers of fiction would call "an exquisitely classic profile," but what the coarse Chicagoers called a very long nose. They were quite discontected with the award. The beauty was, not only followed in the streets, but laughed at, ridiculed, and hooted. This unpopularity she attributes to a firm of caricaturists, who sought to make money out of her by selling caricature portraits. She is represented with a proboscis, instead of her lovely Greek nose. And so she has done what no Englishman would dare do. She has commenced an action for libel against her traducers. It is • a very inte-esting and novel point of law. With us our ' comic pwera seem to prove that, at all events, in the case of a public man there is no limit to the ridicule which may be provoked except what is fixed by the capacity of the caricaturist. I do not know whether it is otherwise in America, or whether a candidate at a beauty show might not be subject to the liabilities of a public woman. The case will come before the superior court, and English as well as American lawyers will be interested in the result.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held yesterday morning, at the. offices, Bridgewater-street. Mr. John Simpson presided, and there were present the Rev. Father PenneHey, T. Norman, J. Pritchard, P. Briscoe, and F. Rigby (clerk).

div.head: PRECEPT.
div.p: THE PRECEPT.

The CLERK said last year the balance in hand, on the 29th September, was £66 is. 21., and the Board drew a pre- cept for £2OO. But the Board had really a balance of £133 because the grant which was earned the previous year came In on the sth October. That day, after the payment of all claims, the Board would have a balance of £l5O. He had, therefore, drawn up a precept for £l5O, which struck him would be quite enough. The election came on in January, and in the event of there being no contest, the funds would be quite sufficient to cover the cost, while if there was a contest, the b •st course would be to issue a precept fer the sum spent. Mr. PRITCHARD moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, a motion that a precept for £l5O be issued to the overseers.

div.head: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.

THE ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the members of the Widnes Choral Society was held in the SiMql9 Cross Board School, on Thursd,iy evening. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. Carey, the vice-president of the society, was elected to the chair.

div.head: TILE ANNEAL REPORT.
div.p: TILE ANNEAL REPORT.

Mr. W. S. Callender, secretary and treasurer, read the annual report, as follows —"it: will be within the recollec- tion of the members that on the presentation of their an- nual report last year, your committee had the unpleasant duty of announcing that the season closed with a deficiency of £l5 7s. With this debt before them, and the evident fact that the hold of the society upon the public was on the wane, the committee entered upon the past season with con- siderable diffidence and distrust of the ultimate result. By strict econonly, but more especially the generous conduct of Mr. Argent, who for the firet half of the season gave his services, your committee are glad to be able to say that they have not only nearly met the ordinary expenditure of the season, but also succeeded in wiping off the debt with which the season opened. They must also not omit to mention that by donations and the payment of double fees several mem- bers of the society generally contributed to this desirable result. The society gave two concerts during the season, the opening one taking place on November 30th, the music rendered b,ing a number of glees. Miss Stewart, of Bir- kenhead, as on former occasions, most generously placed her services at the disposal of the society, and was ably assisted by Messrs. George Barton and Eaton Batty. The nett result of this concert NV LIS a balance to the good of £7 17s. 51. At the second and closing concert of April 12th the music selected for the first part was Rovaini's "Stabat Mater," and Macfarren's "May Day." Miss Stewart agein undertook the treble solos, and in cm- junction with Miss Frances Armstrong and Messrs. Tuer and Morel, succeeded in winning the approbation of a some- what critical audience. Your committee are glad to report also on this occasion a balance to the good of .£4 14s. 6d. Thu number of members on the books is 76, consisting of 36 ladies and 40 gentlemen. This is a reversal of last year's figures, the ladies then totalling 45 to the gentlemen 35. The committee sincerely trust that this season the members may again be reversed or at least equalised, as a full complement of the treble and alto parts is so essential to the success of the society. The average attendance of members at rehearsals has been about 45. Your com- mittee believe that the results of the season from one point of view have been a considerable gain to the musical knowledge of the members, and that the so- ciety has greatly contributed to the advancement of musical culture so far as the immediate neighbourhood is concerned. In conjunction with the kindred societies of Frodshain and Runcorn, and at the invitation of the latter, it was the pleasure of a number of the members to take part in what has since been by , co:npetent judges pronounced to be the most efficient ren- dering of "Judas Macabnis" ever submitted for approval to an audience in this neighbourhood. Your committee think that to Mr. Argent is especially due the sincere thanks of the society for his generosity at the commencement of the season and for his efficient labours as conductor. They would allo ask you to accord to the members of the Runcorn band a hearty vote of thanks for their kind assistance at the two concerts given during the season. Before closing this report your committee lay before you certain recommendations touching the Society for the future. They have decided to the best of their judgment, and should the members happily confirm these recommendations, they will, the committee think, greatly strengthen the position of an institution which has already (lone somewhat to foster the love of music in the town, and which is also one of the sadly too few humanizing agencies I in the district."

div.head: FINANCIAL REPORT.
div.p: FINANCIAL REPORT.

The financial rpport showed that the receipts during the season bad been £73, and the expenditure £75 is Bd, leav- ing a balancc of £2 is 8d against the society. The reports were unanimously adopted on thc m3tion f the CHAIRMAN.

div.head: AN IMPORTANT CHANGE.
div.p: AN IMPORTANT CHANGE.

The CHAIRMAN said that the first qt.eetion to be on- sidered was whether the society should go on or not. The committee had met on the previous Tnursday, and after carefully discussing the whole subject had Come pretty unanimously to the conclusions which Mr. Callender would lay before them. It must, he said; be obvious to everyone that it was impossible to continue the operations of the society on its present basis. The expenses were heavy, and the subscriptions net sufficient to meet them. They wanted the society to be entirely self•supporting, and some thought it should either be so or they should give it up.— The SECRETARY read the recommendations of the commitee, which were that the subscriptions should be raised to is 61 for the gents and 5s for the ladies, that Mr. Argent's services be continued, and that open rehearsals be substituted for concerts.—The CHAIRMAN said he thought the increased subscriptions would cover the ex- penses. He would not like to go round the neighbourhood asking for subscriptions. As to the open rehearsals, it was thought that it would be very nice if the society could work up some good music and then invite their friends to come and hear them without any charge. It would be a far better thing than having concerts and selling tickets. Mr. Argent had been consulted on the subject, and he concurred with the committee. Besides, he thought that if the open rehearsals were substituted for the concerts the society would not be ambitious to have a band, and they would Mot have to go about the neighbourhood with their hats in their hands ask- ing people to buy tickets.—After a little further discussion, it was decided, on the motion of Miss COOPER, seconded by Mrs. Boz.ro. that the society be continued, and that the member's subscriptions be raised to is. J. and ss. respect- ively.—lt was further decided, after a little opposition, '6 that open rehearsals be tried during the season, each mem- ber being entitled to bring two friends, and that tickets la. sold sufficient to fill the room." The motion was made by Mr. MORRISON, and seconded by Mr. KIDD.—It was also re- solved to open the season with a soiree. The president, Mr. M. Taylor; vice-president, Mr. Carey; secretary and treasurer, Mr. Cellander ; and librarian, Mr. T. Davies, were each re-elected to the respective offices. The meeting shortly afterwards separated.

THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION AT WIDNES. Having concluded their deliberations at Soutbport, on Wednesday, the members of the British Association organ- ised a number of excursions into the surrounding country on Thursday, and the manufacturers of Widnes invited a party, which was limited to a hundred persons, to visit several of the works of that town. About 50 gentlemen and ladies availed themselves of that invitation, and left South- port by special train at ten o'clock, on Thursday morning, arriving at the chemical centre an hour later. Every arrangement for the comfort and convenience of the visitors had been made, and in the event of wet weather, carriages were engaged to convey them to the various places. For- tunately, the weather, although some4vhat threatening, cm- tinued fine, and immediately on alighting on the platform, the visitors were conducted to the works of Messrs. W. Gos- sage and Son. West Bank, which ate the largest of their kind in the kingdom. Under the guidance of Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, the proprietors, the party spent a pleasant hour and a half inspecting the multi- farious processes through which soap passes before itreaches the hands of the shopkeepers for sale to the public. Mr. Gossage aud Mr. Timmis gave lucid descriptions of the various machinery, dzc., the greatest interest being shown in the cutting and stamping of the bars of soap by hand and steam power, and in the making of boxes by machinery. Three machines are used in the mak- ing of an ordinary "soap box," such as may be seen in any grocer's shop. The man in charge of the first machine, who is supplied with wood of the proper size and thickness, makes three sides of the box; by the second machine the fourth is fixed, and the bottom is nailed by the third. Men with hammer and nails then add a few "finishing touches," and the box is passed on to the packers, materials for the lid being placed inside. Messrs. Gossage manufacture 40 different kinds of soap, which they ship to every quarter of the globe. The party then adjourned to Lacey-street school- room, where Mr. J. W. Fowler, of the Central Hotel, had prepared a repast of a most enjoyable description, the table being set out in very creditable style, while the waiting was all that could be desired. Mr. F. H. Gossage occupied the post of honour, and there were present His Excellency Don Arturo de Marcoartu, Rev. George Bond, M.A. (Farnworth), Rev. Wm. C. Hudson, BA. (Oxon), Rev. R. Harper (Widnes), Major Gant, Captain Walter Cairns, Lieutenant H. V. Evans, Professor Frank Clowes, D.S.C., Dr. O'Sullivan (Burnley), Dr. A. T. Arthur, Messrs. Percy Bell, J. Carter Bell, Jno. Holden Davis (Widnes), Mrs. Eccles, Miss Mary Evans, Mr. and. Mrs. J. C. Evans, Mrs. E. A. Eccles, Messrs. John Fox,l Holbrook Gasket', jun. (Widnes), Mr. and Mrs. C. T. Hey- I cock, Messrs. Richard Howarth, John Fred. Heyes, B.A. (Oxon), A. Vernon Harcourt :(Oxon), Mark W. Hyde,l Lees, Moses, F. Mylina, Mathieson (Widnes), Hugo M. Muller, James L. Mnspratt (Widnes), Henry Foster Morley,' Miss Orbell, Mr. John Pye, Miss Patrick, Miss Parke, Messrs. Walter F. Pankhurst, Matthew Percy, J. C. Round, G. Robinson, J. C. Stevenson M.P.,Robt. div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

In two cases the children had been sent to the iudustri.il school.— The report was adopted.

That Miss Jane Clark be appointed head mistress of the Oakland-strect infant school, at a salary of MO per annum; the engage- ment to date from October let, 1833. That the following monitors be enaged at the :ileum's Cross school, viz., Bessie Glover, Ellen Beecham, Minnie Gillow, at salaries at the rate of £5 per annum; the engagements to date from October Ist, 1883. div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE FINANCE COMMITTEE.
This committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £299 17s. Bd., and the recommendation was adopted.

THE LOAN OF £9,643. A letter was real from the Local Government Board, dated 7th September, adverting to a letter from the Widme School Board stating that they had heard nothing from the Widnes Local Board as to the paving and digging at the Warrington-road schools. The Local Government Board stated that, having regard to the uncertainty that there would appear to be as to the time within which the unex- pended balance of the loan would be required for the works alluded to, and to the period which has elapsed since the amount was advanced, they considered that the balance should be remitted to the Public Works Loan Commissionere. —After a short discussion on the subject, it was decided to repay the balance, and not to proc:‘ed with the flagging-and paving.

div.head: INSTRUCTION OF MALE PUPIL TEACHERS.
div.p: THE INSTRUCTION OF MALE PUPIL TEACHERS.

A letter was read from Mr. Thorn is &lowan, master of the senior boys' department, Simms Cross school, calling attention to the subject of instruction to male teachers. He said it wee now 12 months since the teachers were informed 'that the pupil teachers were to be taught in central classes. Daring that time the males had been without the benefits of the collective teaching. The teachers would be glad to learn that the Board could see their way to offer the same advantages to the males as were at present offered to the females.—The subject was referred to the committee.

div.head: FAILURES AT TUE EXAMINATION.
div.p: FAILURES AT TUE EXAMINATION.

The Rev. Father FINEGAN Slid it appeared that four of the female pupil teachers had failed to pass their examina- tions. He did not wish to go into the details, but his ob- ject was to know if something could net be done tor the girls. It seemed that it was not from a want of competence that they bad not passed, but from a want of observance of the rules during the examination, and the Inspector bad come down and marked them as failures. Owing to being marked failures they would have to remain in the same position of pupil teachership as they did last year, and the little sum of money that would otherwise have accrued from the examination would be lost. If the Board could let them go on another year he thought it would soften the trouble and grief that these poor girls and their parents felt. The CLERK said he did not think the Board could deal with the affair because it was entirely in the hands of the Education De- partment. He believed that so far as the pupil teachers were concerned, the inspector was going to recommend that they serve the year over again, but there was no othcra.l in-., formation of the fact.—Tho Rev. Father FINEGAN said he wished the girls could go on and be advanced —The CHAIR- BUN said it was desirable that they should do so. Mr. BROCK said that at the same time the girls were to blame. —lt was eventually decided to memorialize the Education Department on the subject, in favour of the Rev. Father Finegan's suggestion. The Board shortly, afterwards rose.

div.head: :4etter to the Clitay.
div.p: :4etter to the Clitay.

OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. ' Sir,-1 was under the impression that Mr. Westbrook had exhausted himself, and it can only be because he so fully recognises the danger that our National Church is in that he again takes up the pen. I have more than once in this discussion tried to point oat—first, that the Radical portion of the community will not accept any historical or tradi- tional rights that Churchmen cairn to have in the phrase, "State Church ;" and, second, that it is in consequence of the slavish ignorance in which it has pleated the priests to keep the people that, now their eyes are opened, they are crying out for a complete severance of Church from State; • and also that the presumptuous and arrogant style of be- , haviour they adopt towards those outside the Church pale is simply so insultingly condescending that it is not to be borne with any longer. Mr. Westbrook sees fit to ignore all • these "abuses," and, sneaking in a shamefaced fashion by • them, finds rest for the sole of his foot upon the authority of a few Liberals who, he supposes, are favourable to the ceetinuance of a State Church. For him to quote Mr. Gladstone is satisfactory to me; quite so, I accept it as evidence that he does not believe the authorities of his own Church, who look upon the foremost statesman of this age as nothing but a "Jesuitical fabricator of un- truths." Remember, Mr. Gladstone has distinctly given us to understand that governments must act according to the requirements of the spirit of the age, and with this we can rest and be thankful, knowing full well that when the people insist, the government will give all that is asked for; and I have sufficient confidence in the people to be able to say that they will never ask for anything that will be to the national prejudice. And now to my friend's latest speci- men of defence; I had almost said, of special pleading. I wish to say nothing offensive, nothing to hurt my friend's feelings; but really this latest smacks. so much of priestly casuistry, that I am afraid this discussion mast has e led Mr. Westbrook to pore over books of a Dens or Ligurian character. "There never was a Church of Rome in England." Mr. Westbrook knows as well as any one that this is but a mere play on words—that Pope Gregory I. sent forty monks with Augustin at their head to convert the English Pagans, and from that day to Bluff Hal's was one continued system of subjection to the Romish Church. Indignity after indignity was heaped upon England's kings by the Pope, .even to the compelling our monarch to hold the Pope's stirrup. Excommunications and Bulls were issued without end for the sole purpose of humbling England's throne; and these fulminations were always supported by what Mr. Westbrook is pleased to call the English Church. Thomas Beckett, a wretch loaded with every honour by his royal master, having once gained all that his ambition could hope from the king, became one of the most captious and troublesome villains that ever dis- turbed with priestly pride the peace of kingdoms. When Stephen Langton was made Primate agaiast the wishes of John, the weak and wicked Lack-land, who had appointed John de Grey, this was another instance of Popish supre- macy. Innocent laid John's kingdom under the berm, churches were shut up, sacraments superseded, the dead were buried in the highways. In 1209 he excommunicated John, absolving all his subjects from their allegiance, and . when Randolph, the Pops legate, arrived in England, the king's courage broke down, and he submitted, promising to submit himself entirely to the judgment of the Pope, and as compensation for all the trouble he had given to the Pops instantly paid over eight thousand pounds. The Pope's legate kept England's crown and sceptre five whole days, and then returned them as a special favour of the Pope. Does this loek like waiting for the consent of the crown? I _ defend not the Popish Church. Eneland's blackest days were seen while under that mind-enslaving and most de- graiing priestly incubus. We only changed it for another of a less immoral character. During the years to which I have referred, fabulous sums of money were given and bequeathed to the Church—whether it be called of England or of Rome— for- messes and for' prayers for the dead. Large sums to day are received by her clergy, for which the duties via, praying for souls out of purgatory, expected, are not rendered. Our own parish church was, like the Grammar School, filched and diverted from her original purpose by the saintly and pious Reformers, and down to our day priestly intolerance, allied with venerable country squires, has managed to persuade the poor and ignorant to remain satisfied with the position in which it has pleased God to place him. I hope I have said enough to convince my friend that on the question of mere words we need not argue; but on historical facts he must either quote or accept the argument as rendered to him. And now one more reason for disestablishment, and I have done for the present. Oaf readers must be the judges as to who has right on his side. For a number of years past the English State Church has been torn by dissensions of a very ludicrous character. The Prayer Book has been brought forward as an authority for all sorts of childish and Popish acts; whether the priest should face the congregation or turn his back to them; whether the service should be intoned or read in a plain clear voice and manner; what sort of drapery the eriest should wrap him- self in—all these, and others equally silly and brein soften- ing, questions have been enough to cause the Church to stand out clearly as a laughing-stock for the whole world. Lord Beaconsfield attempted to deal with this in his "Public Worship Regulation Act," but failed completely. The clergy appealed to the Prayer Book for proof in aid of their right to take Protestants' money while doing Romish work, snd they are successful. Disestablish them, and the con- gregation of each church will have the right to move on to better mental pabulum; disendow the Church, and rsen of brains only will be selected to teach the pe.ple. No more shall we see men entering the Church on account of its kid glove respectability; no more will younger sons be ap- pointed to fat livings because they dare not degrade their family connections by entering trade.—Yours, Warrington, Sept., 1883. CLIFFORD DIX.

Sir,-1 suppose that a criticism is often easier than a per- formance, but I am led to think from some of the corres- pondence on this subject which has appeared lately in your columns, that there is little difficulty in supplying matter especiaily adapted for stricture. 'The incongruities pervad- ing most of the literature of the Liberationists seem to offer special attraction, and their greatest and best efforts end in illogical conclusions and an irresistible appeal to common- sense judgment for ridicule and censure. It is only just to say that every man, as a citizen, is entitled to an opinion on the affairs of the nation, but your corer spondent "Clifford ' Dix," in his reasoning on this subject, appears to have fol- lowed with studied steps the old lines above referred to. For example, in his first letter he says "the Reformation robbed the Romish Church of all the property Which the Protestant Church now cells her own ;" and further on he states that "no matter how the Church acquired it, no matter who left it to the clergy, it must be taken back again and given to the people," not to the Romish Church, mind ! but to "the people," by which he means "the nation." So that while "Clifford Dix " deprecates with highly moral dignity and disgust the rebbery from the ' Romish Church, he advocates a theft of the same property from the Protestant Church for distribution among all, in- cluding Theists, Atheists, Materialists, Agnostics, Jews, and lufi'els. I have no doubt that this division of spoil would take place in the exercise of that " moral right" which lot,berationists are so fond of preaching, but your readers will kindly note that a new kind of morality is here in- vented and warranted free from that pernicious element allied justice. No legislative expediency must overpass the boundary line of right and wrong." "Clifford Dix" also dis- qualifies the Prince of Wales as a holder of patronages be- cause he sh" Pigeons: we shall he told next that every man who ea's cheese is a mouse. While on the subject of the enor- inous wealth of the .Church, he further remarks that one•third of the !Itheable property in the king- dom has Came into existence 'during the last century. What of that? Betl presume this also must go with the Reform i ation plunder n the great moral distribu- tion. The Manchester &amour and Times of January 20th, 1879, says, "The origin of tithe was privapterivaan;tle voluntary." Glebe lands—" These endowments were not ' bestowal by the State they Were the offspring of 'liberality." Then " Cliff )rd Dix " tells tie that the Church is stagnant. Do not the figures supplied by your correspon- dent "H. J. Westbrook " prove the reverse. U ufortuencaatuelgye for Liberationists they do not always agree. Why? B I read in the British Quarterly Review, Jannary, 1831, that they gladly again recognise tne quickening of spiritual life 'in the Epieconal Church during the last 40 years." Again 4' Clifford Dix" refers to some " shot- comings" and abuses 'Connected with certain local churches, and suggests that these should remind "our Conservative friends of the necessity of attending to the beam in their own eyes." (Have I Clifford Dix's" permission to inform Mr. Gladstone; tie is also a Churchman but not a Conservative.) This h intended as a rebuke to " H. J. Westbrook's " retort and rreterence to a " few little episodes connected with a cer- .tain dissenting body ;" hut has " Clifford Dix" forgotten that be was the first to see a " beam," when he said " that -one of the main arguments relied on by Diesenters in their Crdeavours to disestablish the Chinch is that the person, look too much after the loevee and fishes." Perhaps the fact of his holding no " brief," as he say, for the defence

they pay for all their spiritual needs and operations, for doing which they may honourably boast; and for this reason, no one has the slightest right—much lees any priest or Churchman—to remark upon their internal affairs. On the part of my opponent it is all the more impertinent and censurable, because he cannot be ignorant of the piteous representations constantly made regarding the straighLued, if not poverty-stricken, condition of large numbers of the clergy. Then, too, if the Noncon- formists suffer bondage, as he alleges, it is self-imposed and therefore bearable; yours is a chafing, grinding, humiliating thraldom, fastened upon you by an alien power—a Parlia- ment comprising a gamut of the most discordant beliefs, views, notions, and also no beliefs whatever. How you kick, and writhe, and groan, under your bondage, the nation knows to its cost, by the odious diequiet that is occasioned and the malicious wranglings that incessantly prevail. Not only is night made hideous by them, but the glorious sun- lit day—not passing over the blessed Sabbath either. I have already taxed your space so largely that I hardly know how to ask for more. But this contention is weighty; and the transcendent importance of what I now wish to submit—important to thoughtful, honest, and truth-loving men—will be my plea for appending it. Let "Church- man," and such as he, heed to it—it is uttered by no foe of the Church; the writer is the Vice-Principal of St. Mary's Hall, Oxford, the Rev. Edwin Hatch. He says, "From the wider extension of tithes to all holders of land, whether originally Church land or not, it may be questioned whether the Church, from its ownpoint of view, has not lost more than it has gained ; for the fixing of a definite amount of offering tended to check the free flow of liberality. It substituted a tax for a gift, and in doing so it quenched the spirit of which it should have been the offepring. And from the appropriation to the clergy of that which was originally intended to be divided between the clergy and the poor, the Church has probably been a looser in a far more serious way, for it has ceased to be the great almoner, the central source from which the waters of charity were dispensed, as in its early ages, to the sick, the friendless, and the poor. Hospitals, infirmaries, and poor-houses have passed, for the most part, from her hands. Private individuals and voluntary societies, State institutions and municipal corporations, almost all of them outside the specially ecclesiastical organization, do the work which the Christian Churches, as such, once set themsely3s to do, and for which tithes and other offerings supplied the material means. To limit tithes to their ori- ginal area or to recall them to their original purpose, is as impossible as to toll back any other tide of history, and to reproduce with all its circumstances a bygone century. But the Church of modern times will be wise in time, and es- pecially wise in face of the vast hostile population which has grown up round its walls, if it learns to depend less and less upon that which, however innocent its origin, is now only a system of compulsory taxation, and depend more upon the memory and the practice of that earlier time when with no other material aid than the free offerings of its members, it humanized and Christianised a heathen world." The reading of this ought to make "Churchman" ashamed of his taunt against Nonconformists as to "the loaves and fishes "—the latter, you see, are turning as a canker in your vary vitals; you have clutched at tithes and endowments —" property, pruperty "—until they are shrinking and slipping from your grasp. When you might have converted your glebes and estates into mon3y you scorned that task; now you feel the pinch and stress of bad harvests, and are sorely distressed thereby. "sour grapes" is a taunt that rebounds, and should now be for ever buried. But so it is, that after men have persisted in ages of unfair, exclusive legislation they superciliously treat those wbom their arrogance or selfishness leads them to injure. And there is very littleeenspecteetion that such men will open their eyes to admit the evidence of truth until the course of events puts an end for ever to the national establisbment of sectarianism and the support of an anarchical Church. When that time arrives, Englishmen of all churches will then do full justice to each other's merits and excellence, charitably estimate each other's defects, and boldly resolve to borrow each other's fragments of apostolicity. Warrington, S)pt., 1883.

On the same subject your correpondent "Ob- server" seems to have had no instructions and to be likewise without a "brief," for he says, "Why Mr. Westbrook should have attacked the dissenting bodies at all is past my comprehension." Innocent surprise! So much for " Oba server's" comprehensive qualities. Your correspondent, "Dissenter," writing from Frodsham, in supporting the theory of "Loaves and fishes," asserted with sorrow " that he was troubled with rates for the support of this National Church," and" helped to pay the piper, but never got any of his music " ; and further complained that "never but once in six years had the Church of England clergyman called upon him to enquire after his body or soul," but being a workingman and unable to invite the minister of his parish to a "drawing room patty" w a "lawn tennis match," he presumed that was the reason. In your issue of the 25th ult., I asked "Dissenter " to name the "rates " which he stated "were collected regularly enough from him" for the support of the national Church, and enquired I also whether he intended to convey by his letter that the ! workingmea of his parish or neighbourhood were not visited Iby the minister of the Church of England. I say if "Die senter " does not wish to be so understood he had no right , to insinuate that a "drawing room party " is necessary to I secure the clerical services; and I repeat that the reason why "Dissenter " is not." called upon" by the clergy appears I obvious and justifiable. It is perhaps needless to add that "Dissenter" has not yet replied, and it may not be a very dangerous stretch of imagination to conclude that inability has something to do with his reserve. He also remarked in his letter that "cause and effect generally go togelher."
