"In love and war all things are fair," said one of the captors. e "And is this love," he asked, "or war ?" The pretty ones looked at each other with a laugh, but gave no other answer than by one putting a white rose into his coat, while the other demanded half-acrown. "Pardon me: you said a shilling!" "If six were taken! But I amereally almost ashamed to take half-a-crown from a person so distinguished!" "Let me be quick then, or the half-crown will get to half-a-sovereign !" said, Stephen, and he got out his purse. Both the sisters clapped their hands. "I thought he was only joking," said one. " Ala!" re- joined the previous speaker, "If now he would only take the whole half-dozen ae the same price, how happy he would make us both, wouldn't he? After that, nobody could re- sist us, wnatever price we chose to ask. Think of the glory before vtu, and pay the money quick! Six half-sovereigns —five pounds!" "We shall tell everybody of Mr. Fronde's generosity—we asked one shilling a piece, and he offers ten." " Ah, ladies, if I could only reckon up my store by the aid of your admirable system of arithmetic, I don't know what I mightn't do, what extremities of beneficence touch, when sotempted! But my arithmetic—confound it t—re- verses yours." 1 Stephen was, however, so tickled with the simplicity, or ' the something else of the young ladies, that declining the larger proposal he actually produced a half-sovereign, and , surrendered it to the thenceforth lawful owners, for his one ' rosebud. As be went his way a sadder and wiser man, mentally resolving that no thumbscrews, or other equally effective if less terrible looking instruments in such hands should wring even a sixpence more out of him, ho looked back, and saw Miss Vandeleur waiting and watching for the close of his business with the noblemaa's daughters. A thought struck him, and he at once acted on it. Another of the aristocratic Flower Brigade challenged him to buy a button hole. "But you see I am provided." "Oh, give me that for the Charity, and buy another for yourself." Stephen laughed to find that even in the little trick he meant to play Miss Vandeleur, he was helped by an uncon- scious fellow conspirator, • so gave his rose, paid his shill- ing, and was duly buttonholed again. And a third time the same trick was played, so that when he had gone the round, forgetting entirely the mission con- fided to him, he found himself returning alone, aad face to face with Miss Vandeleur; who waited to expose him in all the enormity of his behaviour, while yet unconscious of its true extent. But at the very moment of his return, the lest of the rose sellers, amused with Stephen's trick (for he had been obliged in her c Ise to put her up to it), told it to another, and that one to the lord's daughters, who presented to Miss Vandeleur the iden- tical rose Stephen had paid for so expensively; with lauda- tions on his genet ens character; and his plan of buying and giving away, and after all keeping only one for himself. If ever Miss Vandeleur's face suggested incipient and gathering thunder; if ever her eyes shot fl ashes of indignant and scathing lightning, it was now, as Stephen made full but not quite remorseful confession of his guilt; but de- clared he would really behave better for the fu'ure, if for- given. The Countess, who kept carefully in the back grennd, sit- ting by the Wheel of Fortune, which was reeerved for a while, saw something was wroag, met rose tq intervene. But Miss Vandeleur took care to antipate her, by con- doning the offence for the moment, and sending him a second time on his mission. But while he sought only to prey, he Wee himself inceo4% antly preyed upon, at least by atteSepts. A timid young lady ',tucked up boldness to invite his at- tention to A vase---a superb specimen of Staffordshire pot- tery ; but he stopped her before she could tempt him with the price, by saying— "l have promised a lady, under pressure of course, to buy nothing except from her." The timid young lady looked as though that had settled the question, and drew back. Net so a near neighbour, a baroness, who had overheard; but not seeming to have done so, challenged him to buy a water-colour drawing, and held it for him to see its beauty. , Her own face was so charming, and had in it so little of the boldness she assumed as a part to be played, and there- fore well played; her hair, dressed more exquisitely'than he had ever seen hair dressed before, in little curling knots close fitting to the shape of the beautifully-formed head, so attracted him, that if he looked at the picture at all, be realised only the image of the fair Baroness, and heard only the sweet, fascinating, but still womanly and modest tones of her voice. lie felt ashamed of the answer he must give, and which he did give—his pledge to buy only of one lady, pleading, "She asked me, insisted—promised on the one hand, and threatened en the other—so how could I resist? I sac- cumbed, and gave my word of honour." " That is my own painting," gently insinuated the Baroness; as though she had not caught the point of his logic. " Ah, that makes my ease ilarder stili," reniarked Stephen, with a half attempt at a sigh. "'But honou; ! My honour is pledged: and you would not have ma break faith with a lady ?" "And here's a hand screen, also of my work. Buy that for her, and see, that you did not consider such a purchase could possibly be an infringement of the compact." Stephen laughed as he replied, " I'm afraid she'd say I was a Jesuit; that I had broken faith with her, and would refuse after all to take the gift." " Still the merit and solace of the intention would be yours," persisted the Baroness. " And as to the picture, I'll take it back with pleasure, and so you will be deubly a benefactor of the charity !" Again Stephen laughed, as he said— " Ah, but my honour—my truthfulness, where would they be? I could not with any satisfactiou give even to charity a gift so contaminated. But I promise you, that as I have not yielded to you, I will not yield to anyone; or if I do, I'll come back for the screen, and express my re- morse for appearing even to listen to so charming an advocate for the charity, with se bard a heart." A sm le answered his parting bow, and the moment he had left her sent one of her satellites after him to see where he might come to a standstill, and so discover who was the goddess who had so ingeniously secured him beforehand, and to whom he had proved apparently so faithful. Other interruptions of the same kind Stephen fought through more easily, but they served so as to hinder him in his mission, that when again he came in sight of Miss Van- deleur he was alone, no victims in his train. But not so his task-mistress. Her name, her relations with the Herlaxtons, and her large fortune had got noised about, and her beauty and spirit did the rest. Stephen found her surrounded with young dandies and old beaux, to whom she was handing out single flowers at a guinea a ' piece; and though often appealed-to, as if seriously, for a month's credit, answered as seriously she would be happy to oblige them on any occasion but this. They were pertinacious in their questions, and Stephen, taking a position near enough to hear, but where he was concealed fro.n her, listened for Mime time to such dialogues as the following : " Don't you ask too much?" "Can't say, but I take no less." "Were they all made by you?" "No, but mostly by ladies of much more distinction and merit. And if lam obliged to bring out such facts I shall raise nay price. Consider: that to bring here such lovely things we have ransacked the world over—" . "In person ?" interrupted one. "In spirit, which is much better," she replied. "But not se expensive." - " I am no so sure, if the present moment is to be taken into account," rejoined Miss Vandeleur. Then there was a laugh at the last questioner's over- throw ; whe, however, not only joined in the mirth, but went on, delighted perhaps with punishment from such an execntiener. "Did you make any of them ?" "Some!' "Would you kindly oblige by individualising which ?" "I can refuse nothing to a good customer, but business first, pleasure afterwards." She held out one hand with a fairly well imitated flowee of the Stephanotis, in a pretty but by no means costly vase, and put the other forward for the money,

saying, "Five guineas!" and she got it. "Now then for Miss Vandeleur's own particular flower," said the buyer. She produced another Stephanotis, but altogether of a finer character— one that really rivalled the beauty, and even (through some artful contrivance) the scent of the ori- ginal, and said, "That is mine." It elicited universal admiration for the flower, and uni- versal mirth for the again discomfited purchaser of the pre- vious one. Professing his desire to buy Miss Vandeleur's, he offered in vain his own for half the price ;and then made a virtue of necessity, and gave it back to the Charity and its clever agent. What was the price of Miss Vandeleur's own artistic prb- duction was now asked by two or three voices. "It is really a high compliment you pay to me, even while I know your object is nine—toi improve the funds of the Charity. -Therefore, I shall not say one word in depre- ciation of all the fine things you might be inclined to think and say about my one poor offering, but simply propose to put it op to auction for the highest bidder." This was received with acclamation, and the previous Purchaser a little maliciously proposed, amid cries of "sham,," to begin with— "A guinea!" " Five !" said a quiet observer, who had not previously spoken. " Does the vase go with it? " asked a voice. "Of course ; but we'll sell the flower first," said Miss Vandeleur. Six---eight—ard ten guineas were offered, and still the fair hand did not fAi. "Coins," Ste said, " let's be generous, even though we deal with the funds of the Charity. The vase shall go with the next bid " "Twelve guineas!" oriel the previous purchaser; and so mad. peace with Miss Vandeleur, and carried away his pur• chase in triumph. But f•ir one circumstance Stephen would have enjoyed this exhibitien. It hid, however, for him a serious draw- back. Mies Vandeleur was, he thought, a good deal too profuse in her smiles to some of the young men that flut- tered their little wits about her.

div.head: SAD BATHING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD BATHING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

At the Devonshire Hotel, on Monday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstanees of the death of John Illidge, 11 years of age, son of Alfred Midge, a labourer, living at 31, Cawdor-street, Runcorn. After eating his dinner on Friday, Midge left home to play, telling his mother that he would return for his books in time for school. Although he had often been cautioned against bathing in the river, the boy proceeded to "No man's land," and the tide being on the flood, he, with a number of com- panions, undressed and entered the Mersey near Castle Rock. A flat had been " sanding " near the locality, and had left a large hole, which Illidge. who was unable to swim, desired one of his friends, named John Hill, aged twelve years, to show him. Hill did s but evidently in a frolicsome spirit. Illidge, instead of avoiding the place went into it, and then seizing Hill round the legs, climbed up his body until he was riding on his shoulders. He then fell backwards into the water, and Hill swam to the shore. A boy named Ed- ward %Forret], twelve years of age, seeing that Illidge WAR making attempts to stand upon his feet, but without success, swam to his aid, and standing almost up to ' the nostrils in water, endeavoured to pull Midge into a , shallow pot of the river. Illidge, however, was in the tidal current, which swept his feet off the sands, and Worrall was powerless to drag him away. He called to his companions on the bank, who were hurriedly putting on their clothes, to help him, but thy were frightened, and did not do so. Worrell then became alarmed for his own safety and swam to the chore. A boy named Whitehead called to Midge to come out of the water but he replied. "Oh, John, John, I can't," flung up his 1111119 and sank. The boys shouted out to a man on a flat that there was a boy drowning, but his only reply, so it was stated in evidence, was to curse them. The body of the unfortunate boy was found on the sands at Weston Point, on Saturday morning, by a man named Ueorge Clarke. In answer to a question from the Coroner, Hill said the reason he did not go to Worrall's aid when attempting to rescue the deceased, was because they were ton far away for him. He could not swim the distance. The jury p Isstd many encomiums upon the bravery of Worrall, and returned a verdict of " Ace:, dently drowned whilst bathing."

CHAPTER XX.—A COMPACT. Hearing accidentally from Mr. Caxton that be had left I Stephen and Miss Vandeleur in ~the library, the Countess had hastened thither; moved by the thought that something might be passing between the pair which would wonderfully lighten her difficulties, and which, it was just possible, her presence at a critical moment might make decisive. But when she was with them she could not but notice a certain constraint showing itself through their affected air of gaiety, and seeming readiness to enter into any kind of gossip—as if to keep her aloof from anything serious— affecting them. She accepted the position, and changed to an attitude that still had the same aim in view, to bring them nearer together. "Well, my dear, I have altered my mind about the Fancy Fair; and if it will really please you that I go there, then go I will." "I am so pleased." said Miss 'Vandeleur, kissing the Coun- I tees warmly. "And perhaps now a certain gentleman may spare me the many shafts of wit and satire he has been doubtless polishing to let fly at me, for going to such a frivolous place, on such frivolous business." I "That hardly represents the case, for I myself all the ! while intended to go," said Stephen. . "But you must not ask me to take any part," said the Countess. "I have no spirits for that kind of thing." "But which is the very kind of thing to give spirits. Why I already feel myself a sort of millionare in the cause and behalf of the charity," responded Miss Yandeleur. "And who can held feeling elevated at the prospect of such a pinnacle? Do come, my dear Countess, if only to see that Stephen does not incite me to cheat in delivering up the prizes from the Wheel of Fortune; or if he does, and I succumb to his naughty advances, then of course you I will interfere, and bring us both back to the paths of duty, and pecuniary, and all other sorts of ismocence." The Countess laughed heartily, then shook her head, and then yielded. But now Stephen had something to say, "I have forsworn gambling; how then can I undertake to turn a wheel for so nefarious a purpose, if that is the dignified post you are so good as to assign me ?" "Will you do it, sir, or not ?" demanded Miss Vande- leur ; "or must I apply in some other aad more dignified quarter?" She might not have meant an allusion to Lord Harlaxton, but Stephen thought she did; and while he disliked the remark for her own sake, he could not make up his mind to see them so brought together in public. "I consent, but am rather a pressed man than a volun- teer," hs replied. "But there is one condition!" "In favour of the pressed man then I hope, though his chance does not seem very promising." "It is this: That you promise ma that what you do buy you buy solely of me. You are my retainer, will be in all my secrets, and I can't think of you going about to en- courage other women, and setting a bad example generally to all the ladies and gentlemen I expect you to bring to my house of business." "May I go the length of buying a button hole from a lady." Mies Vandeleur looked at him with a grave deliberative air, then turning to the Countess, said, "I think we may accord that boon, though he does not go down on his knees to ask us." "I think we may," said the amused Countess. "Very well,l prorniee," f3M4 Stephen, "But don't, sir, let me see yon with more than one in your coat." "Your slave—since that appears to be his fate for the day—shall be found loyal." "And you shall be rewarded, as you may deserve," re- joined Miss Vandeleur, g-aciously. There the little group moved to go away and break up, the Countess' hopes once more reviving, even from such small encouragement as the last few minutes afforded.

div.head: CHAPTER XXI.—TwE Fewer FAIR.
div.p: CHAPTER XXI.—TwE Fewer FAIR.

Oddly as it may sound, Stephen had never yet attended one of these fashionable exhibitions of philanthropy. This was partly due to his dislike to what he heard of the ex- treme abandonment of all the ordinary reticence, and natural delicacy of the sex, to the business of money-making. A licensed saturnalia for the ladies he had once called it (when no ladies were present); while on another occasion hs had gone the extreme length of denouncing prominent memners of these bazaars, or fairs, as Social Brigands who were per- mitted to act without danger to themselves, the costly farce, entitled "Stand and Deliver! "

"But be had another—a more personal, and on the whole, probably a RION influential reason—he had no money to spare in such ways. He was therefore delighted to find that quite unconsciously Miss Vandelenr had re- moved that difficulty from his path; and that he need net spend a siagle shilling with her, while prepared with a shield to defend himself from all other predatory ladies. So that be went to the place of meeting—the Duke of Wellington's Riding School, Knightsbridge—in capital suirits; for he would be able to watch unsuspected Miss Vandeleur's proceedings, and especially bow she treated the gentlemen who were sure to fl )ck to her. For his attitude was still determinedly the sanse—to watch, and at last get to understand her thoroughly; taking care meantime not to commit himself, partly an considera- tion of his brother, but also in obedience to his secret mis- giving that she was too like him in the faults and deficien- cies he was inclining to take te heart, and to remedy; and therefore the last person he ought to marry, even though the path should be honourably open to woo her. At his entrance he saw her husilv engaged in the disposal of her flowers in all kinds of grac4ul and elegant vases. The hour being yet early, few visitors had arrived. He paused at some d'is.ance, unnoticed, to observe bow she went into the business, as though her heart and soul co- operated. _ _ .

Stephen could not but admire the rapidity with which the deft fingers formed one group after another, each one im- proving as she went on in the arrangement of colours, and in the display of characteristic forms. Pausing a moment to retire a little back, like an artist from his easel, to study critically the effect, she caught sight of Stephen, and a lively colour instantly suffused her face, to her own extreme annoyance. So unwelcome was it to its owner that it soon disap- peared, and with it the emotion and thoughts his appearance at a moment she happened not to be thinking cf him, had eslled forth.
She alvanvd with her accustomed frank, not to say audacious, rustin?r to him, and said aloud, as if for the benefit of two pretty girls, her next door neighbours, the daughters of Lord Magmus,-7-
, " Itemember our compact! You have promised to buy nothing from anybody but me."
"May I, if need be, mention what I am to receive as my part of the harg tin ?"

s The col.)ur again seemed to be rising to her cheek from his significant manner and tone, which brought back the incident of the Billiard R)ona : but her will was strong, she checked it as sht answered— I•

"Did you ever hear of a Kni;ht, on being admitted for the time to do service to a lady, bargaining like a huxter ?" "I think I have, bat I own he was not a favourable specimen of the great order of Chivalry." "Come, then ; be yourself the bright example !" "Your slave is all submission, on your own terms," said Stephen; with a gesture of his up-raised arms and hands that suggested he was salaaming to a mighty queen or prin- cess, and which was so received.

" That is well ; we are satktied, and now whit does the Honourable Stephen Chandos Fronde mean to buy from me, rot for my own sake, but for the sake of so inestimable a charity?" "Really, T have quite forgotten what charity. Do you happen to remember?" Miss Vancleleur could not restrain a hearty laugh at his cool impudence; and would have liked ta have given him a rejoinder in his own spirit, but visitors were fl3cking in, and business must be seen to. So she simply repeated the question, , "What de you mean to buy of me "Nothing " How is that ?" "I am too poor to offer a price commensurate with the interests of the charity, and the inestimable condescension of the charming lady who officiates; and, therefore prefer to stand apart entirely, and help others to fulfil my duty and their own by one and the some act." "Ah, that's all very flue!" "Perhaps it may comfort you if I 33Y when all your cue- tomers have gone home, and the Fair like other vanities is at its last gisp, and you are wondering what to do with the shabby and useless remainder, and you are ready to sell „at any price, perhaps I may bargain with you; and so without hurting my pocket set up some casterm enger for life by the precious gift." • " But if vou are going to be so shabby as regards your- self," said Mks Vandeleur, " I expect all the more devotion and self-sicritice through you as re,:ards others." Nothing," replied Stephen, " shall be too pitiful for them to take, or too costly for them to pay for,l if it rests with me, depend upon it. But you must be the true M4gician ; I only your insignificant helper. At your 'open sesame' I already see banks on all sides opening their coffers."

"If you se a banker kidnap him at any risk to begin with, and bring him here." So she sent him to make a round of the place, and in- veigle hy one artifice or another any of the gentlemen he found " dawdling " .bont any of the other stalls, to come to hers.

He went obediently, and Miss Vandeleur, notwithstand- ing her sense of the necessity of close attendance to busi- ness, watched his proceedings at the stall where the tw, pretty and somewhat fast daughters of Lord Magnus " im- pounded him" as he pathetically complained to them, by coming one on each side, and insisting on his purchasing half-a-doaen button holes for his coat, single but fresh buds, artistically yelled in maiden's hair fern, to set an example fur the good of the charity, and— Only a shilling each, white roses or red !" " Ah, ladi s, I am rotricted by the hard mistress I serve for the day to the purchase of a single oae.'?
TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT WOOL- WICH ARSENAL.

Woolwich had an experience on Monday morning the like of which no town in England ever had before. By some means, not yet explained, the rocket factory within the arsenal enclosure caught fire, and there was in it at the time a large number of war rockets of formidable dimensions. The largest were 6-inch rockets, carrying a solid iron bead weighing twelve pounds; and there was also a number of 24-pounders and projectiles of lighter construction. The flames spread rapidly, and in a quarter of an hour the rockets began to ignite and to fly in all directions. The scene was both grand and terrifying. Some of the missiles burst in mid-air, others shot to great distances, and as the fire increased they crashed out of the building in flights of a dozen to twenty at a time. This terrible bombardment lasted about an hour, but the casualties are fortunately confined to two deaths. Many marvellous escapes are, however. reported,stray rockets hav- ing travelled several miles in different directions. One fell into an infant school in Plumwead village, another partially wrecked a grocer's shop, whilst a third dropped into the pre- mises of a draper, in High-street, Woolwich, when many persens were in the shop, but non were injured. Some of the 24 pounder war rockets travelled five miles, the 16- pounders two miles, and the 9-pounders one mile. There was also a number of 6-inch rockets, which carry a solid iron head weighing 12Ibs. a distance-of eight miles. Many of the dangerous missiles went as far as Ilford, Charlton, El ith. and Eltham. One went through the arsenal wall, and another through the roof of the Old Forge, Royal Arsenal, where many men were employed. As soon as the danger was fully realised, the workmen were sent home to their wives and relatives anxiously awaiting them outside the three arsenal gates. The two persons killcd were employed examining and repainting the rockets when the explosion oc- curred in the shed, which was a store for war rockets re- turned from all parts of the world.—An official inquiry into the origin and circumstances of the explosion at the Royal Arsenal Rocket Factories was commenced at Woolwich on Tuesday. It is expected that the investigation will occupy several days. In the afternoon the Coroner for West Kent opened an inquest at the Town Hall, Woolwich. After the jury had viewed the bodies of the deceased and the site of the explosion, the injttiry was adjourned. The inquest on the bodies of the two men killed by the explosion of rockets at Woolwich Arsenal was brougkt to a close on Thursday. No evidence was given to account for the accident, and the jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and commended the action of the police and the officials of the arsenal.

The first meeting of the coursing season commenced to- day for Lancashire and Haydock Park, where the attend- ance was good—quite equal to any previously seen. The weather, though threatening in the morning, was really 'fine. The meet was on what is termed the lower ground. All the trials, of which there were 39, were disposed of by 4 30. To-day the meet was on the higher field, which is in magnificent order, having been turned over since last season and grass got from it, which gives it the appearance of a large bowling green. The attendauce was tnuch larger than on the opening day, and the weather was fine, though the wind blew almost a gale the whole time, thus causing the sport to be not so good as expected, as it interfered with the running of the hares, a large proportion being killed before they could make their escape. There were, however, some splendid trials, and the day's proceedings passed off well, being brought to a close soon after 4-30. Return ap- pended

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.,
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 1883.,

FILTHY Horsss AT Yi'aitstuvoTos.—John Cross, Rome and Crown-yard, was summoned to Warrington Police Court, on Monday, for allowing two of his houses in Ship- yard to be in an unsanitary state.—Mr. R. Norman, nuisance inspector, deposed to the spouts, roofs, and drains of the houses being defective, and to the walls and ceilings being in a filthy state. He said that the defendant bad had a notice served upon him respecting the houses, but they were still in the same condition.—The Mayor said that such places as these often proved hotbeds of fever. The defendant would have to pay the costs, and if at the end of 14 days the work was not done a fine of ss. per day would be imposed. A CONFIRICED THIRF.—At Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Michael Welch, a young man, of no fixed residence, but who has been lodging in Warrington about a week, was charged on remand with offering for pawn a pair of trousers and other articles at the shop of Mr. Valentine Morton, Bridge-foot, and refusing to give a satisfactory account of .how he came by thsm.—On Thursday week the prisoner went to Mr. Morton's shop and offered the articles for pawn, but as he gave no satisfactory account of bow he came by then the manager, Mr. Kerr, sent for a policeman. On being taken into custody the prisoner made a number of conflicting statements, some of which had been proved to be absolutely false. The Chief Constable had received a letter from the Stockport police authorities stating that the prisoner had been convicted of felony there and sentenced to three months' imprisonment, and that he was a confirmed thief.—The prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of £1 and costs, or go to prison for a month. _ :- PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR, RUNCOUN- MR JOHN SIMPSON ON ReILIGIOUS LIBERTY. To defray the cost of a heating app tratue which was xed in the Greenway-read Primitive Methodist Chapel in December last, and to assist the funds of the Runcorn cir- cuit of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, a bazaar was opened in Itancorn Public Hall on Tuesday morning. The committee, of which Mr. John Fleet is the honorary secre- tary, hoped to realise about £2OO by the sale of the thou- sand and cne articles of the bazaar, and the receipts at the varleas excellent entertaiuments provided. Eighty pounds will be required to clear off the debt for the heating appara- tus, and the rest will be added to the circuit fund, upon which there is now a heavier call in consequence of an ad- ditional married minister having been appointed to the dis- trict. Just previous to the death of Mr. Elijah Billingsley, which cast such a gloam upon the congregation of Green• way-road Cirapel, that gentleman Reis engaged in preparing for the production of some grand musical entertainment with the object of raising the money required. Other means had to he adopted, and when the first shocit of grief was passed it was decided that a bazaar would be the most zuitable and probably the most successful means of obtaining the desired object. With that willingness with which they enter into every good cause, the ladies at once commenced to prepare for the greed event, and the result on Tuesday was a num- ber of stalls well stocked with a 'variety of articles for house- wifery use, and the adornment of the parlour and the person. Handy little cabinets found a place amid charming cushions and cunnicgly-worked antimacassars in lace and woel, while fire screens • and hand fans, Shet- land shawls and shawls of every :description, crockery and tinware, gipsy tables and buffets, mirrors and drawings, dohs and dolls' beds were mixed together in attractive con- fusion. The stalls were as follows :—(No. 1), Mis. Pick- well, Mrs. Faulkner, Mrs. Miles, Miss Miles, Mi 33 Pickwell, Wise Faulkner ; (2), Mrs. Booth, Mrs. Fleet, Mrs. Patin, Miss Hoxworth. Shingler, Ahab Sayle, Janes Stubbe, and John Fleet. he Rev. Geo Hack having offered up prayer, the Rev. J. latcawaar. introduced Mr. Steirsow to open the bazaar. In one respect, he seid, it gave him great pleasure to take the -part that he was doing that morning—(hear, hear)—but in other respects he • alw rys tell that he would rather occupy any place than that one. He had often thonght that although one had a feeling of helping in a good c tuse when opening a bazaar, yet it was a position that he should always wish to avoid if it were possible to do so. When he sailif it were possible, he meant if he really felt he was justified in declining the post; but, unfortunately, whenever he had been asked to tahe the position he did that morning, he had generally felt he could not fincl in his heart to do so. (Hear, hear.) The reasons that had been given why he should consent had seemed to outweigh all reasons which he could bring for- . ward against it. (Hear, hear.) Ard so be had had to does he was asked. Some years ago he engaged to open a bazaar for their friends in Greenway-road and Regent-st., but just when the day arrived, or the day before, he was called away through the death of a near relative, and could not take the position that he had promised to take. Partly ore that • account he felt he could not refuse Mr. Pickwell and Mr. Broadhurst when they came and asked him to take that p.wition that day. Bazaars in Runcoru were generally got up for some good purpose—some good cause—and he sup- posed it was found that they were generally tolerably stic- ceseful, or they would not have so many of them in the town and neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) Certainly the object for which they wished to raise money in connection with this bazaar was, he thought, a very good one, which most benefit all of them, and in which they could all enter very feelingly. With regard to the heating apparatus at the chapel, he was sure they would all admit that it was very desirable to have a place of worship comfortably warmed. (Hear, hear.) One day a man went to him and said he had come about the heating apparatus which was out of order. " he replied, "I don't see what I have to do with it, and if a man's eating apparatus is out of orderal think the best thing for him to do is to go to the dentist." (Laughter.) Bnt the heating apparatus in a chapel was a very different affair, and he thought they could all sympathise with their friends, and wished to help them in carrying out a proper method of warming the place where they met sabbeth alter Sabbath and dry after day to worship God. (Hear, hear.) The other obnct which was named in connection with the bazaar was the circuit fund, the uses for which Mr. Simpson explained, aud went on to ask how wls it raised? It was raised from various places in the circuit by quarterly col- lections, but as they might quite suppose when the money had to come, to a very great extent, from those who, however, they might wish to do so, had not got it in their power to give very largely—they might fancy that sometimes when those who bad the management of the financial matters rant quarter after quarter, they found unfortunately a balance on the wrong side of the book. It was So in the present case. They could not go on without a good circuit fund, and as the congregations in the different parts of the circuit were not able to raise the full amount required quarter after quarter, they called upon their friends to help them, and he thought it was a very proper thing to do. In connection with the circuit in which Mr. Pickwell and Mr. Miles were stationed he understood they had recently taken a second married minister. That entailed considerable addition to the expense that they had had to meet hitherto, and so they came and asked the public to help to raise a little fund to tide them over the present, hop- ing that after a while things would greatly improve, and they would find themselves in a very different position. He felt that it was a very cheering thing in going up and down the country to ,see such a large number of places of worships, (Hear, hear.) He often felt very glad that they did not belong to the same denomination of Christians, (Hear, hear.) Some people seemed to think that if they were all joined together in one crowded body that they would be very much better. He did not think that was so, because if there were 20 or 30 people met together they would very soon find, not only w;th regard to politics, but with regard to many points in connection with religious matters, that personal opinions differed very much, avid he thought it was a very good arrangement that different persons whose views to a great extent accorded with each other's, should be able to meet together and have ministers of their own trying to do all the good they could in their own way. That was a prin- ciple which seemed to him acknowledgedin this country ae a matter of course. They did hear more or less about some kind of persecution even in England. They heard daily about the persecution which the Salvation Army had had to coneend with in various places. He thought it was a very sad thing that any body of Christians, whether he agreed with them or not, should in this enlightened coun- try be persecuted. (Hear, hear.) Why should not any number of Christians be allowed to worship' God and try to do good in their own way without being persecuted. In a country where the laws were made by the people them- selves, they might expect that there would be full religious liberty. And yet if they read the accounts of what was ping on in Switzerland, where the Government was a re- public elected by the people, the people themselves making the laws, they actually found that it was contrary to law to worship God and to try to do , good according to the dictates of conscience. (Hear, hear.) That seemed to him an extraordinary state of things. Of course they knew that in this country the isuorant and un- educated mob of people had very often wrestled with those,' who were trying to do good. But when persecution had taken place in England according to law, it was a different thing to Switzerland. The laws of this country were not made, as was generally supposed, by the people themselves, but by some few, who were not always the immediate repre- sentatives of the people. And yet we had according to the law perfect liberty of conscience; not toleration. We were not tolerated. (Hear, hear.) How thankful we ought to be for such a boon when we looked. at such a country as Switzerland, where they might expect to find perfect liberty of conscience! They ought to do each one in their Own sphere everything they possibly could to promote good and kindly feeling amongst the different religious bodies, and he thought everyone would admit that each one of them in the position in which God had placed them ought to do everything they possibly could for the good of those around them. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in -declaring this bazaar open. (Applause.) The Rev. E. Wiaroeits said he felt that Mr. Simpson was • worthy of their very best thanks for his services that day. Mr. Simpson felt that too, and because he felt that be was always ready to contribute to the suppert Of every good institution in the town and neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) There were many people who professed liberal views, who were not liberal when asked for help. They were liberal eentirnentally but not practically. HARVESTING OPERATIONS AROUND WARRINGTON.

A correspondent writing on Wednesday says :—I have to- day had a short run through a portion of Lancashire and Cheshire, and was rather astenished to find that there is so much grain and clover out. Going from Manchester to Warrington, I found a field or two of grain out at Stretford. At Fliston I also came upon wheat and clover ; and touching the south point of Chat Moss' new Cadishead, there are some acres of grain still out. AftePcrossing the Glaz 3 the quantity of grain which is oat on the north aide of the line is rather considerable ; it will take some days to clear it. On the western side of Rixton Moss there is a still greater pro- portion of grain out, not half the crop being carte'!, and there are several fields of wheat to cut. There is grain more or less out all the way to Warrington. The quantity of clover hay which is down and in various stages of making is very - I large. This must suffer by the weight of rain, for in places ' which are not well drained the water stands in patches upon the land. Unless the weathertakes up soon a great portion of this, the bulk of the second crop of clover, will not be worth much. Turnips and mangels keeptheir color well; and potatoes which have decayed naturally are a good colour in the haulm. On the south side of the Mersey, near Warrington, there are still several crops of clover hay unhoused ; and between Warrington and Thelwall there is much grain in the fields. Ploughing and potato digging are going on briskly. From Lymmt to Heatley there are a number of fields of clover and grain unhoused, and looking up th e Bollin there is much need of fine weather before the crops that are down there can be carted away in good condition. From Dunham Massey eastward to Broadheath there is a great amount of grain ta be housed, and some fields are only partly reaped. There is a great weight of clover down here for a few miles and it itlying on the land in every stage of the process of 'taking, but mostly in big cock. Some of these crops are heavy. It will take 'about a fortnight's good weather to see the crops cleared in this neighbourhood. Green crops are looking very well,. and petato tops ap- pear to be quite free from disease. There is na great weight of grass.
IA MM.

SALE OF PROPERTY AT LYMBL,—A goodly number of• persons gathered in the Plough Inn, Lymrn, on Wednesday afternoon, when Mr. Thos. Sutton, of Warrington, brought under the hammer eleven lots of property on the estate of the late Mr. Forrest. The competition for the various pro- perties was very slow, and the auctioneer expressed his sur— prise that there was not much more bidding, as the property was in choice lots, and the vendars were willing to sell at very Tow prices Only one or twe of the lots were disposed of. The solicitors for the sale were Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley. . _

ST. HELENS JURY Lrsrs.—Ast the St. jieiens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, the assistant overseers of the following townships presented the lids of persons qualified to serve on juries, viz.: Eccleston, Windle, Parr, Sutton, Rainford and Bold. The lists were sanctioned after the erasure of the names of a few persons who wereeaither dead or exempt from the duties of jurors owing to their being over sixty years of age. • MARRIAGE OF Ma. JOHN Haves—The marriage of Mr. John Hayes, to Miss Harriet Stanfield, which took niece at the Earlestown Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, on Tuesday, was attended by a very large number of interested persons. Mr. Hayes was formerly mining engineer, under the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and resided in Earlestown. He was well known and much respected in local musical circles, and on the recant severance of his connection with the Earlestown Musical Society (of which he was the con- ductor), the members presented him with a tangible token of their esteem. He at present, follows his profession at Maryport, Cumberland. The nuptial ceremony was per- formed by the bride's brother, the Rev. J. C. Stanfield, of Bristol, assisted by the Rev. J. M. Fairbourne, of Earles- town. The happy couple left the sacred edifice amid the well-wishes and congratulations of many friends. GOOD TEMFLARS' MRETING AT EARLESTOWN.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Tern- plars held their weekly meeting in the lodge-room, Bridge- street, on Monday evening. There was a good attendance, and Bro. Henry Warburton, W.C.T., occupied the chair. Three new members were initiated, and several other candi- dates nominated. Arrangements were made for a return visit of a number of the members to the Ashton lodge next week, and a committee was appointed to draw up the pro- gramme. According to the quarterly programme the night was set apart for "Bits, chips, and clips," and a goodly numb,r of the members read interesting and amusing; !eCt.OiS called from various sources. Bro. John Warbur- ton gave one or two LancaAire dialtct readings; Bros. W. illiams and A. Allison gave recitations, and a song was given.hy Bro. Bassett. A very pleasant evening was spent.

A COW SHOCIONOCY MTITILATED AT LYMM: A LAD IN CUSTODY.—A valuable cow belanging to Mr. D. Foster, farmer, of Lymm, had such serious injuries inflicted upon it on Thursday afternoon that yesterday morning Mr. Foster was compelled ta have it slaughtered. It seems that about five o'clock on Thursday afternoon Joseph Kelley, a lad about 16 years of age, who has lately been employed by Mr. Foster as farm servant, told 11 at the farm that while he was driving the cows home. from the field one had broken its leg and was lying in the road. Mr. Foster, who had ben away from home in the afternoon, went to look at the anim tl about 10 o'clock in the evening, and found one of its legs dreadfully mutilated, as though by s)tne sharp instrument. The limb was nearly severed. He al- lowed it to remain where it was tintil yesterday morning, when he found it necessary to have it slaughtered. The lad K,lley subsequently, on being interrogated, tmae sevcra, conflicting statements as to how the cow came by its injuries. During the aftesnoon he had been engaged " dabbing " hedges with a billhook, and one of his statements was to the effect that when he was driving the cows home he swung the billhook round and it accidentally slipped out of his hand, inflicting the injuries on the cow. The lad was taken into custody yesterday afternoon.

A WARNING TO WORIMEN.—John Birmingham and John Haggerty, two workmen, were each summoned before the S. Helens Polica Court, on Friday, et the instance of their employer, Mr. C. J. Bishop, for neglecting their work. It was stated that the defendants absented them- selves from work on those days without notice, whereby Mr. Bishop had sustained a loss of £1 in respect of each. They were ordered to pay the amount of loss sustained.
The abolition of quarantine for mail or Australian stearnass

arriving at Cyprus is officially announced. The Dublin correspondent of tha Daily News mentions a rumour that Mr. Parnell has been murdered by an Oranoe- man, and says it seems certain that he has been wounded. No particulars are to hand. Patrick O'Donnell was committed yesterday afternoon for trial on the charge of murdering James Carey, by Mr. Flowers, at Bow-street. Mr. Poland prosecuted, and Mr. Sullivan again appeared for the prisoner. It is stated this evening that an agreement has been _ _ _
arrived at between the Liberal and Conservative parties at Limerick to coalesce against Mr. Macmahon, the Parnellite candidate, Mr. Spaight (Conservative) receiving the united vote.

TILE CABRA SHOOTING CASE.-At an inquest on the body of Mr. Mooney, the victim of the Cabra Shooting case, held on Thursday, in Dublin, a verdict of death from gun- shot wounds received on September 16, was returned. The prisoners have been returned for trial for manslaughter.

CAPTURE OF TEE ABSCONDING BARIIISTER'S CLEM:C— R turns out that Danks, the defaulting barrister's clerk, was not apprehended at Worcester, as had been reported.. lie was, however, traced to Worcester, where he defraud:A

a public-house keeper, and was later on tracted to Bromq-, grlve, where he was arrested by a Birmingham deteaive late on 1 hursday night. The foundation stones of the ao;th-eastern pi.r of Peter- borough Cathedral were laid yesterday, on solid rock 12 feet below the surface. Doubts are entertained as to the _

stability of the western piers since the discovou that the old foundations are not laid on rock • and test holes have been bored, the result of which will b repeaod to the re- storation committee next week. MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT PRESTON.—About nine o'clock on Thursday evening a woman named Elir,a Alston, aged 45, wife of a labourer, was found dead, in her house, Lower Pitt-street, Prestan, in a large pool of blood. She had received a sum of money the day before and had gone abou: drinking' with a man, name unknown. The police appre- hended the man, who denies all knowledge of the affair. SHOCKING FATALITY IN CHESHIRE.—Mr. H. Churton, coroner for West Cheshite, held an inquest at Wettenhall, yesterday, on the body of Mary Hough, aged forty-three years. The deceased, after dressing on Wednesday morn- ing, went to the rain-water tub to draw water. Her presence being missed, her husband went to look for her and found her immersed, head downward, in the water-but. Death resulted from suffocation. The verdict was in accordance wl'ala these facts. A RAILWAY CARRIAGE ON FlRE.—While the up mall ; train was proceeding to Dublin from Sligo on Thareclay night a first-class carriage containing two gentlemen was discovered to be on fire. The flames broke out from the window-slide& of the door, which Was quickly one mass of fire. Fortianatelv before the filmes spread to the interior of the compartment the train pulled up at Elgeworth, and the tire was extinguished. thus preventing what might have been a similar c itastrophe to the recent one in England. 'I HE OPPOSITION TO THE PARNELLITE CAIIPAIGN.—The Orange,nen wh had assembled in Dungannon in opposition to the Parnellite campaign which is being conducted bys Messrs. O'Connor and small, M.P.'s, continued on Thursday to hold the square, of which they took possession on Wed- nesday night. There were at least 5,000 Orangemen present at the demonstratlon, which pissed off without any serious breach of the peace. The authorities had made sufficient preparations. A detachment of the Border regiment, 300 police, and about 50 men of the 16th Lancers had been drafted into the town. Earl Spencer, who arrived on Wednesday at Downhill, Coleraine, the seat of Sir • Henry Bruce, Bart., M.P., on Thursday visited and inspected the navigation works now in course of construction at the mouth of the Bann. His excellency was presented with several addresses. The Lord- Lieutenant has received a threatening letter in connection with the opening of the electric tramway at Portrush, the construction of which was strongly opposed by residents in the district. A reward has been offered for the detection of the writer of the letter. MORE EXTRAORDINARY FRAUDS IN BIRMINGHAIL—TWO more extraordinary frauds came to light in Birmingham yesterday morning. It is reported that the clerk of a well- known firm in the town has absconded with £2,000 or £3,000, and that two other Birmingham banks have been de- frauded to a considerable extent by a Birmingham trades- man named Albert Westley, owning property in Birming- ham and other parts of the country. Westley was charged with four different forgeries on the Birmingham and Mid- land Bank, and the Worcester City and County Bank. It was stated that he had obtained sums of money from the banks by means of bills of exchange with forged accept- ances. The prisoner, who shed tears in the dock, was re- manded. _

A BIGAMOUS CLERGYMAN.—Yesterday morning, at the Birmingham Police Court, Thomas Morris Hughes, 43, clerk in holy orders, Be!grave Square, Gravelly Hill, Bir- mingham, was charged with committing bigamy by irter- marrying with Mary Ann Morgan, 54, Wycliffe-road. Small Heath, his wife, Charlotte Hughes, nee Harmer. being alive. The pr;soner is a man of medium height, fair com- plexion, and of somewhat dissipated appearance. He was attired in ordinary clerical dress. Hughes pleaded guilty to the charge and the conduct of the case was a good deal simplitied;but the evidence adduced revealed an extraor- dinary career of duplicity, licentiousness, and crime. The court was crowded. The prisoner, who was undefended, did not appear to be much affected by the position which he occupied, but stood up, arms folded, mil gazed un- concernedly around the curt.—Richard Clarke, coroner for Shrewsbury, deposed to the prisoner being married to his wife on the 16th November, 1860, at the Registry Office, Elwards sad she wa3 present at the second mo on the 15:h February, two and a half years ago, at Birm...ham. His second %:fe was living .:: with her mother. She waO now a lunatic, having been driven mad by Lio prisoner's mduct.—A detective produced the two marriage cartijf'ates, and stated that he appreheocl.il the prisoner at Aston on the ..Btlj inst., where ha was living with the cook from a clergyman's house at Worcester, for whom he hatbeen officiating. When aa..'''sted the prisoner said, "It is qite trus."—He now pleaded gu and wastrt committed for trial at tha assizis, saying th it tie ti.;.l been grossly misrepresented by the local press. Bail was not ap • plied for.
ORANGE ATTACK ON T. P. O'CONNOR.
REPORTED SHOOTING OF MR. PARNELL.

A Leeds correspondent, telegraphing at noon yesterday, says :—Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr., has justarrived here from the Dungannon demonstration. , He was escorted to the station there by the military and armed constabulary. Orange mobs threatened to sraash into his train at every station where he stopped, and with difficulty we: e prevented striking him with their shillelaghs. As he was changing carriages at Portadown the mob rushed upon him, and he was only rescued from personal violence by the interposition of two Orange clergymen. The Press Association's Dublin correspondent, telegraph- ing yesterday, says :—No confirmation has yet reached Dublin of the rumour to the effect that Mr. Parnell h es been shot at. The bon. gentlemen has for the past eight days been in London, and was to leave there yesterday to attend the convention of the National League, which is to be held at Leeds to-day, and in which town he is announced to deliver a lecture to-night.
SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST WORK- MEN.

Arthur Warburton, a respectable-looking, middle-aged man, residing at Nicholson-street, and Thomas Pemberten, of Fountain-street, Latchford, were charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with stealing three cart beds and a quantity of irenwork, valued at about £2, the property of Mr. John Lunt, Latchford.—Mr. Percy Davies, who ap- peared for the prosecution stated that the prisoners had been in the employ of Mr:Lunt for some time, Pemberton working as a carter and Warburton as a blacksmith. During that period they had in Mr. Lunt's time been working for their own gain, and appropriating to their own use articles which belonged to Mr. Lunt. As there were three other men who ought also to be in the dock he would, after pro- (keine' sufficient evidence, ask for a remand for eight days. —John Norris, a lad, said he bad been apprenticed to Mr. Lunt about four months. About ',ay° months since three eart beds, which ware lying in Mr. Lunt's yard, were put into Pemberton's cart by the prisone 3, and conveyed to the King's Head, Towns-end. Subeequently. at night, Warbur- ton, Thomas Rimmer, and Thomas Williams, broker, had been engaged making a cart on the latter's premises, and the material used belonged to Mr. Lunt The ironwork had been made at Mr. Lunt's; and then carried away in dinner baskets and. bags, witness carrying some of the iron away, and Warburton carrying other iron. During the time the men had been working on the cart at Williams's, witness had held the candle for them. The men had told him not to tell what was being done, offering to give him something if he would keep it a sec-et. He believed that Pemberton got a shilling and a drink ;or conveying the cart beds to the King's Head, but he did not think he knew that they were being stolen.—Pemberton was then dis- charged, there being no evidence against him—The Chief- Constable asked for a warrant fOr the apprehension of Wil- liams, the broker, whom he described as an "old scholar," saying that he refused to produce the cart when asked to do so by Inspector Singleton. The evidence against him ap- peared to be very damning, as he must have known that the things were stolen.—The case was then remanded till Mon- day, a warrant being granted for the apprehension of Wil- liams, who was in court during the hearing of the charge. On Tuesday, Williams was brought before .Major Cart- wright, on warrant, charged with having, on the Bth August, fraudulently received from Arthur Warburton and Thomas Rimmer a cart-bed and a quantity of ironwork, value 303, knowing them to have been stolen.—The Magis- trates' Clerk said that a man named Arthur Warburton had been remanded an a charge of steal•ing the ironwork belong- ing to the cart, and there was a warrant out against another person.—Prisoner said he knew nothing about the theft. He paid £l2 for the cart, of which about £6 went for timber bought at Messrs. Naylor?s, and £5 for springs and ironworl —Mr. Percy Davies: But you must have known about the ironwork.—Prisoner : It is not for ma to know where he got the iron from. I arranged with the men to make me a email cart for carrying furniture.—Prisoner was remanded until Monday next and admitted to bail, himself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO each. .

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELIINS.—A miner named Thomas Thompson, who lived in higher Parr-street, St. Helens, was killed in the Sherdley Colliery, on Thurs- day. Deceased was engaged removing some stuff which had fallen prior to propping up a defective part of the roof, when another fall took place immediately over him, and he was crushed to death.

LIQUIDATIONS BY ARRANGEMENT.—(FrOM Friday night's Gazette.)—W. Butterton, Warrington, boot and shoe maker; A. H. Hitchin, Over, otherwise Winsford, furniture broker; (From Tuesday's Gazette) C. Pierson, Dickinson-street, Man- chester, surveyor, auctioneer, and estate agent, residing at Knutsford, and curving on there the business of a farmer; J. Gore, Wigan, innkeeper; S. Beaton, Westfield-street, St. Helens, printer. THE NATION/FL REFORM Uettoer.—The Executive Com- mittee of the National Reform Union are preparing for the work of the coming winter. The objects of the Union are —(1) The, dissemination of political knowledge and the furtherance of Liberal organisation, especially in the county constituencies; (2) the promotion and agitation of any lead- jut question which an important section of the party may from time to time place before the nation, and in regard to which it may be thought desirable to move and instruct public opinion." The attainment of the first of these objects is effected by means of lectures and publications. As lec- turers the Union has upon its list upwards of BO gentlemen, whose services are at the disposal, during the winter season, of affiliated and subscribing branches, which at the present time number 297. The Union has recently added several new publications to its list, including Mr, Gladstote's speech on the Parliamentary oath.

True, he could not detect any particular preference, but the thought brought back all his own previous misgivings about her, and about the scene in which she was so enjoy- ably engaged. He went io her; and the bthers, some knowing him, and the remainder seeing he was a friend of Miss Vandeleur's, gradually edged away, and left them the opportunity of a brief conversation. "You are getting on I sae," was the first comment. "And strange to say wit'amit the valuable help I was promised !" was the reply. • "Then you have, in addition to your seecee, the pl sa- surable conscionsueee of being able to say, Alone I did it I congratulate you." She saw he was angry, and found no difficulty in dis- covering the cause. But before she could decide whether her next move should be eonciliatory or the reverse, he turned the scale by saying, in a low voice, "I see one coming who can pay, and must be made to pay, and who will no doubt be very content to pay, under the circumstance. Come down heavily upon him!" "Who is that ?" "Lord Harlaxton! Good bye; lam tired, anl shall go home. Can Ido anything for you by the way ?" "Yes; take the Countess with you. She, too, is very tired, though she has been most amiable." Stephen looked at her for a single moment. His Owe go- ing, he thought, might have suggested to her something likely to make him change his purpose. But her getting rid of the Countess Left him no alternative but to suppose she was glad to be left by herself, free from the eyes of her friends, ready as he imagined to join the "saturnalia of licence" before spoken of. He obeyed her with careful reserve; and with a few words to his mother to ewer the abruptness of his depar- ture, they went away; and Miss Vandeleur—stern, defiant —saw them go, and turned with fresh stniles to greet the new corner, Leed Harlaxton. But instead of at once following Stephen's advice—to come down heavily upon him, advice spoiled, perhaps, by the circumstances under which it was given, she merely welcomed him in the usual manner, but rather more cor- dially ; and entered upon familiar conversation, narrating in her liveliest manner such incidents of her own experience as she chose to dwell en, bat principally on those that bad occurred around her at other stalls; and in doing which her two pretty neighbours bore a very large share for Miss Vandeleur, like most of us, could keenly detect, and rnerei- lessly expose, those faults in others of which she was her- self guilty. Lord Harlaxton was delighted to find her so amnsing, and in such high spirits, while also noticing her avoidance of any pecuniary appeal to him on behalf of the Charity, which seemed to him a trait of peculiar delicacy and refi le- meat. So he said, when a pause occurred, "Now to business; I know I am a victim, but quite re- signed. So tell me, what you expect in return far one of those charming flowers I am to consider my own, and which really appear to surpass their originals!" "Only a blank cheque!" said Miss Vandeleur, with a laugh. The Earl laughed too but with some misgivings. Did she really mean what at:a said? And if he gave the cheque, would she till it up with ten, fifteen, or twenty guineas, or even more? Well, he would trust her. She would not do anything outrageous. But a lucky alternative occurred to him. "I don't usually, you know, carry my cheque book about with me, but as I have a little loose cash —" " Oh, but f can readily aceomodate you. Hare are writing materials. Step inside. There is a chair and a table. I anOejot written cheques even from people I don't irilOW. Can (then object to take one from Lord Harlax. ion?" He was caught and knew it; and repented his over-hasty behaviour and too flattering estimate of Miss Vendeleur's reticence in business matters. So he allowed her to lead him like a lamb to the slaughter, wrote out his blank cheque, and handed it to her, which she filled up, and then handed to him to look at, saying, "Mind, you can easily write another, if you think I have not been sufficiently mindful of your lordship's generosity of heart, or the very great claims of the Charity to your particular favour." "One hundred guineas!" said the Earl aloud. Then concealing his annoyance he merely said, "Miss Vande- leur does things so grandly it is an honour to be her asso- siate !" Avoiding to spoil the effect of that by any less im- portant matter, he speedily departed. And she was left alone. With a deep sigh, she sat down on the chair he had vacated, and seemed for a few moments absorbed in painful thoughts; during which all the triumphs of the day, all the enjoyments of the occasion died out, and left behind a sense of inexplicable weariness, and disgust with herself, her customers, and the whole world. But she was roused by the sight of an Illustrious _Personage coming her way, and presently stopping before her. Assuming a becoming attitude, she waited for him to speak first. I'm told Miss Vandeleur dispenses the most charming things in the Fair, but that she asks unconscionable prices, which it must be obvious I can't afford ! Miss Vendeleur laughed. "Besides, the ladies have stripped me bare before I could get here, or knew the treasures that were yet to tempt me. But come, what is the price of this 7" And the speaker took up the first vase of fbwers that lay nearest to his hand. "Twenty guineas only." "Twenty guineas! Be candid_ Did it really cast two? Did it cost one ?" "Supposing," began Miss Vandeleur, "that to be the case, does not your price is adapted to the occasion? The one marks the Charity's sense of the exalted honour done to it by the very exaltation of the price; the other its belief in the pleasure your little it cost the Charity !" The Illustrious Flowage laughed heartily, as he ob- served, " Well, if I am to be once more bamboozled into buying what I don't w.lnt, and therefore must pay heavily for as a matter of course, let me have at least something worthy to be kept in remembrance of so charming, and, in every sense, winning a young lady !" Miss'Vandeleur blushed a little at the compliment, and draw from under a cover a very beautiful and really valuable vase, filled with an assemblage of flowers that made the beauty of the vase more impressive, from their wondrous perfection of form, their mingling of delicate colours, and their artistic truth te their originals. "The vase your -- —can judge of more truly than myself." "I know it and its origin. English, but of the finest Wedgwood and Fiaxman ware. And as to the flowers —" "They are mine." " Your own handiwork ?" " Entirely." "I am conquered! Be merciful! Say fifty guineas !" "I am much too loyal a subject. One hundred is the least • but I really thought—" "Ak, that'll do. Keep it for me ;I'll send you a chequer Let us shake hands in token our strife ends happily." And again Miss Vandeleur was left alone; and to the thoughts and feelings that had before affected her, and which made all else be quickly forgot. The place was now full, the air hot and stifling, and she wished heartily the day would end, and she get home. But she braced herself for fresh exertion as she saw some lady acquaintances coming towards her; when to their astonishment and alarm they saw her hastily put out her hands against the stall, as if to keep her from falling, then totter back to the chair, and there drop, and lose for a time in unconsciousness all sense of the things that troubled her. (To be continued.)

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers, I', Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Sept. 27th):- Notwithstanding the cheapness of money no marked effect was visible on values generally until to-day, when the hank rate was reduced to 3 per cent., on which some firmness ',sisal- fested itself, yet the changes in p; ices of the leading stocks do not show any decided movement. No doubt the approach and the arrangement of the account which terminates to-day has lied a restricting influenee on new business, and business being curtailed, doubtless values have lacked me element of buoyancy. Foreign s'ocks are a little irregular, but with a favourable numerical balance in alterations. One or two stocks which up to yesterday were slighlv lower, have had their record reversed, and exhibit a fractional advance on the week. Egyptians: Uelfied unchanged; preference 4 higher, and Detre 4iower. Quotations compared with Thurs- day last are in no instance more than 4 or 1 changed either way. Mexiean Railway Sto,ks have retrain come in for a ham- msrine, prices being forced as low as 75 to 734; from this, however, they have rallied quickly to-day to 774 784, or a fall (on balance) of 74 since Thursday last. Consensus of opinion from reports e of different papers appears to point to higher values being looked for. The vaeous descriptions of misce laneous shares have produced a very small aggregate of transactions, and the general balance of changes in quotations is adverse. Coax., IRON, &C., AND MINING.-Hardly any transactions reported till yesterday and to-day, when a few lots of Bole- kows. Ebbw Vales, and Palmer's Shipbuilding A changed hands. Prices again show an adverse majority of changes. Higher-Palmer's A 14. Brown's 4 to 1, Cammell's 4. and Thera's Bu'phur and Copper 1-16.
